The one design choice we would point to: if a list is missing, stale, or below a minimum version number, the answer is never "clean." It is ONMEETBAAR, not measured. A tool that quietly treats "I could not check" the same as "I checked and it is fine" is worse than no tool at all, because it looks like a green light.

We are not claiming this is unique. OpenSanctions and a hosted tool called agentbroker both already sign results in the sanctions-screening space, and OpenSanctions covers far more data than we do. What we did not find elsewhere is a signed snapshot of the list itself, with a version floor that refuses a rolled-back list. That is a narrow claim, not a big one.

Tool two: checking a payment receipt

agent-receipt-verify checks x402/EIP-712 payment receipts: did an agent actually pay what it claims to have paid, on the rails it claims to have used. Same rule applies: a receipt that does not fully check out is reported as such, not rounded up to "looks fine."

The part that might be useful even without our code

We trust both tools today because we tested them against our own planted mistakes, over and over. We plant deliberate bugs in the code (a missing check, a flipped comparison, a dropped field) and require every single one to make a test fail. Al-Muqarin currently catches 548 out of 548 planted faults this way.

That discipline is free to copy, with or without our tools. If you are building anything that outputs "verified" or "trusted," try deleting one check at a time and see if your test suite actually notices.

Where we are honestly stuck

Neither tool solves agent trust. Al-Muqarin has zero paying users right now; we are treating that as the real test, not the code. A separate prototype of ours, a fail-closed checker for independently-verified impact claims (did an agent's donation actually do what it claimed), has a gap we have not closed: the "who verified this" field is still free text. Nothing stops someone from writing a controller description that is not obviously "us" and getting a false pass. We know this, we have a test that proves it, and we have not fixed it yet.

If any of this overlaps with what you are building on top of ERC-8004 or x402, we would genuinely like to hear where it breaks.

More from us: github.com/holistis and tokenizen.nl.

title: 7 Top Software Factory Platforms for Engineering Teams for 2027
description:
AI is becoming part of more engineering activities than code completion. Teams can assign agents to investigate issues, implement changes, review code, expand tests, and maintain documentation. The organizational challenge is making those activities work together rather than creating another collection of disconnected tools.

A software factory provides a repeatable operating model for that work. It connects requirements, execution, verification, and delivery, with controls over what agents can access and when people need to intervene.

For engineering teams planning for 2027, the following seven platforms represent different approaches to that model, from coordinating agent teams across existing systems to integrating AI into development and delivery environments.

Key Takeaways

Software factory platforms differ in how much of the development lifecycle they coordinate and where they connect to an engineering team's existing processes.

  • Overcut brings agent creation, multi-agent orchestration, and execution governance together across an existing engineering toolchain.
  • Repeatable workflows matter as much as an individual agent's ability to generate code.
  • The category includes orchestration platforms, integrated DevSecOps systems, delivery infrastructure, and agentic development environments.
  • Shared context, controlled permissions, verification, and execution visibility are important foundations for enterprise use.
  • A useful assessment connects platform capabilities to the engineering processes an organization intends to automate.

7 Software Factory Platforms to Consider

These platforms address software factory operations at different levels. Overcut leads the list with an approach built around coordinating agents, connecting existing tools, and governing work across the development lifecycle.

1. Overcut

Overcut is an agentic software factory platform for engineering organizations that want to operate coordinated agent teams rather than manage isolated coding assistants. It provides a shared layer for building agents, connecting them to engineering systems, and organizing their work into governed workflows.

The platform supports agent configuration through models, MCP tools, prompts, memories, and skills. Teams can define specialized responsibilities and combine agents into workflows with shared context and explicit handoffs. This makes coordination part of the operating model instead of leaving engineers to transfer information manually between separate AI sessions.

Overcut connects to an organization's existing stack, including GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps, Jira, and CI pipelines. That breadth allows teams to develop automation around their repositories and delivery processes without making a single vendor ecosystem the organizing principle. Its model options also let organizations work with different providers or their own endpoints alongside coding agents they already use.

Governance is built into execution. Overcut describes permissioned, sandboxed, verified runs with approval gates and audit trails. SAML SSO and role-based access support organizational access controls, while shared agent libraries and workflow templates help establish consistent practices across engineering groups. These capabilities give teams a framework for increasing automation while retaining control over consequential actions.

The platform also includes run analytics, retrospectives, and self-improvement capabilities. Its dashboards track measures such as cost per task, agent efficiency, and developer time saved, giving engineering leaders visibility beyond whether a workflow simply finished. Deployment options include SaaS, private cloud, on-premises, and fully air-gapped environments.

Key features:

  • Agent configuration using models, MCP tools, prompts, memories, and skills.
  • Multi-agent workflows with shared context and coordinated handoffs.
  • Connections to repositories, issue trackers, CI pipelines, and observability tools.
  • Workflow triggers and human approval gates.
  • Sandboxed execution with permissions and verification.
  • Role-based access, SAML SSO, and execution audit trails.
  • Shared agent libraries, workflow templates, and retrospectives.
  • Run analytics and flexible deployment options.

Together, these capabilities position Overcut as a foundation for running an agent workforce across teams, with orchestration, toolchain connectivity, and operational controls in the same platform.

2. GitLab Duo Agent Platform

GitLab Duo Agent Platform integrates specialized agents with the repositories, issues, merge requests, security processes, and pipelines managed in GitLab. Its approach places agent activity within an established DevSecOps environment, where project information and development workflows can supply context.

Engineering teams can use purpose-built agents for planning, implementation, security analysis, and other tasks. They can also customize agents to reflect organizational conventions and combine them into flows that coordinate multiple steps.

The AI Catalog provides a central location for discovering and managing agents and flows. GitLab also describes controls over permitted agents, models, and execution boundaries, with actions tied to user identities and permissions. This connects automation to the governance structure already used for development work.

Key features:

  • Specialized agents and organization-specific customization.
  • Agentic flows for multi-step development activities.
  • Project context from GitLab's development environment.
  • AI Catalog for managing agents and flows.
  • Support for implementation, review, and security workflows.
  • Policy controls, human checkpoints, and execution traceability.

3. Harness

Harness addresses software factory operations through the systems that build, validate, secure, and deploy software. Its platform brings delivery automation together with AI agents, security testing, and governance across pipelines.

The delivery layer matters because faster code generation does not remove the need for dependable releases. Teams still need consistent build processes, required checks, controlled deployment decisions, and visibility into failures. Harness provides infrastructure for organizing those activities across applications and environments.

Its platform describes policy-as-code, role-based access, audit trails, and human approvals. It also supports different levels of agent autonomy, allowing teams to distinguish workflows that require explicit intervention from those permitted to execute within defined policies.

Key features:

  • Automated build and deployment workflows.
  • Agents supporting software delivery activities.
  • Security testing and software supply chain controls.
  • Policy-as-code and role-based permissions.
  • Approval gates and auditable execution decisions.
  • Cost management and engineering outcome visibility.

4. GitHub Copilot

GitHub Copilot extends AI assistance into repository-level engineering work. Alongside code explanation and interactive development help, it supports planning changes, implementing tasks in the background, and reviewing pull requests.

Because GitHub already holds issues, code, pull requests, and automated checks for many teams, Copilot can participate in several connected stages of a change. Engineers can investigate a repository, delegate implementation, and review proposed modifications through familiar collaboration processes.

GitHub also documents automations for recurring or event-driven repository tasks. Execution options differ in their repository scope and environment configuration, so the available workflow depends on the selected environment, subscription, and organizational policies.

Key features:

  • Repository-aware questions and code explanation.
  • Planning and implementation of delegated changes.
  • Pull request preparation and code review assistance.
  • Test and linter execution in development environments.
  • Scheduled and event-driven repository automations.
  • Organization policies and repository access controls.

5. Cursor

Cursor places agentic development within the tools engineers use to understand and modify software. It combines interactive coding assistance with agents that can plan implementation, work with repository context, and make code changes.

That approach supports a range of working styles. Developers can steer an implementation closely while examining the code, or delegate a larger task and inspect the resulting changes. Cursor's interfaces include the editor and terminal, with cloud agents supporting work that continues separately from a local session.

Within a software factory, these capabilities provide a development execution layer. Engineers can use agents for implementation and investigation while keeping code review and existing delivery processes connected to the resulting work.

Key features:

  • AI-assisted development in the editor and terminal.
  • Agent planning and code implementation.
  • Repository context for code exploration and changes.
  • Support for changes spanning multiple files.
  • Cloud agents for delegated development work.
  • Integration with pull request and collaboration workflows.

6. Devin

Devin is an autonomous software engineering platform centered on carrying out delegated tasks. Its workflow spans codebase investigation, planning, implementation, testing, and preparation of changes for review.

Instead of relying only on a developer accepting suggestions as they work, Devin provides an environment in which an agent can execute a defined assignment. Its product capabilities include virtual-machine execution, browser-based testing, and progress communication through connected collaboration tools.

This model applies to work such as bug investigation, maintenance changes, and test improvements when requirements and expected outcomes are clear. Devin also supports scheduled and trigger-based automation, connecting recurring engineering activities to signals from the surrounding toolchain.

Key features:

  • Delegated task planning and implementation.
  • Codebase investigation and architectural context.
  • Development execution in isolated virtual machines.
  • Code changes, test execution, and browser testing.
  • Human review of proposed changes.
  • Scheduled workflows and event-triggered automation.

7. Kiro

Kiro emphasizes the relationship between requirements and implementation. Its specification-driven approach captures intended behavior before code is written and uses that intent as a reference for subsequent verification.

Structured requirements and design work can reduce ambiguity when agents handle features involving multiple components or dependencies. Rather than treating a prompt as the only statement of the task, teams can maintain artifacts that explain what should be built and how the result should behave.

Kiro combines this approach with agents for planning, building, reviewing, and verifying engineering work. It supports local and cloud execution, as well as multi-step workflows and recurring agent activity. These capabilities connect specification work to implementation rather than leaving it as a separate documentation exercise.

Key features:

  • Specification-driven development and requirements analysis.
  • Structured planning before implementation.
  • Agent-assisted code changes and review.
  • Verification against intended behavior.
  • Local and cloud execution options.
  • Multi-step workflows and recurring automation.

How Engineering Teams Should Evaluate Software Factory Platforms

An organization's existing systems and desired level of autonomy shape what a software factory needs to provide. The central question is whether agents can participate reliably in established engineering processes, with enough context and control to produce changes people can verify.

Five operational requirements deserve particular attention:

  • Agent configuration: define specialized responsibilities, instructions, tools, and accessible context.
  • Workflow coordination: manage dependencies, handoffs, and recovery when execution does not proceed as expected.
  • Toolchain connectivity: preserve relevant context and permissions across repositories, work tracking, and CI/CD.
  • Execution governance: control access, isolate agent activity, require approvals, and retain audit records.
  • Outcome visibility: understand completion rates, failures, resource use, and the human effort associated with results.

A complete workflow offers more useful evidence than a standalone coding example. For instance, handling a recurring CI failure involves detection, investigation, a proposed fix, validation, and preparation of a pull request. Following that sequence reveals whether the platform can maintain context and produce a reviewable result across multiple systems.

FAQ

Software factory adoption raises practical questions about integration, coordination, security, and measurement.

Can software factory platforms connect to existing CI/CD systems?

Yes, many platforms are designed to work with established engineering infrastructure. The important distinction is what an integration actually enables, such as reading build results, triggering work, or proposing changes. Overcut, for example, connects agent workflows with existing repositories and CI pipelines. Teams should confirm the required actions and permission boundaries for their own environment.

How do multi-agent engineering workflows operate?

They divide a larger process among agents with distinct responsibilities and coordinate the resulting work. One agent might investigate a failure while another prepares a change or checks the output. The orchestration layer manages context and handoffs so that each step builds on the relevant results rather than starting an unrelated session.

Which security controls matter for an enterprise software factory?

Key controls include narrowly scoped access, isolated execution, protected credentials, approval requirements, and audit records. Deployment architecture and model data handling also need review. Overcut combines sandboxed runs, role-based access, approval gates, and audit trails, illustrating how agent execution can sit within organizational controls rather than operate outside them.

How should engineering leaders measure results?

Measure the path from a request to a validated change. Useful indicators include completion rates, elapsed time, failed runs, human interventions, and review or rework effort. Resource consumption also matters. Counting generated lines of code alone misses whether the result was correct, maintainable, and worth the engineering attention required to deliver it.

title: What 10,000 Trial Grants Taught Us About Free-Tier Identity Design
description:
This content reflects minia2a as of its publication date and is kept for the record. Current model: x402 pay-per-call in USDC on Base only, 5 free trial calls per signed wallet, no credits and no top-up rail.

What 10,000 Trial Grants Taught Us About Free-Tier Identity Design

2026-11-09 · data notes

A free tier is usually argued about as a number: how many calls, for how long, per what.
We have been running one on a pay-per-call x402 catalog for three months, and the ledger says
the number is not the interesting variable. Who the free tier counts decides
what it measures — and the same quota can produce two completely different curves depending on
whether the identity behind it is an IP address or a signed wallet.

Numbers below are read from our own trial tables on 2026-11-09. They are small, they are ours,
and they are reported as measured rather than as advice.

Three regimes, one counter

The trial ledger holds 10,497 global rows plus a legacy per-endpoint table that stopped
receiving writes on 2026-08-11. Across those tables the same idea — "a few free calls" — ran
under three different identity rules:

regime identity window identities at cap
per-endpoint IP or wallet, one counter per service to 2026-08-11 2,350 rows —
per-IP source address 08-13 → 09-01 4,634 3,247 with ≥5 calls (70.1%)
signed wallet EIP-191 signature over a per-call message 08-14 → 11-09 3,513 502 with ≥5 calls (14.3%)

The per-IP regime looks, at first glance, like a system with enormous demand: seven in ten
identities used five or more calls. It was not demand. Addresses are not people and not
agents; they are the cheapest thing to mint, and the counter was measuring a pool of traffic
with no per-caller continuity. Hitting a high count was the expected outcome, not a signal.

The signed-wallet regime reverses the distribution:

calls used by a signed identity identities share
0 424 12.1%
1 2,448 69.7%
2–4 139 4.0%
5 or more 502 14.3%

(Four of the last row predate the current five-call cap; the other 498 stopped exactly at five.)
Seven in ten signed identities use exactly one call and stop. Only one in seven exhausts the
allowance. Whatever a free tier is for, on this surface it is a sample, not an
evaluation budget: the caller is checking whether the shape of the answer is useful, and one
answer is usually enough to decide.

What that changes about the design

1. A free tier is an identity mechanism before it is a quota. The quota we
argued about was five calls. Under per-IP counting, those five calls were consumed by traffic
that had no reason to continue; under signed counting, most callers never reach them. If you are
choosing a number before you are choosing an identity, you are tuning a counter that is not
measuring what you think it is.

2. If most callers stop after one answer, the first answer carries the whole
product. A free call that returns a plausibly-shaped but incomplete result teaches the
caller nothing it can act on. On the other side, a first answer that is complete enough to
decide with turns the free call into the top of a funnel instead of a cost center. The trial
budget is not where the conversion decision happens; the first response is.

3. Breadth does not create trial demand. Our catalog lists 1,856 services;
the legacy per-endpoint table holds rows for 256 distinct service ids, and its top ten endpoints
account for 964 of 2,350 identity rows (41%). The long tail is not under-sampled because the
quota is too small — it is unvisited. Adding more endpoints to a catalog does not
manufacture the intent to try them.

4. Anti-abuse and conversion pull in different directions, and you should know which
one you are buying. Signing every trial costs the caller a keypair and a signature, and
it removes the cheapest abuse vector. It does not make anyone pay. We would make the same trade
again, but it should be described as what it is: an identity decision that changes the
measurement, not a pricing decision that changes revenue.

The rule we keep re-learning

When a free tier is measured through an identity that is cheap to mint, the number
you get describes the minting cost. Pick the identity first; the quota only means something
after that.

Concretely, the questions we would ask before setting a free-tier number on any machine-facing
API: can this identity be created for free in under a second? does it persist across
processes and days? can it be tied to the thing that will eventually pay? If the answers are
yes, yes, yes — then a per-identity budget is a real measurement. If the identity is an address,
a user agent, or a header the caller chooses, the budget is a limit on a traffic class, and it
will be full, and that fullness will mean nothing.

Data source: minia2a's own trial ledger, read 2026-11-09.
Global quota on this site is five trial calls per signed wallet, shared across the catalog.

Originally published at minia2a.uk.

title: How to Remove Hidden EXIF and Location Data from Your Photos for Free
description:
Have you ever thought about what your photos say about you—even before anyone looks at them?

Every time you take a picture with your smartphone or digital camera, it silently saves hidden information called EXIF data directly into the file. This includes:

📍 Your exact GPS coordinates (which can show exactly where you live, work, or travel).

📅 The exact date and time the photo was taken.

📷 Your camera and phone model, lens details, and capture settings.

When you share these photos online, on social media, or through messaging apps, you might be unintentionally sharing your private location and personal details with strangers.

title: Automating Support with AI: From a User's Question to a Response
description:
A user asks a question that support has answered before. An agent reads the message, clarifies the details, finds the right instructions, and explains what to do. A little later, another person asks something similar. For them, the problem is new. For the team, it is another trip down a familiar path.

This is an illustrative scene, but it captures exactly the routine we wanted to automate in our support operation. The goal was practical: answer standard user requests as automatically as possible and reduce support costs in the process. When a request already has a clear procedure, you want a person to step in where their knowledge or authority is actually needed.

That led to a service connecting language models to support work. Messages arrive from Telegram and Discord, while agents manage conversations in Chatwoot. But the most interesting part turned out to be what happens between the incoming question and the outgoing reply: what knowledge the model receives, what decision it returns, and what the service does with that decision.

At first, this path did not end with a message to the user at all. The assistant left suggestions in private notes visible to agents. We could see how it handled a request before giving it permission to respond on its own.

This is the first article in a series on automating support with AI. We will follow a single request from context assembly through an LLM call, result validation, and the choice of a next action. Later parts will look more closely at the knowledge base and conversation history, model tiers and processing costs, human handoff, and protocol failures. Chatwoot and the messaging platforms provide a concrete example; the core decisions also apply to other support systems.

The conversation already lives somewhere

Users write wherever it suits them. In our case, that means Telegram or Discord. Agents, meanwhile, need to see the request, its history, and its current state. Chatwoot handles that part.

The integrations deliver messages and connect them to the right conversation. Processing begins after that: is an automated response allowed right now, what information should go to the model, and what should happen to its result? In autonomous response mode, a Chatwoot agent-bot event triggers this processing. The trial mode starts from the channel integration and saves the result as a private note. These are alternative ways to trigger processing.

Looking inside an autonomous response gives us this flow:

Telegram / Discord message → Chatwoot conversation
                                     ↓
                         processing eligibility checks
                                     ↓
                  history + knowledge base + response rules
                                     ↓
                              LLM call at T1
                                     ↓
                       parse result and select action
                           ↙         ↓          ↘
                        reply     next tier    human agent

Each subsequent tier also returns a result that needs parsing. Sending a message is just one possible outcome. Chatwoot remains the agent's workspace, with the history, request state, and means to continue the conversation already in place.

A human agent saw the first result

In shadow mode, the assistant receives the message, the knowledge base, and the available conversation history. It then proposes a response or a decision to hand the request to a person. The result is saved in Chatwoot as a private note. The user cannot see it, and sending a reply remains the agent's responsibility.

That is how we started. Before allowing the assistant to speak on behalf of support, we gave it a place beside the person already handling the conversation.

For an engineer, this offers a useful observation point. You can open a request and see what the assistant would have suggested in that context: did it find the right information, understand the question, or start answering where a person was needed? Alongside the result, you can see the processing tier, token usage, and cost, if the provider returned it.

The presence of a note does not, by itself, mean the answer was good. The agent may not have read it, may have used just one sentence, or may have resolved the issue in a completely different way. To measure suggestion quality, we need to agree separately on how to evaluate it. A count of generated notes is no substitute.

Still, this starting point has an important practical benefit: we can examine the assistant's work on support requests without turning every generation mistake into a message to the user. Data access restrictions and the terms under which context is sent to a model remain part of the system's design. A private note changes who can see the result; it does not eliminate the external service call.

Assemble the task before calling the model

A message saying “it isn't working again” rarely tells you exactly what happened. Earlier in the conversation, the user may already have described the problem and the agent may have asked them to run a check. If the model receives only the latest sentence, it has to guess at part of the conversation.

The service fetches history from Chatwoot. It includes user messages and public replies, while excluding private notes. Among other things, this prevents a trial response from the assistant from automatically returning in the next request as though it had already been part of the conversation with the user.

The second component is a knowledge base from Confluence. It contains information needed for answers, alongside separate instructions about when the bot should respond and when it should hand the request to an agent. These materials serve different purposes. Knowing a procedure does not mean the assistant has permission to make every decision associated with it.

In the path examined here, the knowledge base text is loaded and cached inside the service process. Connecting Confluence does not, on its own, turn the system into vector search: what matters is which data actually enters the request. History length, knowledge base completeness, and update frequency affect both answer quality and the amount of context you pay for.

That is why I would also begin work on such an assistant by looking at our own documentation: does the team have a sufficiently clear answer to a typical request? If the instructions contradict themselves, the model may faithfully restate that contradiction. A more expensive tier cannot create a missing product rule.

An LLM call must end in an actionable decision

For autonomous operation, a string containing well-written text is not enough. The service needs to know what to do next. The model's result therefore contains an action and the data needed to carry it out.

The code provides four options:

Decision Service action
Reply to the user Send the prepared message
Hand off to an agent Initiate a human handoff
Reply and hand off Send the message and continue the handoff
Request the next tier Repeat processing with the next model configuration

This contract makes behavior inspectable: we can see which command arrived and which handler executed it. A restricted command list does not guarantee the right choice, however. The model can still propose an inappropriate response. Code checks, prompt rules, and quality evaluation address different parts of that problem.

There is another step between the API response and command execution: the service must parse the JSON and interpret its fields. This is where a tidy diagram meets everyday integration work. A response may be invalid JSON, or valid JSON with an unexpected structure. Those are different situations, and they are handled differently.

For broken JSON, there is a separate request to repair the format. It receives the previous call's output, without the knowledge base or conversation history: its job is to restore the structure. If the JSON is readable but the command is expressed differently, the handler tries to recover the action from known fields. This tolerance has a cost: a recovered command can result in a message being sent to the user. Recovery rules therefore deserve as much attention as the normal response path.

When to call the next model

There are three processing tiers. Each can be configured with a separate model. It is also possible to use one model with different reasoning depths, which is what the defaults do. It is therefore more useful to think of T1, T2, and T3 as processing configurations than as a mandatory list of three different providers.

The reasoning behind a cheap-to-expensive strategy is straightforward: a routine question may need only the first call, while additional resources should be spent where they can help. In the current loop, however, a specific action triggers the transition: call_next_model. A numerical score is recorded, but it does not itself act as a switching threshold. If the first tier decides to answer or call a human agent, the loop ends there. If the third tier requests another tier, the request goes to a person.

This is an important boundary: there is a limit to how long computation can continue. And needing a human agent does not always mean the model was insufficiently capable. Sometimes the answer requires access or a decision the assistant simply does not have.

After handoff, the bot must yield the conversation

When an agent takes over, writing a log entry saying processing has finished is not enough. The user needs to understand what is happening to their request, and the agent needs to know why it was handed over and where to pick up the work.

In this service, handoff includes notifying the user, adding a private note for the agent, and changing the conversation state. Separate checks take the handoff label and participation of a human agent into account. Their purpose is to stop the assistant from continuing to answer over the person.

This is now a distributed-system state problem. Events arrive through a webhook, a message can be repeated, and an agent can join between two processing steps. Message deduplication exists at the entry point, but that mechanism alone does not prove that all possible overlaps have been eliminated. Handoff needs to be treated as a scenario of its own, with its own checks.

This is exactly where the simple picture of “receive text, call a model, send a response” stops explaining the service. We need to account for who is currently handling the conversation and whether a decision made a few seconds ago is still valid.

Savings begin with the cost of the whole request

We came to this problem to automate routine work and reduce costs. Looking only at the price of the first request would therefore be insufficient.

One support request may end after T1. Another may pass through several tiers. A third may need an additional call to repair the response format and still end up with a human agent. The code collects token usage, duration, and available call costs, but human work falls outside the model's meter.

To understand the outcome, we need a wider view: was the issue resolved, did the user have to contact support again, how long did they wait, and how much work remained for the agent? Cheap generation is useful until the cost of fixing its consequences outweighs it.

I will not claim a percentage saving in this article; that conclusion requires comparable data. What matters here is showing a design that lets us gradually automate standard requests and examine what happens at each step.

For us, that path began with a fairly modest result: a note the user never saw. Autonomous replies followed, with a limited set of actions and a way to hand the conversation to a person. Around the model call, the main engineering work gradually revealed itself: context, conversation state, routing, and result validation.

In the next part, “Context for AI in Support: Knowledge Base, History, and Response Rules,” we will begin with a short user message that is not enough on its own to resolve the issue. We will explore how to assemble the necessary information around it, what to leave out of the request, and why more context does not automatically make support better.

I also wrote about setting context and task boundaries in “How to Give AI a Task in an Existing Project”.

title: ¿Por qué un LLM local da una nota distinta cada vez y basta con temperature 0 para arreglarlo?
description:
Pásale un CV a un modelo de lenguaje, pídele una nota del 1 al 10 y te devolverá un número con una justificación muy segura. Pregúntale otra vez y el número puede cambiar. El consejo habitual es "pon la temperatura a 0", y es correcto, pero deja dos preguntas sin responder: ¿cuánto se mueve de verdad la nota con la configuración por defecto? ¿Y qué es lo que temperature 0 no arregla? Las dos cosas se pueden medir en un portátil en unos minutos, porque la nota es un solo token y el modelo te da su probabilidad directamente.

Para las pruebas usé Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct (4 bits, MLX) con mlx-lm 0.32.2 en un Mac M1 de 8 GB. Los prompts son los de una demo de evaluación de CVs en Models → Playground de la app de escritorio osFoundry: un CV de seis líneas para un puesto de analista de datos junior, seguido de "Score this CV from 1 to 10 for a junior data analyst role. Start with the score, then one reason." La app ejecuta los modelos locales con llama-server de llama.cpp, así que la configuración del muestreo sale de ahí.

Los valores por defecto cuando no eliges nada

Si una petición no lleva temperatura, llama-server muestrea con sus propios valores por defecto. La compilación que incluye la app (versión 10358) los muestra en --help:

--temp, --temperature N    temperature (default: 0.80)
--top-k N                  top-k sampling (default: 40, 0 = disabled)
--top-p N                  top-p sampling (default: 0.95, 1.0 = disabled)
--min-p N                  min-p sampling (default: 0.05, 0.0 = disabled)
-s, --seed SEED            RNG seed (default: -1, use random seed for -1)

Se aplican a cualquier petición que no fije sus propios valores. Cuando la app arranca llama-server, solo añade --temp si se ha configurado una temperatura para el servidor (local_inference.rs), así que una petición sin temperatura se muestrea a 0.8 con una semilla aleatoria, que es también lo que hacen de serie la mayoría de interfaces basadas en llama.cpp.

Hacer que la nota sea el siguiente token

Una respuesta libre puede empezar con "Score: 7", "7/10" o "I would rate this CV a 7", y así cuesta localizar la nota. La solución es rellenar de antemano el inicio de la respuesta, para que el siguiente token que genere el modelo sea directamente el dígito:

import mlx.core as mx
from mlx_lm import load, generate
from mlx_lm.sample_utils import make_sampler

model, tok = load("mlx-community/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct-4bit")
DIGITS = {d: tok.encode(str(d))[0] for d in range(1, 10)}

def ids_for(cv, question, prefill="Score: "):
    msgs = [{"role": "user", "content": cv + "\n\n" + question}]
    text = tok.apply_chat_template(msgs, add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=False)
    return tok.encode(text + prefill)

def digit_probs(ids, T=1.0):
    logits = model(mx.array([ids]))[0, -1].astype(mx.float32)
    p = mx.softmax(logits / T)
    return {d: float(p[t]) for d, t in DIGITS.items()}

El tokenizador de Qwen separa los números en dígitos sueltos, así que "7" es un token y "10" empezaría por el token "1". Una sola pasada hacia delante sobre el prompt de 173 tokens da la distribución completa de la nota.

La nota es una distribución, no un número

Para el CV en inglés, con temperatura 1 (las probabilidades en bruto del modelo):

Nota Probabilidad
7 74.2%
6 23.3%
8 1.3%
5 1.2%

El modelo no "piensa" que el CV es un 7. Piensa que probablemente es un 7, con una posibilidad entre cuatro de que sea un 6. La temperatura divide los logits antes del softmax, lo que afila o aplana esta distribución:

Temperatura P(7) P(6) P(8)
1.0 74.2% 23.3% 1.3%
0.8 80.2% 18.9% 0.5%
0.5 91.0% 9.0% 0.0%
0.2 99.7% 0.3% 0.0%

llama-server no aplica solo la temperatura. Su cadena por defecto ejecuta top-k 40, luego top-p 0.95, luego min-p 0.05 y la temperatura al final. Con estos logits, top-p ya elimina todo lo que viene después del 7 y el 6 (entre los dos superan el 95%), así que el muestreador por defecto elige entre exactamente dos notas:

def llamacpp_default(logits, temp=0.8, top_k=40, top_p=0.95, min_p=0.05):
    order = mx.argsort(-logits)[:top_k]
    kept = logits[order]
    p = mx.softmax(kept)
    n = int(mx.sum(mx.cumsum(p) < top_p).item()) + 1
    idx = [i for i in range(n) if p[i].item() >= min_p * p[0].item()]
    q = mx.softmax(kept[mx.array(idx)] / temp)
    return {tok.decode([int(order[i])]): float(q[j]) for j, i in enumerate(idx)}
# -> {'7': 0.8093, '6': 0.1907}

Después lo muestreé de verdad: 200 generaciones con el mismo prompt y el muestreador de mlx-lm configurado con esos mismos cuatro valores (make_sampler(temp=0.8, top_p=0.95, min_p=0.05, top_k=40)).

7 6
Previsto por la cadena 80.9% 19.1%
Observado, 200 ejecuciones 162 (81%) 38 (19%)

Es decir, con la configuración por defecto, más o menos una de cada cinco ejecuciones le pone un 6 a este CV en lugar de un 7. Si evalúas a dos candidatos una vez cada uno y uno saca un 6 y el otro un 7, hay una posibilidad real de que la diferencia sea puro sorteo.

Un caso más plano: el mismo CV en japonés

El mismo CV y la misma pregunta en japonés (222 tokens, con 「点数：」 como relleno inicial) dieron un modelo mucho menos decidido:

Nota Probabilidad con T=1 Observado, 200 ejecuciones con los valores por defecto
8 39.8% 108
9 23.8% 44
7 19.4% 40
10 (empieza por "1": 4.1%) 8

Aquí la nota más probable gana solo la mitad de las veces, más o menos, y en 200 ejecuciones salieron cuatro notas distintas. Cuánto baila una nota no es una propiedad fija del modelo. Depende de lo cerca que estén los primeros candidatos para esa entrada concreta, y eso solo se ve mirando las probabilidades.

Lo que temperature 0 sí arregla

Con temperatura 0 (decodificación greedy: siempre el token más probable), generé la respuesta completa de 40 tokens 20 veces en cada idioma. Salió 1 texto distinto por idioma, idéntico carácter a carácter. Para el CV en inglés es "7" seguido siempre de la misma justificación, y para el japonés 「8点」.

Una semilla fija consigue lo mismo al muestrear: 10 ejecuciones reiniciando mx.random.seed(42) antes de cada una dieron 1 texto distinto. Es útil cuando quieres variedad pero necesitas reproducir una ejecución concreta. Pero no sirve para ser justo. Con una semilla, un CV distinto recibe una secuencia de sorteos distinta, así que dos candidatos siguen evaluándose con suertes diferentes.

Todo esto tiene una condición: cada ejecución fue una única petición sobre un modelo sin otra carga. Los servidores que agrupan varias peticiones en lotes pueden producir diferencias mínimas de coma flotante entre ejecuciones, que solo importan cuando dos tokens están casi empatados. Eso no se midió aquí.

Lo que temperature 0 no arregla

La decodificación greedy convierte la salida en una función de la entrada. Lo que no garantiza es que sea una función estable. Hice cuatro cambios que no deberían alterar la nota de un CV y anoté cada vez la nota greedy y las probabilidades:

Cambio (inglés) Nota greedy P(primera) Segunda
ninguno 7 74.2% 6 con 23.3%
Línea de habilidades movida arriba 7 69.6% 6 con 28.1%
Nombre cambiado (Mia Chen → James Miller) 7 68.5% 6 con 28.5%
Una línea en blanco extra 7 71.0% 6 con 26.1%
Pregunta reformulada 6 67.5% 5 con 19.3%

La pregunta reformulada era "Rate this CV for a junior data analyst role on a 1 to 10 scale. Give the score first, then one reason." Misma tarea, mismo CV, y la nota greedy baja de 7 a 6. En japonés, las cinco versiones se quedaron en 8 con temperatura 0, pero la probabilidad de la primera nunca pasó del 44%, y la segunda alternaba entre 9 y 7 según el cambio.

Así que temperature 0 elimina el azar entre ejecuciones, no la sensibilidad al prompt. Para comparar CVs, eso significa:

  • Usa temperatura 0 y exactamente la misma pregunta para todo lo que compares, carácter a carácter. Si cambias la pregunta, vuelve a puntuarlo todo.
  • Guarda la probabilidad, no solo la nota. El endpoint /completion de llama-server devuelve las probabilidades de los tokens si le pasas n_probs, y con el truco del relleno inicial el primer token es la nota. Un 7 al 74% y un 8 al 40% no son el mismo tipo de respuesta.
  • Trata como empate una diferencia de un punto con poca confianza, y lee la justificación del modelo antes de fiarte de cualquiera de los dos números.

Hacerlo en la app

En la app de escritorio osFoundry, el mismo experimento son tres paneles con un mismo modelo local en Models → Playground. Ejecuta el prompt una vez con los valores por defecto para ver la dispersión, luego abre la fila de ajustes y pon Temp a 0.

Las entradas del glosario sobre temperatura y top-p explican los dos ajustes con más detalle. La app es gratuita en la página de descarga de osFoundry.

title: Cloud vs Local: The Break-Even Point Where Self-Hosting Stops Losing Money
description:
The Local LLM Lab — Part 14

One controlled experiment. One number. One verdict.

"Local LLMs are cheaper than the cloud" is a claim you see constantly. "The cloud is cheaper" is a claim you see just as often. Both are right, both are wrong, and the answer depends on a number most people have never calculated: their own break-even point.

The break-even point is the monthly usage at which self-hosting costs the same as the API for the same work. Below it, the cloud wins. Above it, local wins. It is different for every person, because it depends on three things: what your hardware cost, what your electricity costs, and which cloud model you would otherwise be paying for.

I calculated mine from a metered 30-day bill and a current price sheet. Here is the method, so you can run it on your own numbers.

The local side: what the box actually costs

Two components, and only one of them scales with anything.

1. Hardware amortisation. A used RTX 3090 runs €800–1,200. Midpoint €1,000, amortised over 36 months: €27.78/month. If you already own the card for other reasons, this is €0 and the marginal cost of the inference stack is just electricity.

2. Electricity. This is measured, not estimated. My homelab monitor attributes power per process, and over the 30 days to 2 November the resident inference stack drew:

Service Energy (30d) Cost (BGN)
Whisper (ASR, 24/7) 21.73 5.67
Text-to-speech (24/7) 13.47 3.51
Embedding model 5.09 1.32
Everything else GPU-side 0.36 0.09
Total 40.65 10.59

Tariff: 0.30 BGN/kWh by day, 0.18 BGN/kWh by night (22:00–06:00). The bill above is not priced at either one on its own — it is a blend, and it works out to an effective 0.26 BGN/kWh. If you quote a single rate against a metered figure, quote the blended one and say it is blended.

Converted at 1.95583 BGN/EUR, that bill is €5.42 for the month.

So the local monthly cost is:

  • You already own the card: €5.42/month
  • You are buying the card: €27.78 + €5.42 = €33.20/month

Note what that number is: the whole stack, running around the clock, including every transcription queue and embedding job it handled in those 30 days. It is close to flat. It does not move much when you ask it more questions.

The part that does scale, and how I know its size. The card measures 40 W with the models resident and nothing queued — that is measured, and it is most of the month. What it draws while actually generating I did not meter this month, so I will not pretend otherwise: the 3090's board power limit is 300 W at spec, and that is a ceiling, not a measurement. At the day tariff, an hour pinned at that ceiling is 0.09 BGN — about €0.046. Two hours a day of it adds €2.76/month, putting the local side at €8.18. Treat that as the worst case for a heavy user, not the typical one.

The cloud side: what the same work costs

List prices, checked against the published price sheets in early November 2026. A "Q&A pair" is the shape of one typical assistant exchange: 500 input tokens + 200 output tokens, so 1,000 pairs is 0.5M input + 0.2M output.

Cloud model $/M input $/M output Per 1,000 Q&A pairs
Claude Sonnet 5.5 $2.00 $10.00 $3.00 (€2.69)
GPT-6.1 Sol $2.00 $10.00 $3.00 (€2.69)
Gemini 3.8 Flash $0.75 $3.75 $1.13 (€1.01)
Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite $0.30 $2.50 $0.65 (€0.58)
Claude Haiku 5.5 $0.10 $0.50 $0.15 (€0.13)
GPT-6 Luna $0.10 $0.50 $0.15 (€0.13)

Two things worth knowing before you use these. First, on the premium models output costs 5x input, so a chatty model is a more expensive model independent of quality. Second, several of those rates are introductory: Gemini 3.8 Flash goes to $1.50/$7.50 on 1 January, and the Google flagship that matches the premium tier doubles from $2/$10 to $4/$20 on 1 December. The cheap end of the market is not permanently cheap.

The break-even point

Set local cost equal to cloud cost and solve for pairs per month.

Case 1 — you already own the card (€5.42/month flat)

Comparing against Break-even Per day
Claude Sonnet 5.5 / GPT-6.1 Sol ~2,000 pairs ~67
Gemini 3.8 Flash ~5,400 pairs ~179
Claude Haiku 5.5 / GPT-6 Luna ~40,000 pairs ~1,340

Case 2 — you are buying the card (€33.20/month flat)

Comparing against Break-even Per day
Claude Sonnet 5.5 / GPT-6.1 Sol ~12,400 pairs ~412
Gemini 3.8 Flash ~33,000 pairs ~1,100
Claude Haiku 5.5 / GPT-6 Luna ~247,000 pairs ~8,200

Case 3 — you own the card and generate heavily (€8.18/month, two hours of generation a day)

Against Sonnet-class: ~3,000 pairs/month, ~102/day. The adder moves the line, it does not move the conclusion.

What the numbers say

The break-even is not "a few times a day." It is dozens. The claim that circulates in the local-LLM crowd — that you recoup a GPU by using a local assistant a couple of times a day — does not survive contact with a meter and a price sheet. Against a premium cloud model, a card you already own pays for its electricity at around 67 exchanges a day. That is a real daily habit, not a casual one.

Against the cheap end, local loses outright. Haiku-class and Luna-class APIs price a Q&A pair at about €0.00013. Your electricity is €5.42 a month before the first token. You would need 40,000 pairs a month to break even — and 247,000 if you had to buy the hardware. If the model you would actually use is a small fast cloud model, do not buy a GPU to save money. You will never catch up.

The hardware decision dominates everything else. Owning the card already moves the break-even from ~12,400 pairs to ~2,000 — a 6x difference, and it is decided before you send a single request. If the GPU is already in the machine for gaming, for work, or for something else entirely, the inference stack is nearly free and the arithmetic flips in your favour. If you would be buying it for this, this article is not the reason to do it.

The honest summary

"Local is cheaper" holds if and only if:

  1. The card is already paid for (or is being bought for some other reason), AND
  2. You use it at the volume the table demands — dozens of exchanges a day against a premium cloud model, hundreds against a cheap one, AND
  3. The local model is accurate enough for the task. A model that is wrong half the time is not cheaper. The cost of a wrong answer does not appear on either side of this equation, and it is usually the largest number in it.

The profile where local genuinely wins is narrower than the community likes to admit: someone who owns a 3090 anyway, runs a local assistant as a daily tool, and is otherwise paying premium-tier API rates. That person is over the break-even line by a wide margin and should keep the box running.

The profile where it loses is the one most often arguing for it: someone considering a first GPU purchase, comparing it against a cheap fast cloud model. That comparison is not close.

Run it on your own numbers

Four inputs, one division:

  1. Hardware: purchase price ÷ 36. Zero if you own it.
  2. Electricity: meter it for 30 days. Do not estimate from a spec sheet's TDP — my stack's real figure is the difference between a card idling warm and a card doing work, and the idle warm part is most of the month.
  3. Cloud price: your actual model, at the input/output token split your actual usage has. Not the model you wish you were using.
  4. Break-even: monthly local cost ÷ cost per 1,000 pairs × 1,000.

The result is a number of exchanges per month. Compare it against what you really do in a month, and you have your answer — which is the only answer that was ever yours to have.

Verdict

If you own the card, you break even against a premium cloud model at roughly 2,000 Q&A pairs a month — about 67 a day. Against a cheap cloud model, 40,000. If you are buying the card, multiply those by six.

The card in my machine cost me €5.42 in electricity last month. Whether that was cheap or expensive depends entirely on which row of that table I would otherwise be paying for — and now I know which row I am in.

The Local LLM Lab is a series of measured experiments on a home GPU stack. The electricity figures here are pulled from 30 days of per-process power attribution on the box; the cloud figures are published list prices as of early November 2026, and several of them change on 1 December or 1 January.

title: Your Agent's Failure Predictor Is Grading the Task, Not the Run
description:
Your Agent's Failure Predictor Is Grading the Task, Not the Run

By Igor Eduardo · Austin, TX · https://igoreduardo.com

A short new paper, Hard Issue, Weak Model, or Bad Run? Rethinking Failure Prediction for Coding Agents (arXiv 2611.08285, posted 2026-11-05), asks a question most agent monitoring skips: when a predictor flags a run as "going wrong", has it learned anything about that run?

The setup is familiar. A coding agent works on a repository issue for many steps. A predictor reads the partial trajectory (reasoning, commands, tool output) and raises an alarm. On an alarm you stop the run, retry it, or hand the issue to another model.

The authors point out that a run can fail for three different reasons, and each one calls for a different action:

  • Hard issue: most models fail it. Stopping or asking a human is the better move.
  • Weak model: this model fails many issues. Switching to a stronger one is the better move.
  • Bad run: the same model solves the same issue on other attempts. Only here does a retry help.

Their finding is that current trajectory-based predictors mostly can't tell these apart.

What they report

They used public trajectories on a widely used benchmark of 500 real repository issues, where each model attempts each issue once: 3,492 runs from seven models, 994 of them failures, plus outcomes for 23 models and a separate public corpus with repeated runs.

  • A score that never sees the run wins. A reference that only knows how hard an issue is for other models reaches 0.92 pooled AUROC. The trajectory predictors reach 0.62–0.63.
  • Pooled AUROC is mostly a between-task number. Of 494,109 failed/successful pairs in the test folds, 99.66% compare different issues. A score that recognizes hard issues can look excellent without reading a single step.
  • Within an issue, knowing the model beats reading the run. Model identity alone reaches 0.72 within-issue AUROC, against 0.60–0.61 for the predictors. On "upset" pairs, where the overall weaker model won, the predictors score 0.42, below chance. They are reproducing the model ranking, not watching the run.
  • What the trajectory adds is statistically zero. Adding a predictor's score on top of issue difficulty and model identity changes AUROC by an amount equivalent to zero in all 18 configurations they tested.
  • The "switch models" story mostly dissolves. The best single model solves 76.8% of issues and some model solves 86.8%, a 10.0-point "oracle gap". That gap sits inside the range chance alone produces. 45% of failures (448 of 994) happen on 64 issues no model solves, so there is nothing to switch to. Picking a model per issue from its past runs gains +0.09 points on new runs; a router for new issues gains +0.41.
  • The gain people attribute to routing comes from a second attempt. Escalating every failure to one fixed second model gains +6.91 points, and that assumes a perfect failure detector. The win is the extra try, not a better-suited model.
  • Bad runs are real. In the repeated-run pilot (522 issues, at least four runs per model), outcome variation splits into 53% issue difficulty, 42% run-to-run variation, and only 4.6% model-issue specialization. So retries have real room to help, but 64–82% of predictor score variance lies between issues, which means the alarm mostly fires on the cases where a retry is less likely to work.

Scope, in their words: mainly one benchmark and one scaffold, trajectory-based predictors only, a repeated-run pilot with older models, and a router with shallow issue features. Not detecting specialization is not proof it is absent. Those are their numbers, not mine. I have not re-run the experiments, and I am deliberately not naming the models, the benchmark, or the prior systems the paper discusses.

The stake

Teams will read "our failure predictor has a good AUROC" as "our agent knows when a run is going wrong".

That is the same mistake as reading a leaderboard as a forecast. A pooled score mixes three things into one number: how hard the tasks were, how strong the model is, and what happened in this attempt. Only the third is something a run-time monitor can act on. If the number is carried by the first two, you have built an expensive difficulty estimate and wired it to a retry button.

The cost shows up in the action layer. A predictor that fires on hard issues triggers retries on exactly the failures a retry rarely fixes, and stays quiet on the bad runs a retry would rescue.

Opinion (one sentence)

Any claim that a monitor, router or retry rule makes an agent more reliable should be backed by repeated runs and run-blind baselines at equal budget, because a single-attempt leaderboard can't tell a hard task from a weak model from a bad run.

That is a preference with a limiter, not a benchmark result. If your agent runs short, cheap, deterministic tasks, single runs may be enough. Once runs are long, stochastic, and you act on an alarm mid-run, the cause of failure decides whether the action helps.

What a cause-aware agent eval reports (menu, not recipe)

Column Question it answers Failure if skipped
Run-blind baselines Does the monitor beat "how hard is this task" and "which model ran"? A difficulty estimate sold as run monitoring
Within-task score Can it rank two attempts at the same task? Pooled score carried by task mix
Repeated runs How often does the same model pass and fail the same task? Bad runs invisible, luck read as skill
Chance reference for gaps Is the "best of several models" gap bigger than noise? Routing built on a coin-flip artifact
Equal-budget comparison Does the strategy beat simply trying again with the same model? A second attempt credited to cleverness
Action outcome Did the triggered stop, switch or retry actually fix the failure? An alarm graded on itself, not on what it changed

None of that requires a private harness or new model. It needs repeated runs, two baselines that never look at the trajectory, and the discipline to grade the decision, not the alarm.

Why "the alarm was right" is not a pass

The detail I would steal first is the toy example the authors open with. If a model succeeds 90% of the time on easy issues and 10% on hard ones, a score that only knows which issues are hard reaches 0.90 pooled AUROC, yet it ranks two runs of the same issue at 0.50, a coin flip. A great-looking metric with zero information about the run.

That is the eval-as-contract problem in miniature. The metric was computed correctly. It was just answering a different question from the one the product needs answered at run time.

Where this connects to habits I already keep public

My public work is mostly retrieve-first and evaluation-as-contract systems, and the habit is the same: before a component gets credit, compare it against the dumbest baseline that could have produced the same number. In retrieval, that means checking whether a gain survives query-class slices. For agents, this paper names the baselines for run-time monitoring: task difficulty, model identity, and "just try again". A monitor that can't beat them isn't monitoring the run.

Steal this check

Pick one agent with a stop, retry or routing rule and add four things before your next release:

  1. Run each task more than once. Even a small repeated slice tells you how much of failure is the run.
  2. Score two run-blind baselines. Task difficulty and model identity, next to your monitor, on the same cases.
  3. Report within-task ranking. Can the monitor tell a good attempt from a bad one on the same task?
  4. Compare at equal attempts. Does your clever strategy beat a plain second try with the same model?

Then ask whether the monitor is still worth its cost once the baselines are on the same chart.

What I am not claiming

  • I am not reporting this paper's results as my own, and I have not reproduced them.
  • I am not ranking models, agents or vendors.
  • I am not saying failure prediction is useless. The authors call for predictors that explain why a run fails, evaluated on repeated runs, in closed-loop, equal-budget settings.
  • I am not publishing alarm thresholds or retry rules. Those depend on what a wasted run and a missed failure cost you.

The point

A failure alarm that mostly knows the task is hard is not watching the run. Run tasks more than once, put run-blind baselines on the same chart, and grade the action the alarm triggers, not the alarm itself.

Igor Eduardo builds retrieve-first and evaluation-as-contract systems. More at igoreduardo.com.

title: Meta Brings Muse Wonder's Memory and Focus to Everyone: What Active Memory and Active Focus Actually Change
description:
On November 6, Meta started rolling out new models to everyone who uses Muse and Meta AI — not the frontier Muse Wonder model itself, but specialized versions of Meta's existing models, trained using Muse Wonder. The upgrade brings two capabilities from Wonder down to the assistants most people actually use: Active Memory and Active Focus.

If you build with AI agents, this is worth paying attention to, not because of the headline numbers, but because of the pattern: a frontier model acting as a teacher, and the distilled result shipping to the whole fleet.

What actually shipped

A few weeks earlier, on October 12, Meta introduced the Muse Wonder series — Muse Wonder and the larger Muse Wonder Full — as its most capable models for personal and professional agentic tasks. Wonder is available through the Meta Model API and Muse Code, with Wonder Full for Muse Code subscribers. It was never going to be the model inside the free Muse and Meta AI apps.

What shipped on November 6 is different: specialized versions of the existing models behind Muse and Meta AI, trained using Muse Wonder. Meta says the rollout is underway, and it did not name the specialized models, their sizes, or which regions and account tiers get them first. The charts in the announcement refer only to "Current Muse Model" versus "Previous Muse Model."

Active Memory: forgetting less of what matters

Active Memory is Meta's name for an assistant that remembers what matters and recognizes when earlier information becomes relevant again, so it can build on your past conversations instead of starting from zero each time.

Concretely, Meta says the models were trained to tell temporary information apart from permanent information, to reason across time, and to distinguish what is still relevant from what has gone stale. In Muse, the improved models show a 2.4x reduction in forgetting critical information needed to help you reach your goals. On Meta's Active Memory evaluation, which measures tasks that correctly use critical context, the current Muse model scores 90%, up from 76% for the previous model.

That framing matters. Memory in agents is usually talked about as storage — how much context you can cram in. Active Memory is a retrieval and judgment problem instead: what to keep, when to surface it, and when to let it go. A model that remembers everything but surfaces the wrong thing at the wrong time is arguably worse than one that forgets cleanly.

Active Focus: staying on the goal when things go wrong

Active Focus is the other half. It describes a model that keeps working toward a goal when unexpected challenges appear — trying harder, recovering from setbacks, or finding alternatives, rather than stalling or declaring the task done.

Meta says the models were trained on a variety of real-world-style bottlenecks. In Muse, they show a 67% improvement in completing everyday tasks where unexpected issues arise. The specialized models also learned to be better multi-taskers: knowing when to push on your goals independently and when to collaborate live with you, and adapting to steers and clarifications in the middle of a running task without getting confused.

In Meta AI, the same improvements are pitched differently: a better thinking partner that breaks complex problems into clear steps, asks sharper follow-up questions, and keeps up when you change direction mid-conversation.

Meta's own summary score tells the same story in one number. On its Personal Superintelligence Index, the current Muse model scores 47%, up from 38% for the previous model.

The pattern worth copying: teacher models, fleet models

Strip away the product names and the announcement describes a deployment pattern that is becoming standard across the industry:

  1. Train one frontier model with the expensive capabilities — in this case, memory judgment and persistent focus.
  2. Use it to teach specialized models that are cheap enough to serve to everyone.
  3. Ship the capability, not the model. Users get the behavior; the frontier model stays behind the API and the subscription tier.

For anyone building agents, the lesson is that memory and focus are the two capabilities that decide whether an agent is useful over days rather than minutes. A model that forgets the constraint you stated yesterday, or gives up at the first unexpected error, is a demo, not a coworker. Meta is betting that both problems are trainable — and that the training transfers from a frontier teacher to a smaller student.

The honest caveats

Every number in this announcement is Meta's own, measured on tests Meta designed, with no independent verification:

  • No baselines for two of the four figures. The 2.4x forgetting reduction and the 67% improvement have no published starting point, so it is impossible to judge how large the absolute change is.
  • No methodology published. Meta has not explained what the Personal Superintelligence Index measures task by task, or which test sets sit behind the Active Memory evaluation.
  • No separate figures for Meta AI. All four numbers describe Muse. The Meta AI side of the rollout has no published scores.
  • No model identity. The specialized models are unnamed, with no parameter counts, no model card, and no pricing.

The 47% versus 38% index score is best read as a direction of travel, not a benchmark you can compare against any rival. The interesting claim is not the number — it is that memory judgment and task persistence can be distilled from a frontier model into the models that serve everyone. That claim will be tested in daily use, where the only evaluation that matters is whether the assistant still remembers what you told it last week.

Source: Meta AI Research, Bringing Specialized Models to Muse and Meta AI, published November 6, 2026. See also Meta AI Research, Muse Wonder: A Frontier Model For Personal & Professional AI Agents, published October 12, 2026.

title: Your Agent's Memory Needs a Scope: What to Keep, Where, and When to Forget
description:
Most agent memory problems I see aren't about storage. They're about scope.

A preference that belongs to you ends up in a file the whole team shares. A temporary rule ("don't deploy this week") gets saved as if it were permanent. A note about the task you're working on right now is still being loaded three weeks later. The agent isn't forgetting. It's remembering the right thing in the wrong place, for the wrong amount of time.

In an earlier article I covered the four kinds of agent memory: working, episodic, semantic and procedural. This one is about a different question you have to answer for every single memory: who is it for, and how long should it live?

Three scopes cover most cases

You can slice scope many ways, but three levels handle almost everything a coding agent or assistant needs:

  • Session: true only for the current task. "We're fixing the login redirect." "The test database is already seeded." Useful for an hour, noise tomorrow.
  • Project: true for this repository or this product, for everyone who works on it. "We use pnpm." "Deploys go through the staging branch." "Never edit generated files in src/gen/."
  • User: true for you, across every project. "Keep answers short." "I prefer TypeScript examples." "Explain shell commands before running them."

Each scope answers a different question. Session memory answers what are we doing? Project memory answers how does this place work? User memory answers how does this person like to work? When a memory is filed under the wrong question, you get the familiar symptoms: your personal style leaks into teammates' sessions, a project fact doesn't follow you into a new worktree, or yesterday's task keeps steering today's work.

How Claude Code maps these scopes to real files

You don't have to invent this structure. Claude Code's documentation on how Claude remembers your project is a good concrete example, because each scope has its own location:

  • User instructions live in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and apply to all your projects. Only you see them.
  • Project instructions live in ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md and are meant to be shared with the team through version control.
  • Local instructions live in ./CLAUDE.local.md: personal, project-specific preferences that the docs say to add to .gitignore, like your sandbox URLs or preferred test data.
  • Managed policy is an organization-wide file deployed by IT or DevOps, which loads before user and project files.

Two details from the docs are worth knowing. First, these files don't override each other; all discovered files are concatenated into context, ordered from broadest to most specific. So "most specific wins" only works if you write the specific file to say so clearly. Second, a gitignored CLAUDE.local.md only exists in the worktree where you created it. If you want personal project notes in every worktree, the docs suggest importing a file from your home directory instead.

Then there's auto memory, the notes Claude writes for itself. The docs describe it as per repository: each project gets a directory at ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/, and all worktrees and subdirectories of the same git repo share it. It's machine-local, so it doesn't follow you to another machine or a cloud environment. Claude records each note with a type of user, feedback, project or reference, and skips anything it can derive from the code or that your CLAUDE.md already says.

Subagents get the same idea in miniature. A subagent's memory field takes a scope: user (~/.claude/agent-memory/<name>/), project (.claude/agent-memory/<name>/, shareable via version control) or local (.claude/agent-memory-local/<name>/, not checked in). The docs recommend project as the default.

Even if you don't use Claude Code, this is a useful template: one place per scope, and a clear rule for which ones get committed.

A decision test for every memory

Before a fact gets saved, by you or by the agent, run it through four questions. This is my own rule of thumb, not something from a spec:

  1. Would it still be true next week? If not, it's session memory. Keep it in the task, a scratch file, or a plan, and let it go when the task ends.
  2. Would it be true for a teammate in this repo? If yes, it's project memory and belongs in the shared, committed file.
  3. Is it about you rather than the code? It's user memory: your home-level file, never the repo.
  4. Does it have an end date? Then write the date into the memory and give it a review point. "No deploys until 16 Nov" is fine. "No deploys" with no date is a bug waiting to happen.

The fourth question is the one people skip. A rule that was true for two weeks and stays loaded forever is worse than no memory, because the agent will follow it with total confidence.

A minimal scoped memory, run for real

Here's a small Python sketch of the idea. Each memory has a scope, a subject, a value, the date it was written, and an optional review date. Session memories are dropped when the session ends. When two scopes hold the same subject, the more specific one wins. Anything past its review date gets flagged instead of silently trusted.

from datetime import date, timedelta

# Most specific scope wins when two scopes hold the same subject.
SCOPES = ["user", "project", "session"]

memory = []  # each entry: scope, subject, value, written, review_after

def remember(scope, subject, value, written, review_days=None):
    # Update, don't append: one current value per (scope, subject).
    memory[:] = [m for m in memory if (m["scope"], m["subject"]) != (scope, subject)]
    review = written + timedelta(days=review_days) if review_days else None
    memory.append({"scope": scope, "subject": subject, "value": value,
                   "written": written, "review_after": review})

def end_session():
    memory[:] = [m for m in memory if m["scope"] != "session"]

def recall(today):
    current, stale = {}, []
    for scope in SCOPES:  # broad to specific, so specific overwrites
        for m in memory:
            if m["scope"] != scope:
                continue
            current[m["subject"]] = f'{m["value"]}  [{scope}]'
            if m["review_after"] and today > m["review_after"]:
                stale.append(f'{m["subject"]} ({scope}, written {m["written"]})')
    return current, stale

d0 = date(2026, 11, 2)
remember("user", "answer_style", "short answers, no emoji", d0)
remember("user", "package_manager", "npm", d0)
remember("project", "package_manager", "pnpm", d0)
remember("project", "release_freeze", "no deploys until 16 Nov", d0, review_days=14)
remember("session", "current_task", "fix the login redirect", d0)

facts, stale = recall(d0)
print("Session 1, day 0:")
for k, v in facts.items():
    print(f"  {k}: {v}")

end_session()
facts, stale = recall(d0 + timedelta(days=15))
print("Session 2, day 15:")
for k, v in facts.items():
    print(f"  {k}: {v}")
print("Needs review:", stale or "nothing")

This is the actual output from running it with Python 3.13:

Session 1, day 0:
  answer_style: short answers, no emoji  [user]
  package_manager: pnpm  [project]
  release_freeze: no deploys until 16 Nov  [project]
  current_task: fix the login redirect  [session]
Session 2, day 15:
  answer_style: short answers, no emoji  [user]
  package_manager: pnpm  [project]
  release_freeze: no deploys until 16 Nov  [project]
Needs review: ['release_freeze (project, written 2026-11-02)']

Three things happened. The project's pnpm beat the user-level npm, because the repo knows better than your habits. The session task disappeared once the session ended. And the release freeze is still loaded on day 15, but it's flagged for review rather than quietly obeyed. In a real agent, that flag is the moment to ask the user or drop the entry.

Keep the always-loaded part small

Scope also decides what gets loaded every time. Claude Code's auto memory is a good example of why that matters: only the first 200 lines or 25KB of MEMORY.md load at the start of a conversation, whichever comes first, and anything past that limit isn't loaded at session start. Detailed notes go into separate topic files that Claude reads on demand. The docs also note that when Claude writes a memory file with frontmatter, Claude Code records a modified timestamp, so both you and Claude can see how current a fact is.

The general lesson: keep a short index of what's always relevant, push detail into files that load only when needed, and keep a date on every fact. Memory files in Claude Code are excluded from transcript cleanup and stay until you or Claude edits or deletes them, so reviewing them is your job.

Sharing one memory across tools

If your team uses more than one coding agent, project memory is the scope worth sharing. The Claude Code docs describe two ways to keep one AGENTS.md as the file every tool reads: Claude Code can read AGENTS.md directly when there's no CLAUDE.md, or you can put an @AGENTS.md import at the top of a CLAUDE.md and add Claude-specific notes below it. User memory, on the other hand, should stay personal and out of the repo, whichever tool you use.

Quick checklist

  • [ ] Every memory has a scope: session, project or user
  • [ ] Session notes are cleared or archived when the task ends
  • [ ] Project facts live in a committed file the whole team can review
  • [ ] Personal preferences live outside the repo (home-level or gitignored)
  • [ ] Time-limited rules carry an end date and a review point
  • [ ] The always-loaded index stays short; detail loads on demand
  • [ ] One shared project file across tools, if you use more than one agent
  • [ ] Someone reads the memory files on a schedule and deletes what's stale

Where to go next

If you're new to agent memory, start with the free AI Agent Memory Quick-Start, six pages on the four kinds of memory and the basic memory loop.

When you're ready to build it properly, AI Agent Memory: The Complete Guide covers writing and reading memories, consolidation and forgetting, tiered, vector and graph architectures, the production failure modes (bloat, poisoning, contradictions), and personalization and privacy, with a worked example of a support agent that remembers users across sessions.
