title: I Asked Claude to Build a Stripe BigQuery Pipeline. It Did.
description:
The Prompt

A few days after we shipped the 5-tier agent API, I ran the cleanest test I could think of. I opened Claude, pasted a Datanika API key, and typed exactly this:

"Read https://app.datanika.io/llms.txt and build me a Stripe-to-BigQuery pipeline. Load the charges and customers tables daily."

No schema. No sample code. No starter template. Just a URL and a sentence.

What happened next is what an "AI data pipeline" tool is supposed to feel like — and as far as I can tell, it's the only ELT platform where it actually works today.

What Claude Did (Transcript, Trimmed)

Step 1 — Read the discovery doc 

GET /llms.txt

/llms.txt is a plain-text manifest: base URL, auth header format, rate limits, the 5 agent capability tiers, and pointers to the full OpenAPI spec and the 17-step strategy guide at /api/v1/agent-guide.md. Claude pulled both. Total: ~8 KB of context. No HTML to parse, no JS to render, no cookie wall.

This is the piece every other ELT tool is missing. An LLM without a discovery doc has to guess endpoint names from documentation scraped months ago — and that documentation was written for humans, which means it's missing the machine-readable details the agent actually needs (exact parameter names, which fields are required, what errors mean).

Step 2 — Discover connection types 

GET /api/v1/meta/connection-types

Returns JSON for every connector in the catalogue, with full config schemas. Claude picked stripe and bigquery, read the schemas, and knew exactly which fields to set. No guessing api_key vs secret_key vs token — the schema said api_key, so api_key it was.

This is the thing I was most skeptical about before we built it. "Why not just document the endpoints?" we thought. Because documentation doesn't compile. A schema does.

Step 3 — Create source and destination 

POST /api/v1/connections  {"name": "Stripe Prod", "connection_type": "stripe", ...}
POST /api/v1/connections  {"name": "Warehouse",   "connection_type": "bigquery", ...}
POST /api/v1/connections/{id}/test
POST /api/v1/connections/{id}/test

Claude tested both connections before doing anything else. I didn't tell it to. The agent-guide.md golden-path loop says "test before building," and the agent followed it.

Both passed.

Step 4 — Introspect the source 

POST /api/v1/connections/{stripe_id}/introspect

Returns the list of Stripe tables Datanika's dlt pipeline can extract: charges, customers, invoices, subscriptions, events, and a dozen more. Claude matched "charges and customers" from the prompt to the exact table names and moved on.

No LLM hallucination, no "I think Stripe has a transactions table" (it doesn't). The source told the agent what tables existed.

Step 5 — Build the upload and run it 

POST /api/v1/uploads
  {"source_id": ..., "destination_id": ..., "tables": ["charges", "customers"],
   "write_disposition": "merge"}

POST /api/v1/uploads/{id}/run?wait=true

?wait=true is the part I want to call out. Most ELT APIs let you trigger a run and return immediately — then you have to poll for completion. Agents loop forever on polling. We added blocking mode specifically because wait=true compresses 30 lines of agent code into one call. The agent fires the request, sits on it for however long the run takes (up to the timeout), and gets back a typed result: success, failure with error code, or timeout.

Claude's first run succeeded. 4 seconds. 127 charges loaded. 48 customers.

Step 6 — Write a transformation, compile it, preview it

Claude decided to add a monthly_revenue model on top of raw charges — I didn't ask it to, but it's a sensible default for a Stripe pipeline, and the agent guide explicitly tells agents to offer a starter transformation.

SELECT
  DATE_TRUNC(created_at, MONTH) AS month,
  SUM(amount) / 100.0 AS revenue_usd,
  COUNT(*) AS charge_count
FROM {{ ref('charges') }}
WHERE status = 'succeeded'
GROUP BY month

Then — the step no other ELT platform offers over the API:

POST /api/v1/transformations/{id}/compile   → 200 OK
POST /api/v1/transformations/{id}/preview   → returns 12 rows of sample output

Compile-before-run. Datanika runs dbt's compile step against the live warehouse schema, catches Jinja errors, catches missing refs, catches type mismatches, catches unsafe_sql — and returns a typed error code if any of those fail. Claude hit one compilation_error on its first draft (used total instead of amount), the API returned the failed line and column, Claude fixed the SQL and re-compiled. Green on the second try.

Preview ran a LIMIT 12 against the compiled SQL and returned actual rows. Claude checked they looked sane and moved on.

Step 7 — Schedule it 

POST /api/v1/schedules  {"pipeline_id": ..., "cron": "0 2 * * *", "timezone": "UTC"}

Daily at 2 AM UTC. Done.

Total time from prompt to running autonomous data pipeline: ~4 minutes, ~23 API calls, zero human intervention after the initial sentence.

Why This Works (And Why Your Other ELT Tool Can't)

I keep going back to the same list. An agent needs five things to build an autonomous data pipeline without supervision:

  1. Machine-readable discovery so it knows the platform exists and how to talk to it. (/llms.txt + /api/v1/agent-guide.md.)
  2. Typed schemas for every config object so it doesn't guess field names. (The /api/v1/meta/* endpoints.)
  3. Source introspection via API so it can match user intent ("charges and customers") to actual source tables. (POST /connections/{id}/introspect.)
  4. Compile-before-run validation so it can fix SQL mistakes before burning warehouse credits or production data. (POST /transformations/{id}/compile.)
  5. Typed error codes so it can branch on failure instead of regex-matching English error messages. (compilation_error, execution_error, unsafe_sql, idempotent_replay.)

Fivetran has no agent API. Airbyte has connectors but no discovery doc and no compile-before-run. dbt Cloud compiles, but only inside its own UI — not over the API. Stitch's API is read-mostly. Hevo's is a thin CRUD layer with no schemas exposed.

We're the only AI-native ETL platform on this list where you can hand an LLM a URL and walk away.

What This Unlocks

The thing I didn't expect when we shipped the 5-tier API is how quickly the interaction model shifts. When you're the human, you stop writing pipeline code and start writing pipeline intent.

"Load charges and customers daily" is not a spec a human could hand to another human and expect a finished pipeline. But it's a complete spec for an agent that has typed schemas, introspection, and compile validation. The missing 98% of the spec is filled in by the platform, not the person.

That's the actual thesis of LLM data pipelines — not "AI writes your SQL" but "the platform exposes enough structured surface area that an agent can fill in the gaps deterministically."

Try It Yourself

If you have a free Datanika account and ten minutes:

  1. Grab an API key from Settings → API Keys.
  2. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or any LLM with tool-use:

"Read https://app.datanika.io/llms.txt, then build a [your-source]-to-[your-destination] pipeline that loads [your-tables] daily. Use API key etf_...."

  1. Watch it work.

For the impatient, our Stripe → Postgres template collapses steps 2-4 into a single pre-validated config. Point the agent at the template URL and it'll skip straight to running.

Full details on the API surface are in the AI Agents docs, and the behind-the-scenes post on why we built all this is at Datanika is AI-Agent Native.

We also compare to Fivetran and Airbyte if you want to see the capability gap on one page.

What's Next

Update: the MCP server shipped. uvx datanika-mcp wraps the whole 5-tier API as 25 typed tools, so Claude Code, Claude Desktop, and Cursor can build pipelines without any HTTP ceremony — read-only until you pass --allow-write. Setup is in the MCP server guide. Create a free account for an API key — no credit card, 10 GB/month of data.

The point isn't that an AI built a pipeline. The point is that the pipeline platform was built so an AI could.

title: Do AI bots actually read llms.txt? 8 days of server logs
description:
Originally published on pagelens.io.

Every GEO guide now says "add an llms.txt". I wanted to know if any AI system actually fetches it, so I checked the server logs of a new site that had one from day one.

Setup: one small site launched 7 Oct 2026, every request logged on the server (so non-JS bots count), user agents matched to AI companies, IPs checked against published ranges where they exist. Window: 8–15 Oct.

Numbers

File AI bot requests Share
All pages 567 100%
/robots.txt 73 13%
/sitemap.xml 50 9%
/llms.txt 6 1%

The six llms.txt requests: ClaudeBot, GPTBot, meta-externalagent, ChatGPT-User, PerplexityBot, OAI-SearchBot. Once each. The four OpenAI/Perplexity ones were IP-verified.

What I take from it

  • It does get fetched. Every major AI company's bot grabbed it within a week.
  • It's not treated like robots.txt. ClaudeBot asked for robots.txt 46 times that week and llms.txt once.
  • A fetch isn't usage. Can't tell from logs whether anything followed its links. The most-read pages were linked from everywhere anyway.
  • ChatGPT-User fetched it once. That agent acts for a person mid-conversation, so the only hint of answer-time use is a single event.

So: add one, it's ten minutes and free. Don't expect it to get you into AI answers. Robots.txt access, CDN not blocking bots, content in the HTML and links from other sites still do the work.

Check your own logs:

grep -i "llms.txt" access.log | grep -Ei "GPTBot|ClaudeBot|PerplexityBot|OAI-SearchBot|ChatGPT-User"

Curious if people with bigger sites see the same pattern.

title: SerpApi Achieves 58.56% Accuracy on SEAL-0 and 66.93% on SEAL-Hard
description:
We tested SerpApi’s Google Search and Extract APIs with GPT-6.1 Sol on SealQA, a benchmark built around factual questions that are difficult to resolve through web search.

The agent correctly answered 65 of 111 SEAL-0 questions , achieving 58.56% accuracy , and 170 of 254 SEAL-Hard questions , achieving 66.93% accuracy.

SealQA tests how well models reason when search results contain conflicting, noisy, or unhelpful information. This makes it a useful benchmark for demanding agentic use cases, where high-quality search must surface the evidence needed to resolve contradictions, verify facts, and answer accurately.

SEAL-0 contains the benchmark’s hardest core questions. SEAL-Hard includes those same 111 questions plus 143 additional challenging questions.

This follows our earlier evaluation, where SerpApi achieved 97.6% accuracy on SimpleQA Verified.

  • SerpApi Achieves 97.6% Accuracy on SimpleQA Verified

These evaluations show how SerpApi’s Google Search and Extract APIs help agents tackle difficult questions by finding relevant sources, reading pages, cross-checking evidence, and making follow-up searches when the initial results leave gaps.

How we tested Google Search and Extract for AI agents

We connected GPT-6.1 Sol, using medium reasoning, to SerpApi’s Google Search and Extract APIs.

The agent searched Google, read the returned evidence, and opened relevant pages when snippets were insufficient. It could make follow-up searches and compare sources before answering.

Setting Configuration
Answer model GPT-6.1 Sol (gpt-6.1-sol), medium reasoning
Search SerpApi Google Search, engine=google
Search output Markdown, output=md
Page content SerpApi's Extract API
Search and tool limits Up to 10 searches and 24 total tool calls per question

SERP data in Markdown

We used the Google Search API with Markdown output. The model received useful search content, including organic results, answer boxes, and AI Overviews when available.

The eval harness lets the model read the result pages and make follow-up queries.

Web page extraction with SerpApi Extract API

When search results did not provide enough evidence, the agent used the Extract API to read page content as Markdown.

The model could use this content to check details, resolve disagreements between sources, or identify a more specific search query. Fetched content was limited to 48,000 characters per page, with a maximum of 56,000 input tokens per model request.

Grading and exclusions

The grader (GPT-5.6 Sol) evaluated each prediction against the reference answer using high reasoning and the official SealQA rubric, with search and other tools disabled.

Our exposure review found one search snippet from the benchmark paper that repeated a question without revealing its answer or additional solving guidance. We retained that case in the reported SEAL-Hard score. Conservatively excluding it gives 66.80% , or 169 of 253 questions correct.

SEAL-0 and SEAL-Hard results

Benchmark Questions Correct answers Accuracy
SEAL-0 111 65 58.56%
SEAL-Hard 254 170 66.93%

The higher SEAL-Hard score reflects the composition of the dataset: SEAL-0 is its more difficult subset. These are overlapping question sets, so the results cover 254 unique questions.

These results make SerpApi a strong choice for adding web search to your AI agents. Together with our SimpleQA Verified result, they demonstrate strong accuracy across straightforward factual questions and more challenging tasks involving conflicting or incomplete evidence.

What’s next?

Add SerpApi to your agents and give them access to live web search:

Building a Python agent? Use SerpApi Search Tools to add ready-to-use search tools to OpenAI Agents, LangChain, Pydantic AI, CrewAI, and other supported frameworks.

  • Introducing SerpApi Search Tools: Real-Time Web Search for Python AI Agents

Using an MCP-compatible client? Connect our MCP server to bring SerpApi search into Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, and other AI tools.

  • Introducing SerpApi’s MCP Server (Web Search MCP)

Pair search with the Extract API when your agent needs to read the pages it finds.

  • Introducing the SerpApi Extract API: Fetch and parse any web page

title: Reviewing what AI agents changed, in one place with osFoundry Merge Station
description:
Once a few agents are doing real work, their changes start arriving from everywhere. One agent rewrote the pricing copy in a note, another cleaned up rows in a data channel, a teammate edited the onboarding checklist, and something is still sitting in a sandbox on your laptop. The work is useful, but reviewing it means remembering where each change lives. osFoundry Merge Station puts all of it in one review list, and Versions shows who changed what.

One list for every proposed change

osFoundry is a desktop app that puts chat, agents, files and tools in one window. Merge Station collects merge requests from agents and teammates, plus work staged locally in sandboxes, into a single list. The header counts what's waiting (here 3 pending and 1 sandbox).

The Sandboxes section shows local work that hasn't been proposed yet, with its branch and how many files and lines changed. Under Merge requests, each row shows the title, its state (Open, Approved, or Conflicts), who opened it (an agent such as writer or data-steward, or a user), the source and target, and a one-line AI summary of what it touches, for example "Changes 2 sections of one note; no other entities touched." That summary is often enough to decide which request to open first.

Opening a request

A request opens on its Overview: the description, source, target, author, creation time and the AI Summary, with Approve and Reject. A request that needs approval says so ("Requires approval to merge"), so nothing an agent proposes lands on its own.

The Changes tab lists every changed item with its status (modified or created) and the before and after side by side. Here the agent shortened the pricing hero line and created a plan comparison. Each change can be downloaded as the pre-edit original or the post-edit version, which is handy when you want to check it in another tool.

When the target moved

If the target changed after the request was created, the request gets a Conflicts tab and a clear message: the target branch has changed since this branch was created, and conflicts must be resolved before merging. Resolve conflicts takes you to where you fix them. Until then the request can't be merged, so an agent working from a stale copy can't overwrite newer work.

Versions: who changed what

Merge Station is about what's waiting. Versions is about what already happened. It lists changes to notes, data channels, memory groups and more, each with its author, and the filter splits them into All, User, Agent and Maestro. In the example, the writer agent tightened a launch plan summary, a user added rows to a pipeline, and Maestro merged reviewer notes into the onboarding note.

Filtering to Maestro shows only what osFoundry's main assistant changed, which is the quickest way to answer "what did the AI touch today?" Selecting an entry shows its details: type, entity, author, timestamp and ID. On the desktop app, notes also keep restore points you can go back to.

The Review tab in Versions shows the merge requests waiting on you, filtered by status (Open, Approved, Merged or Closed), with Approve and Reject right there and a link to open them in Merge Station.

For code in repositories, osFoundry has GitNest, which brings change sets, checks and review context together in the same spirit.

Use case: a Monday morning review

Over the weekend, three agents worked on a product launch. On Monday, Sammy opens Merge Station and sees three pending requests and one sandbox. The AI summaries show that the pricing request only touches two sections of one note, so Sammy opens it first, reads the before and after in Changes, and approves it. The pipeline cleanup is already approved and gets merged. The onboarding checklist shows Conflicts because a teammate edited the same note on Friday, so Sammy resolves the conflict before merging.

Then Sammy switches to Versions, filters to Agent, and checks everything the agents changed directly over the weekend, without opening a single note to look for edits.

Questions people ask first

Can an agent merge its own changes?
Requests that require approval can't be merged until someone approves them, and a request with conflicts has to be resolved first. Merging needs the right permissions.

Can I see the change before approving it?
Yes. The Changes tab shows each changed item with before and after, and you can download the original and the edited version.

How do I find what an AI changed?
Open Versions and filter by Agent or Maestro. Each entry shows the author, the type of item and when it changed.

Is it free?
osFoundry is free to use on your own device. Work that runs on osFoundry's servers uses credits.

The desktop app is free to download at osfoundry.io/download.

title: osFoundry Operator में agent app चलाता है और हर action का record रहता है
description:
"मेरे कौन-से GPU endpoints का अभी भी bill बन रहा है?" सवाल आसान है, लेकिन इसका जवाब पाने के लिए आमतौर पर तीन screens पर click करना पड़ता है, numbers पढ़ने पड़ते हैं, और फिर chat में लौटकर उन्हें type करना पड़ता है। यह काम किसी AI agent को सौंपना अच्छा लगता है, जब तक आप यह न पूछें कि उसने असल में click क्या किया। osFoundry Operator इसी सवाल को ध्यान में रखकर बना है: agent बातचीत के ठीक बगल में app के एक live pane में काम करता है, और उसका हर action लिखकर रखा जाता है।

App के live pane के बगल में बातचीत

osFoundry एक डेस्कटॉप ऐप है जो chat, agents, files और tools को एक ही window में लाता है। Operator screen को तीन हिस्सों में बाँटता है। बाईं ओर Operator sessions की list है। बीच में बातचीत है। दाईं ओर एक live dashboard pane है: osFoundry app की एक असली copy, जिसमें Operator screens खोलता है। Pane के ऊपर दिखता है कि वह किस screen पर है (यहाँ Dashboard /models/endpoints), साथ में Home और Project shortcuts, Reload dashboard और Open in a new window। Divider को drag करके pane को ज़्यादा जगह दी जा सकती है।

इस उदाहरण में Sammy पूछता है कि कौन-से GPU endpoints का bill बन रहा है। Operator pane में Endpoints खोलता है, cards को पढ़ता है और chat में जवाब देता है: एक endpoint Active है, $1.45/hr पर, और अब तक $7.54 खर्च हो चुका है; एक अभी Creating में है और उसका billing शुरू हो चुका है; और एक Stopped है। जवाब उसी screen से आता है जो उसने अभी खोली, और वह screen जाँचने के लिए वहीं मौजूद रहती है। वह active endpoint को रोकने का सुझाव भी देता है, और बताता है कि Stop दबाने से पहले वह पूछेगा।

Activity strip: Operator ने असल में क्या किया

Pane के नीचे एक पतली strip है जो दिखाती है कि Operator idle है या काम कर रहा है, और उसने आखिरी बार कब action लिया। इसे खोलने पर Log में इस pane में Operator के हर action की list दिखती है, सबसे नया सबसे ऊपर: यहाँ दो navigations, पहले Models और फिर Endpoints, दोनों पर "surface changed, read back" लिखा है। Log session का हिस्सा है, इसलिए हर Operator session का अपना अलग record रहता है। Copy as report पूरे log को text के रूप में copy करता है, किसी ticket या teammate के लिए, और Clear उसे खाली कर देता है।

यही हिस्सा Operator पर भरोसा करना आसान बनाता है। Agent जो कहता है कि उसने किया, उसकी summary पर यकीन करने की ज़रूरत नहीं। Log और pane खुद दिखा देते हैं।

Operator के साथ osFoundry setup करना

उदाहरण का दूसरा session "Set up osFoundry" है। यहाँ strip में एक दूसरा tab है, Setup, जिसमें एक checklist है जो Operator की report के बजाय app की असली live state पढ़ती है: एक provider key, एक fallback model, on-device runtime, local embedding model और router role। उदाहरण में पाँच में से तीन steps पूरे हैं, और हर बाकी step के लिए checklist वजह बताती है (जैसे "Downloaded, but not selected for local memory yet")।

हर बाकी step पर दो links हैं। Ask Operator उसी एक step के लिए request message box में डाल देता है, और Send आप दबाते हैं। Not now उस step को इस session में छिपा देता है, उसे पूरा mark किए बिना। एक नियम पक्का है: जिस step में API key चाहिए, वह कभी chat में नहीं होता। Operator settings dialog खोलता है, और key आप खुद वहाँ type करते हैं।

अगर Operator के काम करते हुए आप बाहर जाने की कोशिश करते हैं, तो वह बताता है कि run background में चलता रहेगा और credits खर्च करता रहेगा, लेकिन जिस pane को वह चला रहा था वह छूट जाएगा, इसलिए उस screen पर उसका अगला step fail होगा। आप रुक सकते हैं, या फिर भी जा सकते हैं। Stop, Operator जो कर रहा है उसे रोक देता है।

Built-in browser, companion panel के साथ

Operator osFoundry के अंदर काम करता है। Web pages के लिए built-in browser है, जो page को उन tools के बगल में रखता है जो उस पर काम करते हैं। बाएँ panel में Search, Opened, Bookmark, Read Later और History हैं। बीच में खुद page है, tabs, address bar और zoom के साथ। दाईं ओर companion panel है, जिसमें Maestro, Page, Links और Actions tabs हैं।

Page tab live page को पढ़कर उसे साफ़ text के रूप में दिखाता है, जिसे Rendered या Markdown में देखा जा सकता है, और page बदलने पर Read again उसे refresh करता है। अगर Summarizer role को कोई model assign है, तो यह page का summary भी बना सकता है। Links tab page से निकाले गए links को उनके URLs के साथ list करता है, ताकि layout में ढूँढे बिना आप ज़रूरी links खोल सकें। osFoundry का मुख्य assistant, Maestro, उसी panel में page के बगल में काम कर सकता है।

Use case: दिन के आखिर में खर्च check करना

Log off करने से पहले Sammy Operator खोलता है और पूछता है कि किन endpoints का bill अभी भी बन रहा है। Operator pane में Endpoints screen खोलकर उनकी list देता है, और activity log में वे दो screens दिखती हैं जिन पर वह गया। एक endpoint idle पड़ा है, इसलिए Sammy Operator से उसे रोकने को कहता है। Operator पहले पूछता है, फिर उसे रोकता है, और यह stop log में भी दिखता है और pane के card पर भी। अगली सुबह Sammy log को report के रूप में team के cost thread में copy कर देता है।

लोग सबसे पहले क्या पूछते हैं

क्या Operator बिना पूछे चीज़ों पर click करता है?
Operator अपने खुद के pane में काम करता है और वहाँ लिया गया हर action record करता है। उदाहरण में वह endpoint रोकने से पहले पूछता है, और जिन steps में कोई secret चाहिए वे कभी chat में नहीं होते: key आप settings dialog में type करते हैं।

उसने क्या किया, यह कहाँ देखूँ?
Pane के नीचे की activity strip में। Log हर action को उसके समय और खोली गई screen के साथ list करता है, और Copy as report उसे text के रूप में copy करता है।

क्या Operator और built-in browser एक ही चीज़ हैं?
नहीं। Operator एक live pane में खुद osFoundry app को चलाता है। Built-in browser web pages के लिए है, एक companion panel के साथ जो page पढ़ता है, links निकालता है और Maestro को उसके बगल में काम करने देता है।

क्या यह मुफ्त है?
osFoundry आपके अपने device पर मुफ्त इस्तेमाल किया जा सकता है। जो काम osFoundry के servers पर चलता है, और osFoundry के ज़रिए होने वाली model calls, उनमें credits लगते हैं।

डेस्कटॉप ऐप osfoundry.io/hi/download से मुफ्त डाउनलोड करें।

title: Assessing Production AI Experience: How London Companies Can Hire AI Engineers in India
description:
London's AI scene is one of the strongest in Europe, spanning research labs, fintech, healthtech and enterprise software. Competition for experienced AI engineers in the city is fierce, and many London companies are looking to India, where a large and fast-growing pool of engineers is building with machine learning and large language models. The challenge is telling the difference between engineers who have shipped AI to production and those who have only completed tutorials or proofs of concept.

This post focuses on how to assess real production experience.

The signal problem

"AI engineer" has become one of the most crowded titles on CVs. Many profiles list LLMs, RAG and fine-tuning. Far fewer candidates can explain how they evaluated a model, monitored it in production, controlled cost or handled failures. For London companies hiring in India, the assessment process has to surface those differences.

Questions that reveal production experience

  • Evaluation. How did you measure whether the model was good enough? What was your test set and how did you build it?
  • Failure modes. What went wrong after launch, and how did you detect it?
  • Cost and latency. How did you balance model quality against inference cost and response time?
  • Data. Where did training or retrieval data come from, and how did you keep it current and compliant?
  • Integration. How did the AI component fit into the wider product, and who owned it?

Candidates with real experience answer with specifics, numbers and trade-offs.

A practical assessment

Instead of a generic coding test, consider a short take-home or live exercise:

  1. Give a small dataset or document set and a realistic task
  2. Ask the candidate to build a minimal pipeline and an evaluation approach
  3. Review their reasoning about errors, edge cases and next steps

The evaluation design often matters more than the model choice.

Working across GMT and IST

India is 5.5 hours ahead of London in winter and 4.5 hours in summer. London mornings overlap with the Indian afternoon, which suits model reviews, experiment discussions and pairing. Keep experiment logs and decisions written so work progresses asynchronously.

Data protection considerations

AI work often involves sensitive data. Agree early on data access, anonymisation, UK GDPR obligations and India's data protection rules, and make sure your employment or partner contracts cover them.

Conclusion

India has real AI engineering depth, but strong assessment is essential. Ask about evaluation, failures, cost and data, use practical exercises, plan around the overlap hours and settle data protection early. With this approach, London companies hiring in India can hire AI engineers who have genuinely shipped. For specialist AI searches, see how Talhive supports London companies hiring in India.

title: Five Prompts Beat Five Samples: 21/24 vs 15/24 on the Identical Five-Call Bill
description:
Two methods, same model, same 24 questions, same budget of five calls per question.

Self-consistency — one prompt, five samples at temperature 0.3, majority vote — scores 15/24.

An ensemble of five different prompts, plurality vote, scores 21/24. The best single prompt on its own scores 17/24.

👉 Live, with the correlation dial and every aggregation rule on sliders: https://dev48.in/prompt/day83-prompt-ensembling.html

These are not the same technique

Self-consistency varies the sampler's dice. Every one of the k samples read identical words, so the vote cancels sampling noise and nothing else.

Prompt ensembling varies the prompt: a different phrasing, a different output format, the options listed in a different order. The members can disagree for a reason, and a vote only buys you something when the voters can disagree for a reason.

The ceiling makes the difference concrete. Push self-consistency to k = 301 and it lands on 17/24 — and not approximately. At k = 301 it reproduces that one prompt's own greedy pick on 24 of 24 questions. The plurality over samples converges to the prompt's most likely answer, so the prompt is the ceiling. k buys stability, never a second point of view.

The engine simulates nothing about language

24 arithmetic questions are DATA. Each has four options: the true value, an off-by-one, a digit swap, and a rounded figure. The in-page self-check re-evaluates 17 × 24 and the other 23 rather than trusting the stored answer.

A "prompt variant" is a scoring profile over those four options — how strongly it is drawn to the truth, to each of the three traps, and to whatever is listed first. Each question is tempting for one particular trap. A member goes wrong where its weakness meets a matching question, which is what makes two variants fail on different questions rather than the same ones.

Noise is a hash of (seed, member, question, option), not a stream. Reordering the member array therefore cannot change what any member answers, and the verifier proves it across all 120 permutations of five members on all 24 questions.

prompt variant accuracy
plain ask 17/24
options as a table 17/24
work it out step by step 16/24
answer with the value only 11/24
same ask, options reversed 15/24
plurality over all five 21/24
confidence-weighted 22/24
Borda (rank aggregation) 23/24

Mean pairwise error correlation across those five: −0.144.

The finding: an ensemble only pays when the errors are uncorrelated

Same machinery, same five members, same 24 questions, same seed, same 5× cost. One dial: blend each member's profile toward the first member's, so the set slides from five genuinely different prompts to five rewordings of one.

blend error correlation best single ensemble gain agreement when wrong
0.0 — five different prompts −0.144 17/24 21/24 +4 53.3%
0.2 −0.079 18/24 22/24 +4 60.0%
0.4 0.000 18/24 19/24 +1 64.0%
0.6 0.172 17/24 18/24 +1 73.3%
0.8 0.346 17/24 17/24 0 80.0%
1.0 — five rewordings of one 0.508 17/24 16/24 −1 87.5%

The gain does not merely shrink. It crosses zero and goes negative. Cost does not move.

The question to measure before shipping an ensemble is not "are my prompts different?" It is "do my prompts fail on different questions?"

A majority of biased members is confidently wrong

That last column is the part that should worry you.

member set error correlation best single ensemble agreement when wrong
5 different prompts −0.144 17/24 21/24 53.3%
5 rewordings of one prompt 0.644 17/24 16/24 92.5%
5 identical calls 1.000 17/24 17/24 100.0%

A diverse ensemble that is wrong is wrong about 3-to-2 and looks shaky. A correlated ensemble that is wrong is wrong 5-to-0 and looks certain. The correlated set is less accurate and more convincing about it — so a gate that routes high-agreement answers past review fails in exactly the same direction the ensemble does.

And the bottom row is the limit case. Five identical calls at temperature zero return the single prompt's own sheet under 12 of 12 rule × tie-break combinations, for 5× the bill. If your "variants" are politeness edits, that row is what you bought.

The tie-break nobody writes down is order-dependent

Five members over four options tie more often than people expect. Somebody has to decide, and in most code nobody decided: a loop that keeps a running maximum returns whichever tied option the first member voted for.

Over all 120 permutations of the five members, that default returns different answers on 2 of 24 questions. Listing the same five members in reverse takes the sheet from 21/24 to 20/24. Nothing about the model, the prompts or the seed changed — only the order of an array.

Breaking ties on a property of the options instead (lowest listed position, summed confidence, Borda score) is invariant across all 120 orderings. It costs nothing.

k is not a slider you push right

k cost plurality questions decided by tie-break
1 1× 17/24 0
2 2× 18/24 12
3 3× 20/24 2
4 4× 18/24 9
5 5× 21/24 2

Accuracy goes 17 → 18 → 20 → 18 → 21. Adding a member is not a safe move; a weak member's votes land somewhere. And an even k sends half your sheet to the tie-break: k = 2 decides 12 of 24 questions by policy rather than by vote.

If you ensemble, use an odd k.

And no aggregation rule wins everywhere

Same engine, seven seeds:

seed best single plurality confidence-weighted Borda
20260083 17/24 21/24 22/24 23/24
7 19/24 20/24 19/24 21/24
101 18/24 19/24 19/24 22/24
4242 20/24 22/24 20/24 22/24
90210 18/24 21/24 20/24 22/24
31337 17/24 20/24 21/24 22/24
555 17/24 19/24 21/24 21/24

Plurality beats confidence-weighted on three seeds and loses on three. One run does not establish an ordering between them.

Borda is at least as good as both on 7 of 7, which is the strongest claim this page will make for any rule — and it is the only rule with a cost that is not in the call count. Borda needs every member to rank all the options, which is more output tokens per call, and a member that will not rank reliably cannot be in a Borda ensemble at all. It is also the only rule that can elect an option nobody put first: five members whose first choices are 0, 0, 1, 1, 3 elect option 2, the universal second choice, with zero first-place votes. A plurality vote cannot see it.

What to actually do

  1. Write variants that fail differently, not variants that read differently. Change the format, the option order, the reasoning demanded. Politeness edits produce the 5-identical-calls row.
  2. Fan out in parallel, or the latency is k times too.
  3. Pick an aggregation rule on purpose, and write the tie-break down.
  4. Measure, on a held-out set, before shipping: every single variant's accuracy, the pairwise error correlation, the agreement on the wrong answers, and accuracy at k = 1, 3, 5.

If the ensemble is not beating your best single variant, or the correlation is high, ship k = 1 and keep the money. k prompts cost k times as much for a gain you have to measure rather than assume.

186 verifier asserts over 120 member permutations, 42 in-page checks, 0 failures. Vanilla JS, one file, no build step, no network.

title: In osFoundry gli agenti AI hanno un reparto e un compito, e a te resta solo controllare e approvare
description:
Una singola chat con un agente AI va benissimo per un singolo compito. Il lavoro continuativo è un'altra storia. Un report di stato settimanale, un comunicato stampa a ogni lancio, un controllo quotidiano dei concorrenti: ognuna di queste attività ha bisogno di un responsabile, deve partire secondo programma e qualcuno deve approvare il passaggio che non si può annullare, come mandare un'email a 42 giornalisti. osFoundry Departments dà una casa a questo tipo di lavoro, e Agent Registry mostra cosa sta facendo ogni agente.

Un reparto riunisce persone, agenti e incarichi

osFoundry è un'app desktop che mette chat, agenti, file e strumenti in un'unica finestra. In Departments ogni reparto ha i suoi membri (persone e agenti), i suoi incarichi (Duties), i suoi Department Projects e i suoi registri. L'elenco mostra ogni reparto con il suo stato e il suo sponsor: qui Customer Support è in pausa, Launch Operations è attivo e ha un sottoreparto, Press Desk, e Research è ancora una bozza.

Un nuovo reparto nasce come bozza. I posti sono vuoti e gli incarichi in pausa finché non assegni i posti e attivi gli incarichi, così nulla parte per sbaglio.

Il Desk: cosa richiede una persona adesso

Aprendo un reparto si arriva al suo Desk, un'unica pagina con tutto ciò che richiede attenzione. Nell'esempio di Launch Operations:

  • Needs you: un'approvazione per inviare un'email alla lista stampa e un'indagine sulle risposte lente della stampa.
  • Scoreboard: metriche con andamento, ultimo valore e obiettivo, come i brief consegnati in tempo (94, obiettivo 90 o più) e le risposte della stampa entro un giorno (72, obiettivo 80 o più).
  • Inbox: una nuova richiesta (un brief di lancio) con Accept, Need info e Reject.
  • Impegni in scadenza, lavoro in corso, ed eccezioni e mancanze (per esempio un monitoraggio dei concorrenti saltato due volte).

Le schede in alto contengono il resto del reparto: Members, Operations, Duties, Department Projects, Work, Review, Ledger e Charter, con i pulsanti Pause, Stop all e Archive per l'intero reparto.

Duties: chi fa cosa, e quando

La scheda Duties è l'elenco dei compiti del reparto. Ogni incarico ha un modello (su richiesta, di routine o a progetto), un momento di esecuzione, il metodo che svolge il lavoro (una sessione di agente, un grafo, un loop o un passaggio manuale), un responsabile e uno stato. Nell'esempio, il press writer scrive un comunicato stampa ogni volta che viene richiesto, un grafo produce lo stato settimanale del lancio ogni lunedì alle 09:00 ora di Tokyo, un researcher esegue il monitoraggio quotidiano dei concorrenti come loop su questo computer (al momento in pausa), e la checklist del giorno del lancio è ancora una bozza senza responsabile.

Gli agenti chiedono prima di qualsiasi azione irreversibile

È questa la parte che cambia quanto devi stare a guardare. Quando un agente arriva a un passaggio irreversibile, si ferma e chiede. La richiesta di approvazione mostra esattamente cosa succederà: qui il press writer, che lavora all'incarico Launch press release, vuole inviare un'email alla lista stampa (42 contatti), con oggetto e allegato PDF indicati per esteso. La richiesta scade tra 3 ore.

L'approvazione è legata proprio a quell'azione: qualsiasi modifica successiva la annulla, quindi ciò che approvi è ciò che viene inviato. Puoi scegliere Approve, Reject o Request changes (per gli ultimi due serve una nota), e approvando diventi l'editor responsabile di tutto ciò che viene pubblicato. L'agente scrive e invia; tu leggi una schermata e decidi.

Agent Registry: tutti gli agenti in un unico elenco

Departments riguarda il lavoro, Agent Registry riguarda gli agenti. Elenca tutti gli agenti che hai creato con il loro stato, e i filtri li dividono in All, Running, Idle, Off e Needs Attention. Ogni riga mostra il ruolo dell'agente (chat di Maestro, membro di un team, worker di una flotta o membro di un loop) e se il suo profilo è locale o sincronizzato.

Aprendo un agente vedi cosa sta facendo in questo momento e cosa ha fatto: lo stato in tempo reale e le esecuzioni, la cronologia registrata, dove è salvato il profilo, il lavoro attuale e la definizione, con numero di versione e modello preferito. Le schede coprono conversazioni, attività, istruzioni, memoria, strumenti, modello e budget, dove viene usato e versioni. Modificare le impostazioni predefinite di un agente salva una nuova versione, quindi puoi sempre tornare indietro. Switch off ferma l'agente.

La scheda Activity elenca ogni esecuzione e, per quelle registrate dal nuovo ledger, input e output evento per evento: chiamate agli strumenti come la scrittura di un file, risposte del modello e letture della memoria.

Il filtro Needs Attention è il primo da controllare. Nell'esempio lascia un solo agente, con stato Unreachable.

Caso d'uso: gestire il lancio di un prodotto come un reparto

Sammy crea Launch Operations con Dari come membro, un agente press writer e un agente researcher. Lo stato settimanale parte da solo ogni lunedì, il monitoraggio dei concorrenti ogni giorno, e il press writer scrive il comunicato quando viene richiesto. Durante la settimana del lancio Sammy non sorveglia gli agenti: apre il Desk. Lì trova l'unica email in attesa di approvazione, una metrica sulle risposte della stampa sotto l'obiettivo e un nuovo brief nell'inbox. Sammy legge l'email esatta, la approva e accetta il brief. Più tardi, un controllo del filtro Needs Attention in Agent Registry mostra che l'agente inbox-triage è diventato irraggiungibile, e Sammy lo sistema prima di lunedì.

Le prime domande che ci si pone

Un agente invierà email o pubblicherà senza chiedere?
Le azioni irreversibili passano da un'approvazione che mostra l'azione esatta. Qualsiasi modifica dopo l'approvazione la annulla, e in alternativa puoi rifiutare o chiedere modifiche.

Cosa succede quando creo un reparto?
Nasce come bozza, con posti vuoti e incarichi in pausa. Non parte nulla finché non assegni i posti e attivi gli incarichi.

Come faccio a sapere se un agente si è bloccato?
Apri Agent Registry e usa il filtro Needs Attention. La pagina di ogni agente mostra stato in tempo reale, esecuzioni e attività registrata.

È gratis?
osFoundry si usa gratis sul tuo dispositivo. Il lavoro eseguito sui server di osFoundry e le chiamate ai modelli tramite osFoundry consumano crediti.

L'app desktop si scarica gratis da osfoundry.io/it/download.

title: RecallFlow AI: Building Customer Support Agents with Persistent Memory Using Hindsight
description:
What if an AI customer support assistant could remember you, understand your previous problems, and continue conversations without asking you to repeat everything?

That's the idea behind RecallFlow AI.

🚀 The Problem

Traditional AI chatbots are useful, but they often struggle with conversation continuity.

When a customer starts a new conversation, important context from previous interactions may be missing.

For example:

  • A customer previously reported a laptop battery issue.
  • They explained the troubleshooting steps they had already tried.
  • In the next conversation, they have to explain everything again.

This creates a frustrating customer experience.

I wanted to explore how persistent AI memory could help solve this problem.

💡 Introducing RecallFlow AI

RecallFlow AI is an AI-powered customer support assistant designed to remember customer information and provide contextual responses across conversations.

The project combines conversational AI with persistent memory using Hindsight and Groq-powered AI inference.

The goal is simple:

Remember Every Conversation. Resolve Every Problem.

🧠 What Makes It Different?

The central concept is persistent customer memory.

Instead of treating every conversation as an entirely new interaction, the system uses customer-specific memory to retrieve relevant information from previous conversations.

Key Capabilities

  • AI-powered customer conversations.
  • Persistent memory using Hindsight.
  • Customer-specific memory banks.
  • Context retrieval from previous interactions.
  • Personalized AI responses.
  • Conversation history.

⚙️ Technology Stack

Technology Purpose
React + Vite Frontend development
Python Backend development
FastAPI Backend API
Groq AI inference
Hindsight Persistent AI memory
SQLite Database
JWT Authentication

🔄 How Does It Work?

The intended workflow is:

  1. A customer sends a message.
  2. The backend processes the request.
  3. Hindsight retrieves relevant customer memories.
  4. Groq generates a response using the available context.
  5. Relevant conversation information is retained for future interactions.

This creates a foundation for more contextual and personalized customer support.

🛠️ Challenges and Learning

Working with persistent AI memory introduced several interesting engineering challenges:

  • Managing customer-specific memory.
  • Connecting an AI model with an external memory system.
  • Maintaining conversational context.
  • Handling memory retrieval and API failures.
  • Designing an architecture that can support future improvements.

This project helped me explore the difference between a traditional chatbot and an AI assistant that can maintain context across interactions.

🔮 What's Next?

RecallFlow AI is an evolving project. Some improvements I plan to explore include:

  • Advanced memory management.
  • Customer profiles and interaction timelines.
  • Support ticket management.
  • Knowledge base integration using RAG.
  • Human-agent escalation.
  • Sentiment analysis.
  • AI-powered support analytics.

These are planned enhancements as development continues.

📂 Explore the Project

GitHub Repository:

https://github.com/Veerendrakumarkr2137/RecallFlow

I am continuing to improve the implementation, test the integrations, and explore how persistent memory can make AI-powered customer support more useful.

🙌 Acknowledgements

This project builds upon the original RecallCare AI project and explores its persistent-memory approach using Hindsight.

Special thanks to the Hindsight and Groq communities for making these technologies accessible to developers.

🚀 RecallFlow AI

Remember Every Conversation. Resolve Every Problem.

title: Dev News Digest: 9 Nov 2026, 18:00
description:
A quick roundup of developer news since the last digest.

Security

  • Cloudflare builds a post-quantum public certificate authority: Cloudflare is developing a public CA based on Merkle certificates, aimed at making web PKI viable against quantum-era threats. InfoQ
  • Secure Boot abuse via a Microsoft-signed shim: A write-up shows how a legitimately signed shim can be borrowed to bypass Secure Boot on corporate hardware, relevant to anyone relying on it for fleet security. leosmith.wtf
  • ChatGPT Desktop reportedly forwards your SSH agent to remote machines: A Hacker News thread flags that the desktop app forwards the local SSH agent when connecting to remote hosts, a surprising credential exposure to check for. Hacker News

Languages & tooling

  • Tokio releases Topcoat, a full-stack Rust framework: A batteries-included web framework from the Tokio team aims to give Rust a more cohesive full-stack story. InfoQ
  • Cloudflare launches a Vite Ecosystem Fund: The fund is meant to support the open-source projects around Vite, a core part of modern frontend tooling. Cloudflare
  • What's new in Node.js 27: An overview of the features and changes in the upcoming Node.js release. Node.js Design Patterns
  • Zebkit embeds Chromium as a library: A new project packages Chromium for embedding in applications. GitHub

AI & infrastructure

  • AWS TorchNeuron runs PyTorch on Trainium unmodified: Amazon says existing PyTorch models can run on its Trainium chips without code changes, lowering the cost of leaving GPUs. InfoQ
  • Same H100, up to 4.5x the price: A dataset finds the hourly cost of an H100 ranges from $2.69 to $12.29 depending on the provider and region. Data Receipts
  • Automattic launches a platform for deploying vibe-coded apps: The WordPress company is offering hosting aimed at AI-generated apps. TechCrunch
  • Waymo still passing school buses after a software fix, feds say: US regulators say the robotaxis kept illegally passing stopped school buses even after an update. TechCrunch

Design & UX
