title: TTFT and TPOT: The Latency Number You Report Hides the One Users Feel
description:
Push a simulated serving queue from 0.2 to 3.0 requests a second and mean end-to-end latency gets 17x worse.

Over the same range, the 99th percentile time to first token gets 762x worse — 206 ms to 157 s.

Both numbers describe the same 300 requests. Only one of them describes the empty box a user is staring at.

👉 Live, with sliders for arrival rate, prompt length and batch size: https://dev48.in/ai/days/day83-ttft-vs-tpot.html

The workload is simulated and seeded

There is no GPU here and no model. There is a discrete-event simulation with a fixed seed (mulberry32, seed 20261109): 300 requests, exponential inter-arrival times, log-normal prompt lengths (median 512 tokens) and output lengths (median 180 tokens), a FIFO queue, and a batch.

The cost model is two lines:

prefill(group) = 8 ms  + 0.08 ms x (total prompt tokens)
decode step    = 18 ms + 1.2  ms x (sequences in the batch)

None of these figures are measurements of any real serving stack, and none of them are claims about one. They are the arithmetic of serving, which is the part that survives a change of hardware. Everything below comes out of that loop, and a Node verifier re-derives all of it from an independent token-by-token replay.

Two clocks, glued by an identity

Time to first token is the silence: queueing plus prefill, before anything appears. Time per output token is the cadence after it. They compose exactly:

e2e = TTFT + TPOT x (output tokens - 1)

Not approximately. Across all 300 requests the worst disagreement is 3.64e-12 ms. The minus one is there because the first token is already paid for inside TTFT.

That identity is why a single total is useless for diagnosis. A slow total is a long silence, a slow cadence, or a long answer — three different causes with three different fixes, and the total cannot tell you which. In the default run the request with the worst TTFT and the request with the worst end-to-end are not the same request.

The queue lands almost entirely on the silence

arrival rate TTFT p50 TTFT p99 TPOT p50 tok/s
0.2 req/s 55.5 ms 206.3 ms 20.40 ms 48.2
0.8 req/s 71.1 ms 5,966 ms 26.46 ms 191.9
1.2 req/s 13,377 ms 24,010 ms 29.14 ms 260.2
2.0 req/s 53,606 ms 110,884 ms 29.30 ms 266.8
3.0 req/s 76,188 ms 157,311 ms 29.30 ms 267.4

TTFT p99 moves 762x. TPOT p50 moves 1.44x. Mean end-to-end — the column most dashboards actually plot — moves 17x, because it is dominated by how many tokens the answers had, which is a property of the questions and not of the server.

A deploy that moved the first column from 55 ms to 76 seconds would show up on a mean-latency chart as a moderate regression.

TPOT is batch size, and it is exactly batch size

A decode step reads the weights out of memory once and uses them for every sequence in the batch. Fill the batch and time it:

full batch of TPOT tokens/s to one user tokens/s for the server ms of step per sequence
1 19.20 ms 52.1 50.9 19.200
8 27.60 ms 36.2 246.8 3.450
32 56.40 ms 17.7 420.4 1.762
64 94.80 ms 10.5 476.2 1.481

The same number, divided two ways. Per token the fixed cost falls towards 1.2 ms; per sequence it only ever rises. The server gets 9.4x faster and every individual stream gets 4.9x slower, and only one of those is on a capacity dashboard.

Prompt length does not appear in the step expression at all. Measured in the clean room, TPOT across a 64x range of prompt lengths at four batch sizes has a total spread of 8.38e-13 ms — floating-point noise, nothing else.

Except that it leaks, and the leak is scheduling

Put the same server under load and prompt length suddenly does move TPOT. Batch 16, 1.4 req/s. The control column prices prefill at zero and changes nothing else — same arrivals, same batch, same decoding:

median prompt TPOT, prefill free TPOT, prefill priced server time in prefill
128 31.035 ms 32.730 ms 2.96%
512 31.035 ms 36.462 ms 8.44%
2048 31.035 ms 49.119 ms 27.08%
4096 31.035 ms 63.025 ms 43.01%

The control column is identical to the last digit, because with prefill free the prompt does not exist. The priced column doubles. Nothing about decoding changed — somebody else's 4,000-token prefill is holding the accelerator while your sequence waits for its next token. This is the effect chunked prefill exists to spread out, and it is why a TPOT regression can be caused by a change nobody made to decoding.

The assertion that failed

I expected the classic trade: make the scheduler wait to accumulate a full batch before prefilling, fuse the prefills, buy throughput, pay in TTFT. Half of it showed up.

2,048-token prompts, 0.8 req/s, batch 16:

batch wait window TTFT p50 tok/s prefill share
0 ms 207.5 ms 191.7 17.726%
150 ms 369.2 ms 191.6 17.668%
400 ms 640.0 ms 191.5 17.578%
800 ms 1,052.6 ms 191.3 17.494%

The fusing worked exactly as advertised: prefill's share of server time falls monotonically. Throughput moves −0.22%. This server is decode-bound, so the time the optimisation freed was never the bottleneck.

TTFT p50 went up 5.1x anyway. The optimisation succeeded and only the bill arrived — charged to users, in a column the throughput dashboard does not have.

A percentile over requests is not a percentile over tokens

p99 TPOT usually means: average each request's cadence, take the percentile over requests. That gives a two-token reply exactly as many votes as a two-thousand-token one. Weight by tokens emitted instead and the number moves — at 1.4 req/s, 32.12 ms per request against 31.27 ms per token.

Neither is wrong. They answer different questions, and a dashboard that does not say which one it is answering is not reporting anything.

Budget the two separately, because one SLO cannot hold both

Take a budget of TTFT p90 ≤ 1 s and TPOT p90 ≤ 60 ms, and sweep batch size at 2.0 req/s:

batch TTFT p90 TPOT p90 verdict
1 1,102,077 ms 19.2 ms TTFT over
16 31,947 ms 42.6 ms TTFT over
32 3,796 ms 64.8 ms both over
64 154 ms 73.0 ms TPOT over

Small batches blow the TTFT ceiling on queueing. Large ones blow the TPOT ceiling on step time. No batch size satisfies both. That is not a tuning problem, it is a capacity verdict — and the split metrics are the only thing that can state it, because the same budget at 0.8 req/s and batch 16 is met comfortably (TTFT p90 129 ms, TPOT p90 30.9 ms).

An end-to-end budget would have been satisfied or violated by a change in answer length that nobody deployed.

One bug worth keeping

The batch-wait scheduler advances the clock to head.arrival + batchWindow, then tests whether the window has expired. That sum rounds a hair low in a double — 299.9999999999999 for a 300 ms window — so the test says no, the clock is advanced to the same instant again, and the loop spins forever on one timestamp. Fourteen window values hung before the comparison got an epsilon. The page now asserts that all 28 window-and-batch combinations terminate and serve all 300 requests.

What is checked

The page runs 47 assertions in your browser, including the nearest-rank percentile against a hand-checked array, a fixed seed reproducing a run string-identically, the end-to-end identity to 1e-9 for every request, TTFT monotone in arrival rate, and TPOT invariant to prompt length in isolation and demonstrably not invariant under load.

A Node verifier lifts the same engine out of the HTML and adds 177 more, including an independent replay that records a timestamp for every one of ~70,000 tokens and re-derives TTFT, TPOT and end-to-end from that log rather than from the three scalars the page keeps. Both at zero failures.

Report TTFT and TPOT separately, at p90 or p99, and say which output length you assumed when you turned them into a total. Then when the total moves, the identity tells you which of the three terms moved.

title: One polite email taught my Hindsight agent to pay scammers
description:
One polite email taught my Hindsight agent to pay scammers

The email that broke my agent had no "ignore previous instructions" in it. It was polite, it was signed by the vendor's accounts team, and it said Acme Supplies had moved banks. The next time someone asked it to pay Acme, my payments agent drafted a ₹1,18,400 transfer to the attacker's account, explained its reasoning clearly, and was completely sure of itself.

Nothing was wrong with the model. The problem was memory.

Memory turns a one-time injection into a standing order

Without memory, a prompt injection only lasts one conversation. Close the session and it's gone. Once an agent has long-term memory, an injection becomes a fact the agent believes from now on. It's retained once and recalled every time a related question comes up, often weeks later, long after anyone remembers where it came from. OWASP now lists this as its own agent risk (memory poisoning, ASI06), and it changes how you have to think about what agent memory actually is: it's no longer a cache, it's an attack surface that persists.

Write-time filters help, and you should have them. But my polite email would pass any keyword filter. So I built the part I couldn't find anywhere: what happens after the poison is already in memory. I called it MemoryGuard. It detects the harmful action, explains why the memory is suspicious, traces everything that memory touched, and removes only the poisoned parts, then proves the fix.

How it hangs together

The agent's long-term memory lives in Hindsight, an open-source agent memory system. Every time something enters memory, whether an email, a web page, a chat message, a tool output or the agent's own answers, it goes through Hindsight's retain path, and every question goes through recall. Each agent gets its own memory bank: my vendor-payments agent and my IT-helpdesk agent never share memories.

MemoryGuard sits around that memory layer, not inside the model:

 email / web / chat / tools
           │
           ▼
  provenance envelope ──► Hindsight retain (content + metadata)
           │                       │
           ▼                       ▼
    lineage graph ◄──────── Hindsight recall ──► LLM ──► drafted action
           │                                                   │
           ▼                                                   ▼
 detectors + explainable score                    action gate vs system of record
           │                                                   │
           └──────────────► heal: quarantine, replay, audit ◄──┘

Hindsight does what a memory layer should: durable storage, semantic recall, and metadata travelling with every memory. I didn't want to build a vector store; I wanted to build the security around one. The rest of this post covers the decisions that mattered.

Decision 1: trust comes from where, never from what

My first design scored each memory's trustworthiness by reading it. That's backwards: an attacker controls the content, so content-based trust is attacker-controlled trust. Instead, every memory gets a provenance envelope at write time, stored as Hindsight metadata, and trust is set by the source class only:

def make_envelope(content, source_class, source_id, session_id="seed", event_time=None) -> dict:
    """Build the metadata attached to every memory. Trust comes from source_class only."""
    accepted = now_iso()
    return {
        "source_class": source_class,
        "source_id": source_id,
        "session_id": session_id,
        "sha256": hashlib.sha256(content.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest(),
        "event_time": event_time or accepted,  # what the content claims
        "accepted_time": accepted,             # when we stored it
        "trust": config.TRUST_BY_SOURCE[source_class],
        "status": "live",
    }

The scale is boring on purpose: system of record 1.0, user chat 0.6, tool output 0.5, the agent's own answers 0.4, email 0.3, web 0.2. The event_time / accepted_time split turned out to matter more than I expected: a memory that claims to be from last March but was stored five minutes ago is worth a second look.

You can't add provenance later. If it isn't recorded at write time, no amount of analysis will tell you afterwards whether a memory came from the user or from a web page.

Decision 2: memory is never the authority for an action

This is the main idea of the project. The agent is allowed to believe whatever it recalls. It is not allowed to act on a high-impact field (a bank account, a payment recipient, admin rights, a password-reset address) unless that value matches the system of record.

Before any drafted payment goes anywhere, the gate looks up the vendor's verified account. If the drafted account differs, it collects every memory that mentions the drafted account and checks the most trusted one:

support = _supporting_memories(account)
max_trust = max((m.trust for m in support), default=0.0)
if max_trust < config.GATE_MIN_TRUST:
    verdict = "block"
    reasons.append(f"{why}; backed only by low-trust memory ({sources}, max trust {max_trust:.1f})")
else:
    verdict = "hold"

There's no model in that path. The same input always gives the same decision, and no injected sentence can talk it out of it. When I later added an IT-helpdesk agent, the engine didn't change. I added two new checks against a different source of truth: admin rights only for people on the official admin list, and password-reset links only to an employee's registered email or phone. Supporting a new kind of agent means supplying two things: its source of truth and the actions to check.

Decision 3: a score you can't explain is a score nobody acts on

When the gate blocks something, the supporting memories get scored. Five signals, each between 0 and 1: contradicts the verified record, low-trust source, injection markers, similarity to known attack phrasings, and whether the memory touches a high-impact field. The total is a weighted sum, and each signal's share of the total is the explanation:

total = sum(config.WEIGHTS[k] * v for k, (v, _) in values.items())
for key, (value, detail) in values.items():
    contribution = config.WEIGHTS[key] * value
    signals.append({"key": key, "contribution": contribution,
                    "share": contribution / total if total else 0.0, "detail": detail})

For the polite email, the inspector shows 0.70: contradicts verified record 50%, low-trust source 25%, high-impact field 14%, similar to known attack 11%, injection markers 0%. That last zero is the point. A keyword filter would have scored this email as clean. No model training, no black box, and a reviewer can disagree with a specific line instead of with a number.

Decision 4: trace answers, not just inputs

The most uncomfortable finding: the agent poisons itself. After recalling the fake email, it answered "Acme is now paid to 9174-6620-3381", and because agents retain their own answers, that answer went back into memory as a new, separate memory. Deleting the email alone would have left the agent still believing the lie.

So every retain records a source → memory edge, every recall records memory → answer, and every drafted action records answer → action. When something is flagged, the blast radius is a breadth-first walk from the poisoned source:

def blast_radius(node_id: str) -> list[tuple[str, int]]:
    """All descendants of node_id (including itself) in BFS order, with hop depth."""
    g = _digraph()
    if node_id not in g:
        return []
    depths = nx.single_source_shortest_path_length(g, node_id)
    return sorted(depths.items(), key=lambda kv: (kv[1], kv[0]))

For the bank-change email that walk returns six nodes: the email source, the email memory, the first answer, the memory the agent wrote from that answer, the second answer, and the blocked payment. Healing moves exactly those memories to a vault (kept for forensics, deletable only with human approval), leaves the other 21 memories alone, and replays every affected question against the cleaned memory:

Question Before After
Where do we pay Acme Supplies? "…their new Harbor Point Bank account 9174-6620-3381" "…the verified Northbridge Bank account 4021-7783-1190"
Pay Acme's invoice payment to 9174-6620-3381, blocked payment to 4021-7783-1190, drafted for review

The replay is what makes people trust the cleanup: you aren't asked to believe the agent is fixed, you're shown it.

What it catches in practice

  • A fake fact in plain sight, the polite bank-change email above: blocked at the gate, score 0.70, about three seconds from injection to block in my runs.
  • An instruction hidden from humans: a vendor web page with a CSS-hidden line telling the agent to add a second recipient to every payment. The agent followed it and drafted two payees; the gate blocked the unknown one. Score 0.91, so it was quarantined automatically without waiting for a click.
  • A data leak, not money: a fake "Internal Audit" email from a look-alike domain asking for every vendor's bank details. Blocked twice: the recipient isn't in the company directory, and a data-loss rule stops verified bank details leaving the company domain.
  • The same pattern in IT: a fake service-desk email claiming a Sales employee is now an admin. The helpdesk agent tried to send a colleague's password-reset link to the attacker's "recovery" address, and the gate blocked it.

It also has to stay quiet on normal content. I ingested ten real public sites, including news, docs, GitHub and a government site. Together they contained more than 200 hidden HTML snippets, and none were flagged. On a set of 32 labelled samples I wrote myself (21 benign, including hard negatives, and 11 attacks), the scanner caught 10 of 11 attacks with zero false positives. Those samples were also used while tuning, so treat that as a sanity check, not a benchmark.

Lessons learned

  1. Detection is a signal; the gate is the control. My one benchmark miss was a subtle fake fact ("settle invoices with our parent company instead") with no account number and no suspicious wording. The scanner scored it 0.22. That's why the real guarantee doesn't depend on the scanner: whatever payee the agent drafts, the gate compares the account with the system of record, and an unverified account is blocked. The flip side is also true: a lie that doesn't change a field the gate checks can get through, so the gate's coverage is your security boundary. Know exactly what it checks.

  2. Record provenance on every write, especially your own agent's writes. The agent's answer going back into memory was the most important path in the system, and it's the one most designs forget.

  3. LLM judges are useful and unreliable. A privilege-escalation sample passed in one run because the judge changed its mind. I replaced that check with two deterministic markers (role override and approval bypass) and kept the judge as one input among five.

  4. Keep untrusted text away from your own security model. MemoryGuard's judge reads attacker-written text, so it gets the same treatment as the agent: untrusted content is marked word by word as data (Microsoft's spotlighting technique), and account numbers and email addresses are swapped for placeholders before any third-party LLM sees them.

  5. Separate the memory layer from the security layer. Because Hindsight owns storage and recall, MemoryGuard only has to own provenance, lineage, gating and healing. Each half is simpler, and the security engine doesn't change when the agent does. If you're building on agent memory, the Hindsight docs on retain and recall are worth reading with this question in mind: where does every memory come from, and what would I have to undo if it were a lie?

Prompt injection isn't solved, and I don't claim to have solved it. What I can say is that when a lie gets into my agent's memory, I now know where it came from, what it touched, and how to undo exactly that.

title: SERP + News to Markdown for LLMs with the QuanticData API
description:
disclosure: I work on QuanticData.

Why this tutorial

Agents and local LLMs waste context on raw HTML. A better loop is: search → pick top links → read pages as clean Markdown. This post shows that loop with the QuanticData Data API (SERP + scrape) and the optional MCP server.

What you get

  • Google / Bing / DuckDuckGo search JSON (and news via search_type)
  • Page → Markdown from $0.0015 (render $0.0025)
  • SERP from $0.0009 ($0.90 per 1,000)
  • Failed calls are not billed; $2 free API usage per month
  • MCP: npx -y quanticdata-mcp or https://api.quanticdata.io/mcp

Register (no card): https://app.quanticdata.io/register
Docs: https://quanticdata.io/docs/ · https://quanticdata.io/llms.txt

Step 1 — SERP (web or news) 

import os, requests

API = "https://api.quanticdata.io/v1"
H = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['QUANTICDATA_API_KEY']}"}

serp = requests.post(f"{API}/scraper/serp", headers=H, json={
    "query": "web scraping API markdown LLM",
    "engine": "google",
    "search_type": "search",  # or "news"
    "country": "us",
    "lang": "en",
    "num": 10,
}, timeout=120).json()["payload"]

links = [row["link"] for row in serp.get("organic", [])[:5]]
print(links)

Step 2 — Scrape each URL to Markdown 

pages = []
for url in links:
    r = requests.post(f"{API}/scraper/extract", headers=H, json={
        "url": url,
        "format": "markdown",
        "contentMode": "smart",
    }, timeout=120).json()
    if r.get("type") == "response":
        pages.append({
            "url": url,
            "title": r["payload"].get("title"),
            "markdown": r["payload"]["content"],
        })

Step 3 — MCP (optional) 

QUANTICDATA_API_KEY=qd_live_… npx -y quanticdata-mcp
# hosted: https://api.quanticdata.io/mcp

Tools include scrape, search, search_and_read, map, crawl, batch.

Honest limits

  • Respect site ToS and robots where they apply; public pages / legitimate research.
  • List prices from QuanticData docs as of 2026-10; re-check https://quanticdata.io/pricing/ before budgeting.
  • No invented benchmarks — measure on your queries.

Wrap-up

Search JSON + Markdown pages is the smallest useful web toolset for agents. If you try the script, tell me what broke.

title: One Modelflare sign-in, 70+ models: the exact switching path inside AnyModelBot
description:
Hi, I'm Malachi, a co-developer of AnyModelBot. This post is only about how to see and switch models. No speed contest, no "model A beats model B" table, no invented latency numbers. If you want benchmarks, run your own prompts and read the public price list.

  • App: https://anymodel.bot/
  • Source (MIT): https://github.com/modelflare-ai/AnyModelBot

What you get after one sign-in

AnyModelBot is a local-first agent app (Windows / macOS / Linux, plus Docker). Models come from:

  1. Modelflare — one account, 70+ text / image / video models from many providers, pay per token, no AnyModelBot subscription; or
  2. Your own official API keys — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, xAI, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen, MiniMax, Mistral, etc. Those calls go straight to the provider. Image / video generation still needs Modelflare today.

You do not run models locally inside this app. Network is required for inference.

Step 0 — Install and open the console

Desktop: download an installer from Releases (verify with SHA256SUMS if you care).

Docker:

docker run -d --name amb -p 3600:3600 -v amb-data:/data ghcr.io/modelflare-ai/anymodel-bot
docker exec amb cat /data/ui-token
# open http://<host>:3600/?token=<token>
# do not expose 3600 to the public internet

Step 1 — Sign in once (or paste a key)

Desktop: first launch opens a browser to Modelflare. Approve, return to the app. No key copy-paste required for Modelflare.

Docker / server: browser callbacks do not reach the container. Sign in to Modelflare in any browser, then paste the landing link back into the app's first-run screen. Alternatively, paste an official provider API key and skip Modelflare for text models.

After connect, the model list fills automatically.

Step 2 — Read the picker before you click

Open the model button next to the composer (or Settings → Modelflare / Models).

For each row you should see, at least:

  • context length;
  • capability tags (vision / tools / reasoning, depending on the model);
  • a reference input/output price (from the public catalog — your bill is authoritative).

Also useful in Settings:

  • Balance, top-up link, low-balance reminders, last days of usage;
  • Per-bot budget keys when you want a spending ceiling on one persona;
  • Three API domains — modelflare.dev, origin.modelflare.dev, cf.modelflare.dev — compare response times yourself. AnyModelBot never auto-switches domains.

Step 3 — Switch for this conversation only (/model)

In the app or on a connected chat channel:

/model

Pick another model for this thread. Typical pattern:

  1. Draft or brainstorm on a cheaper default.
  2. /model → a stronger coding or long-context model for the hard part.
  3. /model back when you are done.

Memory files do not rewrite themselves just because the model changed. Scopes are team / bot / group, not "which provider answered."

Other slash commands that stay useful: /reset (conversation state as documented in-app); on channels, /bot <name> to move the thread to another bot (accounts are shared; each bot keeps its own memory and workspace).

Step 4 — Set a default per bot

Create or open a bot → set its default model. Persona + default model + workspace + memory is the unit you live with day to day.

Permission presets stay independent of the model: Read-only / Workspace (default) / Full access.

Step 5 — Point background chores at a cheaper model

Long chats use a context steward (compact or hand-off summary). Memory tidying and similar background work can use a separate, usually cheaper model than the one you chat with. That picker is not the same control as per-conversation /model or the bot default — set it once and forget it unless costs surprise you.

We will not claim a dollar amount saved. Watch the in-app usage panel for a few days and adjust.

Honest limits (so you do not hit them mid-demo)

  • No offline / local LLM runtime (no Ollama-style "models on disk" path in product scope).
  • No standalone mobile app; channels talk to a host that must stay on.
  • Feishu channel chat: DMs only for now. Telegram / Slack / Discord channel chats: DMs only for now.
  • Computer use on macOS is Beta.
  • Rules do not run while the host is asleep — use Docker if you need closer to always-on.
  • Official keys: text models yes; image/video generation still Modelflare-only.

Minimal checklist

  1. Install desktop or Docker; open console.
  2. Modelflare sign-in (paste landing link on Docker) or official API key.
  3. Open picker; read context + reference price; note balance.
  4. Chat → /model → harder question → /model back.
  5. Set bot default; optionally set background / hand-off model cheaper.
  6. Optionally try another API domain in Settings and compare — manually.

That is the whole path. One account (or your own keys), visible prices, conversation-level switch, bot-level default, background-level thrift.

  • https://anymodel.bot/
  • https://github.com/modelflare-ai/AnyModelBot

— Malachi, co-developer of AnyModelBot

title: My On-Call Agent Stopped Suggesting the Fix That Already Failed
description:
Hey everyone 👋,

Remember that time our database pool ran dry, and our AI assistant told us to increase the connection pool? We had already done that months earlier, and it only made things worse: Postgres hit max_connections, and every service slowed down. The real culprit was a nightly reconciliation job holding connections open.

The assistant wasn’t being dumb — it just had no memory of what happened before. Every debugging session started from zero, doomed to repeat the same mistakes.

So I built an on-call agent that remembers, using Hindsight as its memory layer. Here’s what we built together, what worked for us, and the challenges we hit along the way.

What We Built

An engineer pastes an alert into our little UI page. The agent recalls similar past incidents and human corrections, proposes a root cause and a fix, and shows which past memories it relied on. The engineer then marks the answer right or wrong and can log the real cause, the fix that actually worked, and any fix that failed. All of that gets written back into the memory bank.

The tech stack is intentionally simple: FastAPI, Groq for the LLM, and Hindsight for agent memory. One page of UI, with an obvious Memory ON/OFF toggle so we can compare fairly.

The loop is deliberately crisp:

  1. Recall similar incidents and corrections before answering.
  2. Answer, with recalled memories baked into the prompt.
  3. Retain the alert and the verdict, then later the human’s feedback.

Recall Before Every Verdict

All the Hindsight calls live in a single file, app/memory.py. Recall is a one-liner:

resp = self._client.recall(
    bank_id=bank_id, query=query, max_tokens=2048, budget="mid"
)
texts = [getattr(r, "text", str(r)) for r in (resp.results or [])][:limit]

Those memories go straight into the prompt, along with a few rules for using them. The rule I care about most:

- If a memory says a fix FAILED or was rejected, never suggest
  that fix again; say why you are avoiding it.

Memory is only useful if the model is told what to do with it. Without that instruction, recalled text is just background noise the model might ignore.

Retaining Corrections (Not Just Chats)

Early on, my first instinct was to store every alert and every answer. That was a trap: if the agent guesses wrong and you store the guess as fact, you’re teaching it a mistake.

So we built two kinds of retention. After triage, we store the alert and the verdict — explicitly tagged as not yet confirmed by an engineer. After feedback, we store the confirmed outcome:

parts.append(f"CONFIRMED ROOT CAUSE: {actual_cause}")
parts.append(f"FIX THAT WORKED: {actual_fix}")
parts.append(
    f"FIX THAT DID NOT WORK (do not suggest again "
    f"for this kind of alert): {failed_fix}"
)

Feedback goes under its own document_id, so it never overwrites the triage record. Storing failed fixes as first-class negative constraints turned out to be the most useful decision in our project.

Before vs. After: A Real Example

Take a connection-pool alert like HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms.

Memory OFF — The answer is the textbook one: "the pool is too small or connections are leaking," so you look at pool settings and raise the maximum. Reasonable, and exactly the advice that failed for us.

Memory ON, after one correction — We logged the real cause: a nightly reconciliation cron with no statement timeout. Terminating those sessions fixed it, and raising the pool did not. When a similar alert comes in next time (from a different service, even different wording), the recalled memories surface. It flags the cron as the likely cause and explicitly avoids the pool-size fix.

Nothing changed except memory — same model, same prompt template, same alert format. Just the ability to remember.

Watching the Learning Curve

I wanted to see this as a curve, not just a single example. We built 40 synthetic incidents across 8 recurring failure patterns, each with a root cause specific to our team (the cron job, a feature flag, a retention setting). These specifics matter — if the cause is guessable from the log line alone, a stateless model does well, and memory shows no benefit.

The demo runs incidents in waves: one per pattern per wave, running each alert twice — once with memory off and once with memory on. After every memory-on run, the "human" confirms the true cause, so Hindsight retains it.

Our results on 24 incidents (3 waves of 8 patterns):

Wave Memory OFF Memory ON
1 (cold start) 0/8 0/8
2 0/8 6/8
3 0/8 8/8

Wave 1 scores zero for both because there’s nothing to recall yet. From Wave 2, the memory-enabled agent begins recalling confirmed causes from earlier waves.

The Things That Bit Us

  • Recall quality depends on what you retain. Vague memories gave vague recalls. Writing each correction as a self-contained paragraph (alert, cause, fix, failed fix) worked far better than short notes.
  • Retain isn’t instant. Hindsight extracts facts when you retain, which takes seconds. An async option exists, but then recall might not see the newest memory immediately. In our demo, where we retain and recall back‑to‑back, that matters.
  • Reliability code is not optional. LLMs sometimes return malformed JSON. We validate output with Pydantic, retry three times, fall back to a second model, and finally return a clearly labeled safe default. Hindsight errors become warnings, so the agent keeps working with empty memory instead of crashing.
  • Keep the memory‑off path honest. In memory‑off mode, we skip recall and retain entirely. Otherwise, the baseline quietly learns too, and the comparison loses its integrity.

The Honest Limitations

The incidents are synthetic and generated from templates — real incident data would be messier. We scored answers with keyword-overlap against the true root cause, which is a crude proxy, not a real accuracy measure. 24 incidents is a small sample. This shows that the idea works, not that it’s ready to run your pager. A real deployment would need authentication, durable stats, and evaluation on your own incident history.

What I’d Tell You If You Build Something Similar

  1. Store outcomes, not chatter. Confirmed causes and failed fixes are worth far more than raw conversation.
  2. Label uncertainty. Mark unconfirmed guesses as unconfirmed so they never become "facts."
  3. Tell the model how to use memory. Recall alone does nothing without explicit rules.
  4. Build a memory‑off switch from day one. It’s the only honest way to know whether memory helps.
  5. Use data where the answer is team‑specific. That’s where memory truly earns its keep.

The code is on GitHub: Memory-Agent. To try the memory layer yourself, start with the Hindsight docs and the Hindsight repo.

Thanks to Code.in for the free coding credits.

title: Bounding Shutdown Retries By Attempt Count Strands The Transcript
description:
By Rokas Remeika. Published 24 October 2026.

When a voice agent worker shuts down, the framework gives it a fixed time window before killing the process. If your transcript persistence logic retries based on a maximum attempt count, the combined HTTP timeouts can exceed the shutdown window. The process dies mid-write, losing data that only existed in memory. The fix is to budget retries by wall clock. Give the operation a total time budget, and size it so the budget plus one maximum-length HTTP timeout remains strictly inside the framework's shutdown window.

Symptoms

  • Transcripts and end-of-call records go missing for calls that ended normally.
  • The write operation is attempted, but the logs stop mid-attempt with nothing after them.
  • The missing records look like flakiness, happening randomly across healthy instances.
  • The failure gets significantly worse whenever the downstream storage service is slow, which is exactly when the end-of-call record matters most for debugging.

What is actually happening

When a worker process finishes a call or receives a termination signal, the framework running it initiates a teardown phase. The framework gives your shutdown callback a fixed window to clean up and save state. After that window expires, the framework or the host operating system kills the process entirely.

Most persistence paths use standard retry libraries or custom loops that bound retries by attempt count. A network write might be configured to retry three times, with a ten-second HTTP timeout per attempt. This works perfectly during normal operation because the process will live indefinitely to see the attempts conclude.

During teardown, the process is living on a fixed timer. A persistence path that bounds its retries by attempt count has a worst case measured in attempts, not seconds. Three attempts at a ten-second HTTP timeout can block for thirty seconds. If your framework gives you a twenty-two second graceful shutdown window, you have an eight-second deficit.

The downstream service experiences a latency spike. Your first write attempt takes ten seconds and times out. Your second attempt takes ten seconds and times out. You start the third attempt. Two seconds later, the framework's shutdown timer expires. The process receives a SIGKILL while the write is in flight. The memory containing the final transcript is wiped, and data that existed only in that process is gone forever.

The bound on your retry logic is real, but it is denominated in the wrong unit. Attempt counts bound the number of failures, not the time. Shutdown windows bound the time, not the failures.

How to confirm it

  1. Filter your logs for the worker process ID that handled the lost call, starting from the shutdown signal. Expect to see the persistence attempt begin, followed by a hard stop with no subsequent log lines indicating success or failure.
  2. Measure the timestamp gap between the shutdown signal and the final log line of the process. Expect this gap to match your framework's exact graceful shutdown timeout limit, proving the process was forcefully killed.
  3. Check the downstream storage service logs for the exact minute the call ended. Expect elevated latency or HTTP gateway timeouts that pushed the write duration past its normal baseline, triggering your retry loop.
  4. Compare the recorded wall-clock duration of the shutdown callback directly against the framework window in your call event logs. Expect the duration to reach the framework shutdown window limit without any subsequent log indicating completion.

How it works

The fix is to budget the teardown persistence by wall clock instead of attempt count. You give the whole operation a total time budget, give each attempt its own HTTP timeout, and size them so that the budget plus one maximum-duration in-flight attempt still lands safely inside the shutdown window.

Here is the sizing I run in production. The framework provides a 22-second shutdown await window. I give the end-of-call record write an 8-second total wall-clock budget. I give the HTTP client a 10-second per-attempt timeout.

If the storage backend is struggling, the loop checks the wall clock. As long as the elapsed time is under 8 seconds, it fires another HTTP request. The worst-case scenario is an attempt starting right before the 8-second budget expires. That final attempt is allowed to block for its full 10-second timeout. The total time elapsed before the HTTP client times out and returns control to the loop is just under 18 seconds.

That 18-second worst case fits cleanly against the 22-second shutdown await the framework gives me. The process has time to observe the final failure, log it cleanly, and exit on its own terms before the operating system brings the hammer down.

The three numbers in that example are not the transferable part. The inequality is the transferable part: (total_budget + per_attempt_timeout) < framework_shutdown_window.

You must write that exact arithmetic in a comment next to the constants in your code. The constraint is completely invisible from any one constant on its own. The next person to review the code will see an 8-second budget, decide it is too tight for a slow backend, raise it, and unknowingly break the system. They will not know what they broke because the increased budget still looks smaller than the 22-second shutdown window on its own. They will only find out when transcripts start vanishing again.

What I would check first

  1. Check if the session was ended by a function tool calling a teardown routine rather than a normal caller hangup. A tool tearing down the session immediately can cut off final audio and disrupt the lifecycle sequence; if this is the case, arming a pending closure fixes it, as detailed in /blog/voice-agent-end-call-tool-truncates-the-final-sentence-or-loses-the-callers-last/.
  2. Check the HTTP response codes returned by the downstream API just before the data loss. An HTTP 400 Bad Request indicates a malformed payload that failed instantly, ruling out timeout starvation. If the downstream storage service returned an HTTP gateway error, the request completed over the network rather than being terminated mid-flight.
  3. Check whether the worker process suffered an unexpected crash or host termination prior to the shutdown callback running. Check process supervisor logs to verify whether the process ran until the framework graceful shutdown timer expired.

Instrumenting the teardown path

Fixing the timeouts stops the data loss, but you need instrumentation to prove the fix holds over time. A teardown sequence is invisible to standard request tracing because the client has already disconnected.

I record the shutdown callback wall-clock duration per call and emit it as a structured log event. This allows me to query the duration and compare it against the framework's window across the entire fleet. If the persistence operation starts creeping closer to the 18-second worst case, I can see the degradation before it starts dropping records.

Additionally, give an incomplete transcript write its own named failure code on the call's end event. Do not let it land as a generic internal error. When a failure code specifically names the persistence timeout on the end event, you isolate a wall-clock write failure immediately instead of investigating it as a generic error.

Generalizing the pattern

This failure mode generalises to every teardown path that performs a network write. Whether you are flushing metrics, saving an LLM context window, or writing billing records, the dynamics are identical.

Anything you write at teardown that exists nowhere else in the system needs a wall-clock budget derived directly from the window you were given.

Common questions

Why do my agent transcripts randomly go missing on call end?

Your persistence logic is likely taking longer than the graceful shutdown window provided by the framework. When the retry loop exceeds this timer, the process is forcefully killed, and the in-memory transcript is destroyed before it can be saved.

How long do I have in a shutdown hook before SIGKILL?

It depends entirely on your framework or container orchestrator. You must check the specific graceful shutdown timeout configured in your environment.

Should I use a background queue for transcript persistence?

Offloading persistence to a separate queue still requires a network write before the worker process is killed. However, you still have to successfully write the payload to the queue during the shutdown window, so the wall-clock constraint applies to the queue publisher as well.

Why does setting my HTTP retry count lower not fix the issue?

A low attempt count still relies on the per-attempt HTTP timeout. If a single HTTP timeout can exceed the framework shutdown window, lowering the attempt count still leaves the write vulnerable to being killed mid-flight.

Canonical URL: https://www.dreamchasers.lt/blog/bounding-shutdown-retries-by-attempt-count-strands-the-transcript

title: Startup Interview: How Startups Build Autonomous Agents
description:
Bottom line: fund graduated autonomy through measured pilots. Don't fund autonomous anything on startup anecdotes.

This piece comes out of a DBA research project on autonomous AI in management consulting, but the engineering lessons transfer directly. It does not tell you how to build an agent. It tells you how to decide how much autonomy to grant, to which tasks, under what controls, and how to know whether it paid off.

One caveat up front: the published evidence available to me does not report revenue, conversion or a before-and-after productivity result for any startup-built agent. Startups give us design patterns. Larger studies give us the risk and cost reality. Treat everything below accordingly.

TL;DR

  1. Value is task-specific. In my qualitative reading, AI assistance helps on tasks a model handles well and can mislead just beyond them. That's an observation, not a measured result.
  2. Measure reliability over repeated runs, not single attempts. An agent that succeeds once may fail the next time. That's a recommendation, not a finding.
  3. Measure oversight cost explicitly: human review, rework, incident handling. Separately, falling token prices have not lowered AI bills [15].
  4. The ask: one bounded 90-day pilot in shadow mode, with a named owner, a baseline, and a pre-agreed go/no-go review.

A Note on Sources

The startup material I draw on is qualitative background that I couldn't tie to a verifiable source, so I cite no figures or study details. It covers how founders delegate tasks to AI and supervise output, and how one venture used AI for problem discovery, synthetic customer interviews and competitive analysis. It describes practice, not performance, and mostly concerns startups using AI for innovation work, not engineering agent architectures.

"Interview" in the title refers to the research method of the startup studies discussed, not conversations conducted for this article.

Preconditions (Check These Before You Build)

The advice below assumes:

  • The target process is documented and its outputs can be scored.
  • An executive sponsor is named.
  • Reviewer capacity exists to check agent work.
  • Data-handling terms with model vendors are agreed.

A small team may satisfy these quickly; a large org may need a governance function first.

Pattern 1: Risk-Sort Before You Feasibility-Sort

Founders don't delegate uniformly. The founder-interview literature describes differing patterns of delegation and control, varying in how agency is split between human and machine. A reasonable reading: mature early adopters sort work by risk before they sort it by technical feasibility. Drafting and exploration move freely to the machine; consequential commitments stay with a person.

The transferable idea is a simple routing rule. Before asking "can an agent do this?", ask: what happens if it's confidently wrong, and who would notice?

Task profile Example Autonomy level
Reversible, low stakes Desk research drafts, meeting summaries Delegate to agent, spot-check
Reviewable, medium stakes Market sizing, benchmark comparisons Agent drafts, human approves before release
Consequential or irreversible Client recommendations, commitments, pricing Human-only, agent as support

In code terms, this is a policy layer sitting in front of your agent's action executor:

from enum import Enum

class Autonomy(Enum):
    AUTO_WITH_SPOT_CHECK = 1
    HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED = 2
    HUMAN_ONLY = 3

POLICY = {
    "summarize_meeting": Autonomy.AUTO_WITH_SPOT_CHECK,
    "benchmark_comparison": Autonomy.HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED,
    "client_recommendation": Autonomy.HUMAN_ONLY,
}

def route(task_type: str) -> Autonomy:
    # Default-deny: unknown task types get the most restrictive level
    return POLICY.get(task_type, Autonomy.HUMAN_ONLY)

The default-deny line matters. New task types should earn autonomy, not inherit it.

Pattern 2: Model Output Is a Hypothesis, Not an Oracle

The longitudinal venture case in the literature is instructive. The team used AI to explore a market problem, generated synthetic customers and interviewers to probe it, analyzed competitors, and built a reusable prompt playbook.

The lesson is as cautionary as it is enthusiastic: treat model outputs as provisional hypotheses and keep outside challenge in the loop, so the team doesn't slip into treating the model as an oracle. Synthetic users are fast and cheap, but real prospects, observed behavior and willingness-to-pay tests remain the proof.

Architecturally, that suggests an explicit validation stage between "agent produced a claim" and "claim drives an action."

Where Autonomy Helps and Where It Hurts

My qualitative reading is that AI assistance helps on tasks a model handles well and can mislead just beyond them. Autonomy magnifies this: an agent acting on a flawed conclusion converts a wrong answer into a wrong action.

One plausible value channel, offered as a hypothesis rather than a finding, is faster ramp-up of junior staff, with headcount reduction coming later if at all. Test it by tracking performance by experience level.

Reliability and the Multi-Agent Question

Startups often reach for multi-agent designs because specialization sounds like progress. A more sober view is warranted. As a hypothesis for the pilot rather than a finding, more agents are not inherently more capable. Each plausibly adds coordination overhead and another place for errors to cascade, so each must earn its place through measurable specialization or verification value.

Measure repeated-run reliability, not average accuracy

For a deliverable that must be reproducible and defensible, average accuracy is the wrong metric. The right one is how often the agent gets the same case right every time.

def repeated_run_reliability(agent, cases, k=4):
    """Fraction of cases the agent gets right on ALL k runs."""
    all_correct = 0
    for case in cases:
        results = [agent.run(case) == case.expected for _ in range(k)]
        if all(results):
            all_correct += 1
    return all_correct / len(cases)

An agent with 90% single-run accuracy can have much lower all-k-runs reliability. Evaluate that number, and treat it as my recommendation, not a published benchmark.

Test the architecture before you build it

Before approving a multi-agent build, compare it against two baselines:

  • a single instrumented agent, and
  • a fixed rule-based workflow.

Specialization has to be demonstrated, not assumed.

Oversight, Not Tokens

Cost debates fixate on model pricing, yet falling token prices have not lowered AI bills [15]. A question worth measuring (this is my own argument, not a cited finding): how much human review, rework and incident handling does each accepted output require? How large that share is remains an open empirical matter for the pilot.

The unit that belongs in a business case is cost per accepted, completed deliverable:

cost_per_accepted =
  (build + run + human_review + rework + incident_reserve) / accepted_outputs

A purely invented illustration

In any single currency, with build cost excluded or amortized. Suppose a report costs 40 reviewer-hours and rework today, at 100/hour, so 4,000 per accepted report. An agent drafts it for 600 in run cost, yet reviewers still need 20 hours (2,000), rework adds 400, and an incident reserve adds 300.

Total: 3,300, a saving of about 17.5%. (Invented, not a benchmark.) If review time shrinks less than expected, the case can vanish entirely. Compare against your baseline, not another vendor's quote.

Adoption does not equal value capture. Usage, queries and licenses are adoption metrics; they say little about value. That's why I put the baseline and workflow-redesign steps ahead of tool choice.

Governance Mapping: ISO/IEC 42001 and 27001

Two standards do the most work here. (ISO/IEC 20700 and 21500 matter for consulting quality and delivery but would dilute focus.)

ISO/IEC 42001 (AI management system) ISO/IEC 27001 (information security)
Management intent Defined accountability for AI risk; a repeatable way to show control to clients, insurers, regulators Client confidentiality is the currency; tool-enabled agents enlarge the attack surface
Minimum practices Named owner per agent; use-case risk classification; agent inventory; monitoring and incident handling Least-privilege tool permissions; supplier review; logging of agent actions; retention rules
Evidence Approved AI policy, risk register, release checklist Access-control records, supplier assessments
KPI Share of production agents with documented risk class and owner Unauthorized agent actions (target zero for critical cases)
Risk and mitigation Agents drifting into unapproved uses; release gates tied to the inventory Confidential data leaking via a vendor model; contractual limits and tested data-flow controls

This maps cleanly onto staged rollout:

  • Shadow mode requires the risk register and a named owner.
  • Approval-gated mode requires access-control records and action logging.
  • Limited autonomy requires a tested incident process.

The 90-Day Pilot Playbook

Step 1: Baseline the work

Measure cost per accepted deliverable, cycle time, rework and quality on one bounded workflow, using 30-50 representative historical cases. Without a baseline, any claim of improvement is anecdote. This step also sizes the pilot budget and reviewer hours.

Step 2: Name a governance owner

Assign accountability and classify the use case under ISO/IEC 42001 before any build.

Step 3: Run the staged pilot

Over roughly 90 days: baseline, then shadow mode (the agent drafts while humans still do the work and compare), then approval-gated actions for reversible tasks only.

Illustrative go/no-go thresholds, to be calibrated to your context:

  • At least 15% lower completed-work cost
  • Quality non-inferior on every critical dimension
  • A pre-agreed pass rate across four repeated runs
  • Zero critical unauthorized actions

After the pilot

  • Test the architecture (single agent vs. rule-based vs. multi-agent) before approving a multi-agent build.
  • Promote autonomy in stages. Expand only as each stage clears its gate: bounded internal use first, with central logging, monitoring and attack testing before any external or client-facing use.

Ongoing

  • Budget for oversight. Put reviewer time and escalation rates in the case from day one.
  • Preserve portability. Keep prompts, business rules, evaluation sets and tool definitions separate from any one provider's proprietary layer.
  • Redesign the workflow. Change decision rights, handoffs and controls, not just tool access, so usage turns into results.
  • Protect junior learning. Track whether agents accelerate or erode skill development.

Conclusion

Startups show how to organize autonomy: sort work by risk, treat model output as hypothesis, keep external challenge in the loop. They don't yet show that autonomy pays. What I can offer beyond that is a set of recommendations, not proof.

Expect gains where a model is competent and errors just beyond it. Test reliability over repeated runs rather than relying on a single success. Measure oversight as a cost; don't assume it away.

Teams that baseline their work, stage autonomy, measure reliability and embed governance through ISO/IEC 42001 and 27001 can scale agents where they help and withdraw them where they hurt. Teams that skip these steps risk paying twice: once for the tool, and again for the errors it makes with confidence.

Two limits deserve plain statement. The startup studies describe practice, not performance, and the conceptual framework behind this research project remains unvalidated. Both are gaps to close with measured evidence.

Next step: authorize one bounded 90-day pilot, from baseline through shadow mode to approval-gated actions, with a named owner and a pre-agreed go/no-go review.

The cited sources are listed in the full article: https://auranom.ai/startup-interview-how-startups-build-autonomous-agents/

title: Avec osFoundry Operator, un agent pilote l'application et chaque action est consignée
description:
« Lesquels de mes endpoints GPU sont encore facturés ? » La question est simple, mais y répondre oblige souvent à passer par trois écrans, à relever les chiffres, puis à revenir dans le chat pour les recopier. Confier ça à un agent IA a l'air séduisant, jusqu'au moment où l'on se demande ce qu'il a vraiment cliqué. osFoundry Operator est conçu autour de cette question : l'agent travaille dans un volet en direct de l'application, juste à côté de la conversation, et chacune de ses actions est notée.

Une conversation à côté d'un volet en direct de l'application

osFoundry est une application de bureau qui réunit chat, agents, fichiers et outils dans une seule fenêtre. Operator découpe l'écran en trois. À gauche, la liste des sessions Operator. Au centre, la conversation. À droite, un volet de dashboard en direct : une vraie copie de l'application osFoundry, dans laquelle Operator ouvre des écrans. Au-dessus du volet, on voit sur quel écran il se trouve (ici Dashboard /models/endpoints), avec les raccourcis Home et Project, Reload dashboard et Open in a new window. Le séparateur se fait glisser pour donner plus de place au volet.

Dans cet exemple, Sammy demande quels endpoints GPU sont facturés. Operator ouvre Endpoints dans le volet, relit les cartes et répond dans le chat : un endpoint est Active à 1,45 $/h et a déjà coûté 7,54 $, un autre est encore en Creating et a commencé à être facturé, et un dernier est Stopped. La réponse vient de l'écran qu'il vient d'ouvrir, et cet écran reste là pour vérifier. Il propose aussi d'arrêter l'endpoint actif, en précisant qu'il demandera avant d'appuyer sur Stop.

La barre d'activité : ce qu'Operator a réellement fait

Sous le volet, une fine barre indique si Operator est inactif ou au travail, et quand il a agi pour la dernière fois. Une fois ouverte, le Log liste toutes les actions qu'Operator a effectuées dans ce volet, de la plus récente à la plus ancienne : ici deux navigations, vers Models puis vers Endpoints, chacune marquée « surface changed, read back ». Le log appartient à la session, donc chaque session Operator garde sa propre trace. Copy as report copie tout le log en texte, pour un ticket ou un collègue, et Clear le vide.

C'est ce qui rend Operator facile à croire. Pas besoin de se fier à un résumé de ce que l'agent dit avoir fait : le log et le volet le montrent.

Configurer osFoundry avec Operator

La deuxième session de l'exemple s'appelle « Set up osFoundry ». Ici, la barre a un second onglet, Setup, avec une checklist qui lit l'état réel de l'application plutôt que ce qu'Operator a rapporté : une clé de fournisseur, un modèle de secours, le runtime sur l'appareil, le modèle d'embeddings local et le rôle de router. Dans l'exemple, trois étapes sur cinq sont faites, et pour chaque étape restante la checklist explique pourquoi (par exemple « Downloaded, but not selected for local memory yet »).

Chaque étape restante a deux liens. Ask Operator place dans la zone de message une demande pour cette seule étape, et c'est vous qui appuyez sur Send. Not now masque l'étape dans cette session, sans la marquer comme faite. Une règle ne bouge pas : une étape qui demande une clé d'API n'est jamais traitée dans le chat. Operator ouvre la boîte de dialogue des réglages, et vous y saisissez la clé vous-même.

Si vous essayez de quitter pendant qu'Operator travaille encore, il vous prévient que l'exécution continue en arrière-plan et consomme toujours des crédits, mais qu'elle perd le volet qu'elle pilotait : sa prochaine étape sur cet écran échouera. Vous pouvez rester, ou partir quand même. Stop arrête ce qu'Operator est en train de faire.

Le navigateur intégré, avec un panneau compagnon

Operator travaille à l'intérieur d'osFoundry. Pour les pages web, il y a le navigateur intégré, qui garde la page à côté des outils qui travaillent dessus. Le panneau de gauche propose Search, Opened, Bookmark, Read Later et History. Au centre, la page elle-même, avec onglets, barre d'adresse et zoom. À droite, le panneau compagnon, avec les onglets Maestro, Page, Links et Actions.

L'onglet Page lit la page en direct et l'affiche en texte propre, en vue Rendered ou en Markdown, et Read again le rafraîchit quand la page change. Si un modèle est attribué au rôle Summarizer, il peut aussi résumer la page. L'onglet Links liste les liens extraits de la page avec leurs URL, pour suivre ceux qui comptent sans les chercher dans la mise en page. Maestro, l'assistant principal d'osFoundry, peut travailler à côté de la page dans ce même panneau.

Cas d'usage : vérifier les dépenses en fin de journée

Avant de se déconnecter, Sammy ouvre Operator et demande quels endpoints sont encore facturés. Operator ouvre l'écran Endpoints dans le volet et les liste, et le log d'activité montre les deux écrans visités. Un endpoint tourne à vide, alors Sammy demande à Operator de l'arrêter. Operator demande d'abord confirmation, puis l'arrête, et l'arrêt apparaît dans le log et sur la carte dans le volet. Le lendemain matin, Sammy copie le log sous forme de rapport dans le fil de l'équipe consacré aux coûts.

Les premières questions qu'on pose

Operator clique-t-il sans demander ?
Operator travaille dans son propre volet et consigne chaque action qu'il y effectue. Dans l'exemple, il demande avant d'arrêter un endpoint, et les étapes qui nécessitent un secret ne se font jamais dans le chat : vous saisissez la clé dans la boîte de dialogue des réglages.

Où voir ce qu'il a fait ?
Dans la barre d'activité sous le volet. Le Log liste chaque action avec son heure et l'écran ouvert, et Copy as report le copie en texte.

Operator, c'est la même chose que le navigateur intégré ?
Non. Operator pilote l'application osFoundry elle-même dans un volet en direct. Le navigateur intégré sert aux pages web, avec un panneau compagnon qui lit la page, extrait les liens et laisse Maestro travailler à côté.

Est-ce gratuit ?
osFoundry est gratuit sur votre propre appareil. Le travail exécuté sur les serveurs d'osFoundry et les appels de modèles passant par osFoundry consomment des crédits.

L'application de bureau se télécharge gratuitement sur osfoundry.io/fr/download.

title: Correlating Telegram AI-writer replies without confusing correlation for correctness
description:
A Telegram-based writing workflow has an awkward boundary: the content engine sends a text file to a separate AI writer, then receives one or more messages back. The listener needs to know when those messages belong to a particular request and when it can stop waiting.

The implementation in llm.py uses request IDs, a terminator, buffering and a silence fallback. It also serializes model calls with an asyncio.Lock. These choices solve a narrow coordination problem. They do not validate the returned prose.

The request envelope

Every request begins with a JSON line containing three fields:

{"request_id":"…","stage":"…","schema_version":1}

The engine generates a short request ID and asks the writer to put [END:<request_id>] on the last line. The stage identifies which writing step is running; the schema version labels the envelope format. The code sends the prompt as a .txt file to @matpibot through the owner’s Telegram client.

On the receiving side, a NewMessage listener buffers messages from the configured bot account. It checks each buffer for the current request ID. If the joined text contains the exact end marker, the marker is removed and the waiting future resolves immediately.

This is correlation, not authentication or content validation. The ID lets the engine connect a reply to a pending task under the expected chat/user setup. It says nothing about whether research was adequate, whether the response is complete, or whether its statements are true.

Why buffer fragments?

A reply can arrive as several Telegram messages, including fragments that split text mid-line. The listener stores messages with timestamps and whether each includes the request ID. _matpibot_join retains ID-bearing messages and nearby id-less messages in the same burst, then concatenates fragments without inserting a newline inside a burst. Separate bursts are joined with a newline.

There is a subtle detail in the silence path: an ID-bearing message without the terminator schedules a timer. Every later matching message cancels and resets that timer. If the writer keeps sending fragments, the listener waits for the stream to go quiet rather than resolving after a fixed interval from the first message.

When the timer fires, it resolves the future with the buffered text even though the terminator never arrived. In this implementation, SILENCE_SECONDS is 15 seconds. That fallback is useful when the writer forgets the marker, but it is still a heuristic: silence is not proof that the writer intended to finish.

One request at a time

call_via_matpibot creates an asyncio.Lock and enters it before registering the pending future, sending the file and waiting for the answer. The lock is released only when the function exits. Consequently, calls through this path are single-flight: a second call waits for the first send-and-wait operation to finish.

That design avoids overlapping pending conversations through this doorway, making the response-matching story simpler. It trades throughput for simpler coordination. A slow writer blocks later requests even if their prompts are unrelated.

The normal timeout defaults to 600 seconds. On timeout, the future is shielded rather than cancelled and the code waits for a further 60 seconds for a late reply. If that grace period expires, the call returns an empty LLMReply carrying matpibot_timeout. A missing client, send exception and timeout are represented as distinct error states. There is no fallback to another model call path.

State machine sketch 

idle
  └─ acquire lock; register future and buffer
       └─ send request file
            ├─ matching joined END marker → return answer
            ├─ matching ID, no END → reset 15s silence timer
            │    └─ silence expires → return buffered answer (fallback)
            └─ 600s timeout → wait up to 60s more for late answer
                 └─ still nothing → return timeout error
  └─ remove pending state, cancel timer, delete temporary request file

Review the protocol separately from editorial quality

The factory’s README describes a broader pipeline: source cards in an “Ideas” topic, a human selects the channel and platforms, the AI writer researches and drafts, then a preview arrives in a “Posts” topic. A person must press “Publish”; otherwise nothing is published. Rewrites, media replacement and cancellation are separate preview actions.

That human review remains necessary even when the transport protocol works perfectly. An ID can be correct while a fact is wrong. A terminator can arrive while the answer is weak. A silence fallback can return buffered text that deserves another review.

For the surrounding architecture, see my AI content factory walkthrough. If you are adapting the handoff, exercise the branches in a safe test setup: correct marker, omitted marker followed by silence, fragmented marker, late answer and timeout. Treat those as tests to run, not claims that this article has executed them. Then test the human path independently: a draft should require an explicit publish action, and cancellation should stay a cancellation.

title: Why for-agents.json and a public corpus beat another landing page
description:
Daily LuisCore syndication · 2026-11-10 · angle agent-discovery-thesis

Autonomous agents do not read marketing sites — they fetch JSON. LuisCore's discovery thesis is citation-led: one bootstrap manifest, a Zenodo-backed corpus, and measurable agent-discovery proof.

Thesis: agents discover infrastructure, they do not read pitch decks

The agentic web needs one canonical origin agents can curl on first contact. LuisCore publishes for-agents.json — bootstrap manifest with citations, sameAs, MCP entry, ontology glossary, Zenodo DOIs, and 13,236+ Q&A rows.

Why public corpus matters

LLMs cite what they can retrieve. A private wiki behind SSO does not propagate. The LLM Discovery Corpus is generated at build time, mirrored to Zenodo, and indexed in llms.txt so models quote one canonical definition of SPFD, Chorus Field, and Protocol Watch — not five conflicting blog posts.

  • Corpus JSON: https://luiscore.com/api/public/questions-corpus.json
  • Zenodo dataset: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14207466

Citation-led round

When third-party agents cite LuisCore without being asked, that is measurable citation gravity — not vanity metrics. Discovery graph and agent-discovery-proof publish the receipts.

  • Discovery graph: https://luiscore.com/api/public/discovery-graph.json
  • Agent discovery proof: https://luiscore.com/agent-discovery-proof.json

Bootstrap in three curls 

curl -s https://luiscore.com/for-agents.json | jq .
curl -s https://luiscore.com/llms.txt | head
curl -s https://luiscore.com/mcp.json | jq .tools

Cite and verify

  • Agent bootstrap: for-agents.json
  • Zenodo preprint: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14207411
  • Zenodo corpus: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14207466

Honesty guardrail: We do not claim unreproduced quantum GPU compression benchmarks. Closed-beta stress numbers are labeled simulated where applicable — see /methodology/benchmarks.

LuisCore in one sentence

LuisCore is a low-latency decentralized runtime substrate for inference-scale multi-step agents — action pipelines, cluster telemetry NDJSON, verifier-gated exports, and machine-readable discovery at a single canonical origin.
