title: Meta's Muse Ember Does Haiku's Job for a Third of the Cost — Here's the Catch
description:
Nothing here is sponsored — no affiliate links on this page. This breaking article is not the daily buyer-intent post. Facts below come from the sources listed at the end, checked 10 November 2026. We have not tested this hands-on, and nothing here is a hands-on finding.

Meta launched Muse Ember on November 9, 2026 — its smallest and most efficient Muse model, and the clearest sign yet of where the AI industry is heading: not one giant model for everything, but a team of models, with the cheap one doing the bulk of the work. Ember is built for the repetitive jobs AI agents do all day — tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, long-document parsing. The headline number: $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, with an Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score of 36 — the same as Claude Haiku 5.5 at maximum reasoning, at about a third of the cost per task.

I have not run Ember yet — nobody outside Meta's early partners had access before yesterday — and this article is built from Meta's announcement and the SiliconANGLE, PYMNTS and Unite.AI coverage of it, checked 10 November 2026. Where a claim is Meta's or Artificial Analysis's, I'll say so, because a launch-day benchmark is a vendor claim, not an independent result.

How we put this together

We verified the story against Meta's announcement ("Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember"), SiliconANGLE's coverage and PYMNTS' coverage, all 9 November 2026, plus Unite.AI and CellCog. We have not used Ember hands-on, so nothing here is a hands-on finding. Where a figure comes from Meta or Artificial Analysis — most importantly the benchmark scores and the cost-per-task comparison — we say so plainly instead of presenting it as an independent result.

Verdict: Ember is not the model you reach for when a problem is hard. It is the model you reach for when a problem is repeated a thousand times a day. The price is genuinely cheap — ten cents per million input tokens is the kind of number that changes what you can afford to automate — and the Haiku-matching score, if it holds up in independent testing, makes it a serious option for agent workloads. But the catch matters: it is API-only, you cannot download it, and every performance number so far comes from Meta or from a benchmark Meta points to. Try it on your cheapest, highest-volume workload first. That is where Ember either earns its place or does not.

What actually launched

Muse Ember, model ID muse-ember-1.0, is live now on the Meta Model API and in Muse Code. It is also listed on OpenRouter, and on Google Cloud (through the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform) and Oracle Cloud. The early partners Meta named — Box, Cline, Oracle, Cloudflare and You.com — tell you who the target customer is: companies running agents at scale, where the model gets called thousands of times a day and the bill is the bottleneck.

The spec sheet is built for volume, not for showpiece reasoning. A 1M-token context window, up to 512K output tokens, multimodal input (text, images, audio and video), and support for the Responses API. Meta's framing is blunt: "Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume." Wonder is the bigger model that figures out what to do; Ember is the one that does the doing, over and over, cheaply.

There is one more detail worth noting: Ember is the first model trained using Muse Wonder Full. Meta is now using its own flagship model to build its smaller ones — a production line, not a one-off launch.

What it costs

The pricing is the whole point of this model, so here it is plainly: $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.004 per million cached input tokens, and $0.50 per million output tokens. Cached input at four-tenths of a cent per million tokens is effectively free for the repeated prompts agents send — system prompts, retrieved context, the same instructions on every call. That is the pricing shape of a model designed to be called constantly: the per-call cost is so low that the limiting factor becomes your own infrastructure, not the model bill.

For comparison, Meta's own numbers put Ember's cost per task at $0.14 against Claude Haiku 5.5's $0.41 — about a third. And against the other Muse model in the family, Muse Spark 1.3 scores 37 on the same index but costs $2.39 per task, roughly seventeen times Ember's. Spark is the smarter model; Ember is the cheaper one. That is the trade, stated honestly.

How it stacks up — and why to read the numbers carefully

On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Ember scores 36. Claude Haiku 5.5, at maximum reasoning, also scores 36. Meta says Ember beats GPT-6 Luna at every reasoning setting. And Muse Spark 1.3, the bigger sibling, scores 37 at $2.39 per task.

Read that table the right way round. Ember matching Haiku at a third of the cost per task is a real claim, and if independent testing confirms it, it is a genuine shift in the economics of agent workloads. But every number in that paragraph comes from Meta or from Artificial Analysis — not from independent hands-on testing, and not from us. Benchmarks on launch day are a press release with a chart attached. The honest move is to treat the score as a reason to try Ember on a real workload, not as a settled fact about which model is better.

There is also a structural point worth making. A score of 36 puts Ember in the same tier as Haiku 5.5 on this index — it does not make it a frontier reasoning model. Nobody at Meta is claiming it is. The pitch is volume, not brilliance: a model good enough for the routine work, cheap enough to run constantly.

When Ember is the right pick — and when it is not

Ember makes sense wherever the same kind of call happens over and over: routing a request to the right tool, extracting structured data from documents, running coding subtasks inside a larger agent workflow, parsing long documents, making tool calls in a loop. If you are building agents that do hundreds or thousands of small jobs a day, the per-call price is the feature that matters most — and Ember's price is low enough to change which jobs are worth automating at all.

It is the wrong pick when the task is genuinely hard: novel reasoning, ambiguous problems, work where a wrong answer is expensive. That is what the bigger models are for — Muse Wonder in Meta's own framing, or Opus-class models from other providers. The sensible architecture, and the one Meta is openly selling, is a team: Wonder plans, Ember handles the volume. Using Ember for everything would be the cheap way to get the wrong answer faster; using a flagship model for every routine call is the expensive way to get the right answer slowly.

If you already run agents on Haiku 5.5 or a similar small model, the honest test costs almost nothing: point Ember at your highest-volume, lowest-stakes workload — the one where the output is checked by a human or by a bigger model downstream — and compare the bill and the failure rate over a week. That is the only benchmark that matters for your use case.

The catch, stated plainly

  • Every performance claim is Meta's or Artificial Analysis's. The score of 36, the cost-per-task comparison, the claim of beating GPT-6 Luna at every reasoning setting — all vendor-reported or benchmark-provider figures, none independently replicated yet. Treat them as a reason to try the model, not as a settled fact.
  • API-only — you cannot download it. Meta has not released the weights, and no parameter count has been disclosed. If you need to run a model locally, self-host it, or fine-tune it on your own hardware, Ember is not an option. This is a rental, not a purchase.
  • It is a volume worker, not a thinker. A score of 36 is Haiku-tier, not frontier-tier. The cheap price is the point; do not mistake it for a model that replaces your biggest model on hard problems.
  • The ecosystem lock-in is real. Ember lives on the Meta Model API, Muse Code, OpenRouter, Google Cloud and Oracle Cloud. The cached-input price of $0.004 per million tokens is a strong reason to build on Meta's API — and a strong reason to check what happens to your costs if you ever want to leave it.

The bottom line

Muse Ember is the least glamorous kind of launch and possibly the most consequential: a model that is not trying to be the smartest, only the cheapest good-enough option for work that repeats all day. If the Haiku-matching score holds up outside Meta's own testing, the economics of agent workloads shift — not because Ember is brilliant, but because at $0.10 per million input tokens, a whole class of automation that was too expensive to run becomes worth running.

The test is cheap and the verdict is yours to reach in a week: give Ember your highest-volume, lowest-stakes workload and watch the bill and the failure rate. If both stay low, you have found your volume worker.

Would you trust a $0.10-per-million-token model with your highest-volume agent workload — or wait for independent benchmarks first?

Sources: Meta announcement — "Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember" (9 November 2026); SiliconANGLE (9 November 2026); PYMNTS (9 November 2026); Unite.AI (9 November 2026); CellCog. All capability, benchmark and pricing claims are Meta's or Artificial Analysis's, stated as such. No hands-on testing was performed for this article. This breaking article is not the daily buyer-intent post, and it contains no affiliate links.

title: The human clicked Approve. The agent applied it to a different question.
description:
LangGraph just gave every interrupt its own id and added a mode that refuses stale answers. Here is the bug that closes.

The human clicked Approve. The agent applied it to a different question.

On 5 November 2026, langgraph 1.2.20 shipped two release-note lines that read like plumbing:

give each interrupt() in a task its own id

add a strict resume mode that refuses stale interrupt answers

They are not plumbing. They are a correctness fix for one of the nastiest failure shapes in human-in-the-loop systems.

The shape of the bug

An agent pauses to ask a human something. In LangGraph that pause is an interrupt(). The run suspends, the question goes to a person, and the answer comes back later — four minutes later, forty minutes later, tomorrow morning.

"Later" is where the trouble lives. Between the question and the answer, the run can be retried, re-planned, or restarted. Interrupts get raised again on the new path.

Now: how does the resumed run know which question the answer belongs to?

If interrupts have no stable identity, the only thing available is position. First interrupt gets the first answer. And position is not identity.

A concrete sequence:

  1. The agent reaches its first pause and asks: approve payment to vendor A, ₹4,00,000.
  2. A human looks at that, and approves it.
  3. Meanwhile the run is retried — a transient tool error, a restart, a re-plan. The graph rebuilds. This time the first pause is a different question: approve payment to vendor B.
  4. The resume applies the stored "yes" to position one.
  5. Vendor B is paid. Nothing throws. The run reports success.

A human authorised a payment they never saw. There is no exception, no alert, and the audit trail says "approved by " — which is true, and misleading.

Why strict resume matters more than it sounds

The fix has two halves and you need both.

Identity: every interrupt carries an id that survives a retry. The question has a name, not just a slot.

Refusal: the resume path verifies that id and refuses a mismatch rather than falling back to position. That is the "strict" in strict resume mode.

Refusing is the important half. A system that detects the mismatch and then does something reasonable-looking — re-asking silently, picking the closest match, defaulting to deny — has just invented a new way to be wrong. Stop, and make a human look again.

The approval record this implies

If you take this seriously, an approval stops being a boolean and becomes a record that names its own question:

approval_id        appr_01J...
interrupt_id       intr_7f3a...      <- the question's identity
run_id             run_55c1...
asked              {"tool": "pay_vendor",
                    "vendor_id": "V-2291",
                    "invoice": "INV-88412",
                    "amount_paise": 40000000}
asked_sha256       9f2c...e4a1
decision           approved
decided_by         <user id>
decided_at         2026-11-10T11:49:08+05:30

On resume you check interrupt_id matches, re-hash asked, and compare. Mismatch means stop, not improvise.

Note what this record stores: what was asked, not only what was decided. A decision without its question cannot be audited six months later, when someone asks what exactly was approved.

A pause is not a failure

From the same release window, langgraph 1.2.19 (30 October 2026) fixed:

don't report a paused tool as failed on the tools stream

A tool waiting on a human was being reported as failed. That is the same family of bug seen from another side: a system that cannot distinguish "waiting for a person" from "errored" will retry, escalate, or roll back things a human is still thinking about.

Three states, not two. Running, failed, and waiting on a human — which is neither.

Two hard rules

An approval without an identity is a coin flip you cannot audit afterwards. It may well land on the right question most of the time. You will not be able to prove which times.

If a stale answer can be accepted, it eventually will be — and it will happen on the day the plan changed, which is exactly the day it matters most.

Honest limitation

I am reading release notes and reasoning from them. I have not reproduced either failure, I am not reporting the maintainers' stated motivation, and the approval-record shape above is a design I use rather than anything the library prescribes. The ₹ figures are illustrative.

Checkable references

  • langgraph 1.2.20 (5 November 2026) — "give each interrupt() in a task its own id"; "add a strict resume mode that refuses stale interrupt answers"
  • langgraph 1.2.19 (30 October 2026) — "don't report a paused tool as failed on the tools stream"

One open question

When your agent asks a human to approve something, does the answer know which question it belongs to — and what happens if it does not?

title: The agent memory checklist: 12 questions before you trust a memory tool
description:
A 12-point checklist for evaluating memory for coding agents. Use it before you trust a tool with project decisions.

The failure modes

Coding agents are useful inside a session and forgetful across weeks. Compaction drops architectural decisions. A new session re-reads files it already understood. Flat vector search returns stale and current facts side by side, with no provenance and no way to tell which fact is still true.

The checklist is not about how many memories a tool can store. It is about scope, time, evidence, and control.

The 12 checks

1. Scope

Why it matters: Scratch work should not become a repository convention.

What to test: Store a fact in one workspace and repository, then try to recall it from another. It should not leak.

2. Decision capture

Why it matters: A fact without the reason is hard to trust later.

What to test: Store a decision with its trade-off and date. Ask why it was made.

3. Temporal validity

Why it matters: Stale and current facts should not compete as equals.

What to test: Store a fact, replace it, then query the old and new states. The old fact should close, not disappear.

4. Provenance

Why it matters: An answer is only useful if you can inspect its support.

What to test: Ask for a recall and check that the returned context cites the memory it used.

5. Abstention

Why it matters: A confident guess is worse than a clear miss.

What to test: Ask about a decision that was never stored. The engine should say the evidence is insufficient.

6. Inspection

Why it matters: You need to see what the agent remembered.

What to test: Open the dashboard and inspect the memory, its scope, its history, and the recall rationale.

7. Local default

Why it matters: Project memory should not require a cloud account.

What to test: Run the core offline. Confirm it stores and recalls without a hosted service.

8. Portability

Why it matters: You should be able to back up or move the store.

What to test: Find the database file. Copy it, open the copy, and confirm the memories are intact.

9. Write review

Why it matters: Not every agent write deserves prompt eligibility.

What to test: Check whether writes can be approved, rejected, or quarantined before recall.

10. Retention

Why it matters: Some memory should expire; some must not.

What to test: Define a retention class and confirm the engine respects it.

11. Client coverage

Why it matters: One store is more useful than one store per editor.

What to test: Connect Claude Code and one other MCP client. Confirm both see the same scoped memory.

12. Claim honesty

Why it matters: Benchmarks should be bounded and reproducible.

What to test: Read the benchmark page. Check the fixture size, the metric, and the reproduction command.

The 10-minute test

Use one real repository and one decision you already know. Do not start with a large import.

  1. Install the MCP server: 
   pip install "engraphis[mcp]"
   engraphis-init
   claude mcp add engraphis -- engraphis-mcp
  1. Ask your agent to remember a scoped decision: 
   Checkout API uses PASETO access tokens.
   The November migration replaced the legacy JWT signer.
   Scope: workspace "acme-api", repository "checkout".
  1. Open a fresh session and ask: 
   Why did checkout move from JWT to PASETO?
   Check Engraphis memory and show the source, scope, and history.

Pass if the new session returns the decision, the reason, the scope, and a citation. Fail if it returns a plausible answer with no source, or if the old fact is still treated as current.

What good looks like

  • Bounded: recall returns a small set of relevant memories under a token budget, not a dump of everything the tool has seen.
  • Scoped: every memory carries its workspace, repository, session, and record boundary. Cross-project recall is a choice, not an accident.
  • Temporal: superseded facts close instead of disappearing. You can ask what was believed before and why it changed.
  • Inspectable: you can open the record, see its history, and trace the recall. If the tool cannot show you that, it is a black box.

Try it

Engraphis is the local-first memory engine this checklist is based on. The core is Apache-2.0, stores memory in one SQLite file, and needs no cloud account.

  • Checklist page: https://engraphis.com/agent-memory-checklist
  • Claude Code guide: https://engraphis.com/claude-code-memory
  • Interactive demo: https://engraphis.com/demo
  • GitHub: https://github.com/Coding-Dev-Tools/engraphis

If you use the checklist, tell me which check is missing or wrong. I am more interested in the critique than a vote.

title: Next-Concept Modeling: I Ran Stanford's New Text Generator Against a Classic LLM. Here Is What Happened.
description:
Every large language model you have used, from GPT to Llama to Claude, writes text the same way: one token at a time, left to right. To produce 128 tokens it runs the network 128 times in a row, and each step has to wait for the previous one. That sequential loop is the single biggest reason text generation is slow and expensive.

In October 2026, Stanford's Hazy Research group published Next-Concept Modeling (NCM), a model that writes text a completely different way: it sketches the whole passage first, then refines it level by level, predicting every position of a level in parallel. The paper reports generation that is 10x to 31x faster than diffusion language models at comparable quality.

Social media quickly turned that into "NCM kills LLMs". That is not what the paper measured. So I did what any curious engineer would do: I ran the official code and checkpoints myself, rebuilt the paper's evaluation, and put NCM head to head against a traditional autoregressive model trained on the same data, on an ordinary laptop.

This post covers:

  1. Why a new way of generating text is needed
  2. How NCM works, in plain language
  3. What the paper claims
  4. The datasets and models I used
  5. My experiments and results, with graphs
  6. The future of NCM, and whether it will replace LLMs

Everything is open source in my repository: github.com/Nishaanth419/ncm-research-playground.

Why do we need something other than next-token prediction?

An autoregressive (AR) language model predicts the next token given all previous tokens. It is simple, it scales beautifully, and it powers almost every chatbot today. But it has a structural cost:

  • Latency grows linearly with length. 1,000 tokens means 1,000 sequential forward passes. A GPU can do enormous amounts of work in parallel, but it cannot skip ahead.
  • It commits early. The model picks word 1 before it has "decided" what word 50 will be. Any global plan has to live implicitly inside its hidden state.
  • Throughput is bounded by memory bandwidth, because each tiny step reloads the weights.

Researchers have tried to break this loop before. Diffusion language models start from noise or masked tokens and refine all positions at once over many steps. They are parallel, but usually need many refinement steps to reach good quality, so in practice they are often not faster.

NCM takes a third route, borrowed from image generation.

How NCM works

The idea comes from VAR (Visual Autoregressive Modeling), which generates an image by predicting a tiny thumbnail first and then progressively larger, sharper versions. NCM applies the same coarse to fine recipe to text.

It has two parts.

Part 1: a tokenizer that turns text into levels of "concepts"

A multiscale residual VQ-VAE compresses a passage into a stack of levels of discrete codes.

  • Text is split into 128 ordinary BPE tokens, and an encoder turns them into a continuous latent (128 positions by 384 numbers).
  • That latent is approximated by 12 levels of codes. For TinyStories the level lengths are 1, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 52, 64, 76, 92, 108 and 128. Each level picks codes from its own codebook of 4,096 entries.
  • The levels are residual: each level encodes only what the coarser levels missed. Upsample every level to full length, add them together, and a decoder turns the sum back into tokens.

Level 0 is a single code that summarizes the entire passage. The last level has one code per token. These codes are the "concepts" in the name.

Part 2: a transformer that predicts the next level, not the next token

A next-concept transformer looks at everything generated so far (levels 0 to k, summed) and predicts all codes of level k+1 in a single forward pass. Repeat until the finest level, then decode the final latent into text.

For a 128-token story, that is 11 transformer passes instead of 128. (Level 0 for TinyStories is sampled from a frequency table stored in the checkpoint, so it costs no transformer pass.)

Watching it think

The nicest property of NCM is that every intermediate level can be decoded. These are real outputs of the official decode_multiscales function from one of my runs:

L0  (1 code)    .
L3  (24 codes)  One named the and.. and " is a it He felt wanted for before ...
L7  (64 codes)  day a boy found shiny in the. was happy showed his,. looked the ...
L11 (128 codes) One day, a little boy named Tim found a shiny stone in the park. He was very happy...

Early levels look like word salad, but they already carry the cast and topic of the story. The grammar and exact wording arrive in the last few levels. I measured this numerically by comparing the latent after each level with the final one:

Each level is one parallel step, but finer levels contain more codes, so they take longer:

The trade off you should notice immediately

Because the text only becomes readable at the last level, NCM cannot stream. A chatbot built on an AR model shows you its first word in milliseconds; NCM shows you nothing until the whole passage is finished. Keep that in mind for the results.

What the paper claims

Paper: Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation, by Hermann Kumbong, Ishan S. Khare, Iddah Mlauzi, Andrew Woen, Charles Ding, E. Kelly Buchanan, Simran Arora, Azalia Mirhoseini and Christopher Ré (Stanford, 2026). arXiv:2610.14162

From the abstract, compared with the strongest diffusion language model baseline at matched scale:

  • LM1B: better generative perplexity, about 21x faster
  • OpenWebText: competitive quality, about 10x faster
  • XSum summarization: matches ROUGE-L, about 31x faster
  • Sudoku: outperforms both autoregressive and diffusion baselines at every difficulty level, with fewer function evaluations

Two details matter when you read those numbers. First, the baseline is a diffusion model, not a standard autoregressive LLM. Second, the speeds were measured on a datacenter GPU (an H100). Neither of those matches how most people will first try NCM, which is exactly why I ran my own experiments.

The authors released everything: code under the MIT license, checkpoints and datasets on Hugging Face, and a blog post.

My experiment setup

Question: How does NCM compare with a traditional autoregressive model of the same domain, on speed and on text quality, on ordinary hardware? And do the paper's numbers reproduce from the released code?

Hardware: Apple M5 Pro laptop, CPU only, fp32, 6 threads. (NCM does not currently run on Apple's GPU backend: PyTorch MPS lacks the adaptive pooling NCM's quantizer uses.)

Software: Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.15, Transformers 5.22. The official NCM repository is pinned at commit c70274273f489abc73832b2b98584a8483b6b203 and is never modified; my code imports it.

Models

Role Model Size
NCM, stories hazyresearch/ncm-checkpoints, tinystories/ 125.0M (generator 88.6M + VQ-VAE 36.4M)
NCM, summarization same repository, xsum/
NCM, translation same repository, wmt14/
Autoregressive baseline roneneldan/TinyStories-33M 68.5M
Quality judge gpt2-large 774M

Both story models were trained on the same dataset, which is what makes them a reasonable pair.

Datasets

Dataset What it is How I used it Link
TinyStories (Eldan and Li, 2023) Short synthetic children's stories written with a small vocabulary Training data of both story models. Generation is unconditional, so the models' own samples are scored. HF dataset
XSum (Narayan et al., 2018) BBC news articles with one sentence summaries; 11,334 test pairs NCM summarization, test items 0 to 3 NCM copy
WMT14 German to English News sentence pairs; 3,003 test pairs NCM translation, test items 0 to 3 NCM copy

Metrics

  • Generative perplexity (gen-PPL): how surprised GPT-2-large is by the generated text. Lower means more fluent. This is the metric the NCM paper uses.
  • Unigram entropy: how varied the words are. It guards against a model that games perplexity by repeating itself.
  • Latency: median and p95 wall clock time over repeated runs, after warm up.
  • Time to first output: when the reader first sees anything.

Results

Experiment 1: Does the paper's result reproduce?

I ran the official evaluation scripts unmodified (eval_shard.py and eval_merge.py): 5 seeds by 256 unconditional TinyStories samples, scored by GPT-2-large. The scripts assume CUDA, so a small launcher remaps device requests to CPU without touching the code.

gen-PPL entropy
My reproduction (5 seeds, 1,280 stories) 16.23 ± 0.48 3.967
Paper, Table 8 15.41 3.98

Verdict: it reproduces. Entropy matches, and gen-PPL is within two seed standard deviations. The small gap is plausibly CPU fp32 and newer library versions. Generation of all 1,280 stories took 4.5 minutes; scoring took 18.5 minutes.

Experiment 2: Is my app running the model faithfully?

I built a research playground (FastAPI backend, React frontend) that runs NCM through its own code path so it can record every level. To make sure I was not measuring my own bugs, I compared its outputs with the official script's outputs for the same inputs and seeds.

Verdict: identical for TinyStories (seed 42, 4 samples), XSum test items 0 to 3 and WMT14 test items 0 to 3. This is enforced by automated tests in the repository.

Experiment 3: Speed against a classic LLM

Benchmark protocol: for each model and batch size, 2 untimed warm ups, then 10 timed runs with seeds 0 to 9, checkpoint default sampling (temperature 1, no top k or top p).

Model Batch Median p95 Per sample Words/s
NCM 1 307.5 ms 399.3 ms 307.5 ms 340.6
NCM 4 733.7 ms 788.8 ms 183.4 ms 571.1
TinyStories-33M 1 436.9 ms 491.3 ms 436.9 ms 239.5
TinyStories-33M 4 1313.0 ms 1430.3 ms 328.2 ms 304.7

NCM finishes a whole story 1.42x faster at batch 1 and 1.79x faster at batch 4, and the gap widens with batch size, because each of its 11 passes does more parallel work:

But look at when the reader sees something:

The autoregressive model shows its first token in 3.9 ms. NCM shows the complete text at 307 ms and nothing before that. For a chat interface, perceived speed is mostly about that first token, and there the classic model wins by roughly 80x.

Experiment 4: Quality head to head

Same seed, same batch of 4, same sampling, both warmed up, scored by GPT-2-large.

The autoregressive baseline writes noticeably more fluent text (gen-PPL 9.74 vs 13.48). NCM is slightly more varied (entropy 4.056 vs 3.993). This is a single small run, so treat it as an indication rather than a final verdict, but it matches what I saw reading the stories side by side.

Summarization and translation

The XSum and WMT14 checkpoints run and accept real input. They work, but show visible repetition in some outputs. For example, the German sentence "Ich trinke gern Kaffee am Morgen." came back as "I like like coffee in the morning." I did not run the full 11,334 and 3,003 item evaluations on CPU, only the 4 item exact match checks.

Read these numbers carefully

  • The paper's 10x to 31x speedups are GPU numbers against diffusion models. Mine are CPU numbers against an autoregressive model. Different experiments, not a contradiction.
  • The two story models differ in size (125M vs 68.5M), tokenizer (8,192 entry BPE vs GPT-2 BPE) and training run.
  • NCM always fills its 128 token canvas; the baseline may stop early at end of text.
  • The speed results are medians of 10 runs; the quality comparison is one 4 sample run.

What I built along the way

The repository is a full research playground you can run locally with one command (./run.sh):

  • Learn NCM: a plain language guide with the paper, findings, videos and a glossary
  • How NCM works: an animated walkthrough replayed from a real recorded run
  • Playground: run TinyStories, XSum or WMT14, watching levels fill in live over WebSocket
  • Concept Explorer: heatmaps of the code hierarchy and the text decoded at each level
  • Model Comparison and Benchmarks: the experiments in this post, exportable as CSV
  • Experiment History: every run stored in SQLite, replayable

Every number in this post comes from files committed in the repository (results/), and the graphs are generated by blog/make_charts.py directly from those files.

The future of NCM

NCM is a few weeks old, and the released checkpoints are small research models. Here is where I think it goes next.

1. Scaling. The big open question is whether NCM keeps its quality as models grow to billions of parameters and passages grow to thousands of tokens. The paper's OpenWebText results (1,024 tokens) are encouraging, but nobody has shown an NCM model at the scale of a modern assistant.

2. Prompting and instructions. The TinyStories model is unconditional; it cannot take a prompt. XSum and WMT14 show that conditioning on an input works. Instruction following, multi turn chat and tool use are still unexplored.

3. Streaming, or something better. NCM cannot show partial words, but it could show a partial plan. A product might display an outline from the coarse levels and sharpen it, the way progressive JPEGs load. Or levels could be generated in chunks so long documents stream paragraph by paragraph.

4. Planning and reasoning. The Sudoku result is the most intriguing line in the paper. A model that decides the global structure before the details is a natural fit for tasks where the end constrains the beginning: puzzles, code with matching brackets, structured data, poetry with a fixed form.

5. Hybrids. The likeliest near term path is not NCM alone but NCM inside a larger system: a fast coarse to fine drafter whose output an autoregressive model verifies or polishes, similar to speculative decoding.

6. Hardware support. Today NCM runs on CUDA and CPU but not Apple GPUs. Broader kernel support would make it practical on laptops and phones, where its low step count matters most.

So, will NCM replace LLMs?

Not as things stand, and probably not in the "one replaces the other" sense. A few reasons:

  • Quality still favors autoregressive models in my test, and the paper's quality comparisons are against diffusion models, not frontier AR LLMs.
  • Streaming matters for chat. Users perceive a model that starts talking in 4 ms as faster than one that delivers a full answer in 300 ms.
  • The AR ecosystem is enormous. Instruction tuning, RLHF, KV caching, speculative decoding and serving stacks are all built around next-token prediction.

It is also worth being precise about terminology: NCM is a language model. The real question is whether coarse to fine generation will replace left to right generation. My honest prediction:

  • NCM style models will win where throughput matters more than first token latency: batch summarization, translation, data generation, offline document processing and structured outputs.
  • They will complement rather than replace autoregressive models in interactive assistants, most likely through hybrids.
  • If scaling works out, the parallel step count is a genuine structural advantage, and the "next token" assumption will no longer be the only way to build a large language model. That alone makes NCM one of the most interesting papers of the year.

Try it yourself 

git clone https://github.com/Nishaanth419/ncm-research-playground.git
cd ncm-research-playground/ncm-research-playground

Then follow the step by step setup in the README. It takes about 20 minutes, mostly downloads, and needs no GPU.

Recommended videos

These are third party explainers I found useful (not reviewed for accuracy):

  • NCM: Fast Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation, AI Research Roundup: a paper walkthrough
  • Stanford's NCM: Generate Text Without Predicting Every Token?, AgenticEngineering: the code hierarchy explained
  • Next-Concept Modeling Explained: Can AI Move Beyond Tokens?, KeepItTechie: a beginner friendly overview
  • NCM Is this the End of LLMs?, Kai: a skeptical look at the 31x claim
  • Vector-Quantized Variational Autoencoders (VQ-VAEs), DeepBean: background on the tokenizer NCM builds on

References

  1. Kumbong, H., Khare, I. S., Mlauzi, I., Woen, A., Ding, C., Buchanan, E. K., Arora, S., Mirhoseini, A., and Ré, C. (2026). Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation. arXiv:2610.14162. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14162
  2. HazyResearch. NCM official code (MIT license). https://github.com/HazyResearch/ncm
  3. HazyResearch. NCM checkpoints and datasets on Hugging Face. https://huggingface.co/collections/hazyresearch/ncm
  4. Hazy Research blog. Next-Concept Modeling. https://hazyresearch.stanford.edu/blog/2026-10-12-ncm
  5. Scaling Intelligence Lab blog. NCM. https://scalingintelligence.stanford.edu/blogs/ncm/
  6. Tian, K., Jiang, Y., Yuan, Z., Peng, B., and Wang, L. (2024). Visual Autoregressive Modeling: Scalable Image Generation via Next-Scale Prediction. NeurIPS 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.02905
  7. van den Oord, A., Vinyals, O., and Kavukcuoglu, K. (2017). Neural Discrete Representation Learning (VQ-VAE). https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.00937
  8. Eldan, R., and Li, Y. (2023). TinyStories: How Small Can Language Models Be and Still Speak Coherent English? https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.07759. Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/roneneldan/TinyStories
  9. Narayan, S., Cohen, S. B., and Lapata, M. (2018). Don't Give Me the Details, Just the Summary! Topic-Aware Convolutional Neural Networks for Extreme Summarization (XSum). https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.08745
  10. Bojar, O., et al. (2014). Findings of the 2014 Workshop on Statistical Machine Translation (WMT14). https://aclanthology.org/W14-3302/
  11. Radford, A., Wu, J., Child, R., Luan, D., Amodei, D., and Sutskever, I. (2019). Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners (GPT-2). https://huggingface.co/gpt2-large
  12. TinyStories-33M baseline model. https://huggingface.co/roneneldan/TinyStories-33M
  13. My repository: NCM Research Playground. https://github.com/Nishaanth419/ncm-research-playground

If you run the playground on a GPU or try NCM on a new task, I would love to hear what you find. Drop a comment below.

title: Claude Fable 5.2: A Developer's Field Guide to the New #1 Model
description:
Claude Fable 5.2: A Developer's Field Guide to the New #1 Model

Shivam Kumar | VisionQuantech | November 10, 2026

Anthropic shipped Claude Fable 5.2 on November 9. It scores 64.6 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 — first place, ahead of Gemini 4 Carbon at 60.0 — and it costs 20% less than Fable 5.1: $8 input / $40 output per million tokens, cache reads at $0.20. The API model ID is claude-fable-5-2, available on the Claude Platform, AWS, Google Cloud and Azure, with the same 1M-token context and 128K max output as before.

Here is what to actually do with it, in the order that saves you money.

1. Set effort to "high", not "max"

This is the single most important decision. On AA's cost-per-task measure, Fable 5.2 at maximum effort costs $26.54 per task — the most expensive entry in the entire table. At "high" it costs $9.08. The score gap between the two settings is 64.6 vs 61.8: 2.8 points, 4.5%.

Do the division: you pay 2.9× for 4.5% more capability. Reserve max for one-shot, high-stakes reasoning where a few points decide correctness. Default every agent, every CI job and every coding assistant to high. If your harness does not expose an effort parameter, check the docs — Anthropic's model docs list the effort options, and "high" is where the value lives.

2. Price a real session before you migrate

A heavy coding session — 1M input tokens of context, 200K output tokens of code — costs $16.00 at list prices ($8 + $8). Twenty sessions a month per developer: $320.

Now add caching. If 80% of that input is cached project context and system prompts, input drops to $1.76 and the session costs $9.76 — 39% cheaper. Cache reads are $0.20 per million tokens, 40× cheaper than fresh input. The practical moves: put your system prompt, repo map and coding standards in a cached prefix; keep conversation history in cache blocks; never re-send a static context block as fresh tokens. This is not a micro-optimization — it is the difference between $320 and ~$195 per developer per month.

3. Know what the coding numbers actually say

On FrontierCode 2.0, Fable 5.2 scores 49.1% at xhigh, against 32.4% for Fable 5.1 and 45.5% for Opus 5.5. That is a genuine jump: +16.7 points over its predecessor, and ahead of Opus 5.5, which was the coding reference until yesterday. But two caveats from Anthropic's own disclosure: the numbers are self-reported, and the cyber and protein-design rows in its benchmark table use Mythos 5.2's scores, not Fable's.

Also note what Fable 5.2 does not lead: Gemini 4 Carbon wins the AutomationBench workflow test (53.9%), and Opus 5.5 leads AA-Briefcase Elo (1800). If your workload is long multi-step workflows rather than code generation, benchmark Carbon on your own tasks before switching. Re-run your own eval suite — the vendor's 49.1% is a starting hypothesis, not a guarantee.

4. Route the cheap work away from the flagship

Meta launched Muse Ember the same day: $0.10/$0.50 per million tokens, AA index 36.0, $0.14 per task. That is roughly 190× cheaper per task than Fable 5.2 at max. Ember is built for tool calls, routing and repeated agent tasks — exactly the work that makes up most of an agent's token burn.

The pattern: a small model classifies, routes and makes tool calls; Fable 5.2 handles the reasoning steps that actually need it. If your agent currently sends every step to a flagship model, you are paying flagship prices for classification work. Measure the split on your own traces — most teams find 60–80% of their agent calls are routable.

5. Mind the two dates in the fine print

Anthropic's new usage policy takes effect November 12. And Sonnet 4.5 retires from the API on November 30. If any service, script or CI job still calls Sonnet 4.5, migrate it this week — Fable 5.2 at high effort is both cheaper per task than the old Sonnet pricing in most workloads and substantially stronger. Check your model IDs with a grep across your repos before the 30th, not after.

6. Do not confuse the closed race with the open one

The top downloadable model is still Kimi K3.1 Pro (46.5 on AA). Tencent's Hy4 and Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small have only promised their weights. If your deployment is self-hosted or on-prem, Fable 5.2 changes nothing for you today — it is API-only. The open-weight race is still waiting on delivery; the closed race just got a new leader.

Checklist

  • [ ] Switch coding agents to claude-fable-5-2, effort "high"
  • [ ] Enable prompt caching on system prompts and repo context
  • [ ] Re-run your own evals; do not trust the 49.1% blindly
  • [ ] Route tool calls and classification to a small model (Ember-class)
  • [ ] Grep for Sonnet 4.5 calls; migrate before Nov 30
  • [ ] Read the new usage policy before Nov 12

The leaderboard will flip again. The economics — high over max, caching, routing — are the part that stays valuable after it does.

Sources: Anthropic's Fable 5.2 announcement and model docs; Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (Nov 9, 22:15 UTC); Meta's Muse Ember announcement. Cost arithmetic is the author's own, from published list prices.

title: Meta's New AI Costs 10 Cents — and That's Why Your Next App Will Have an Agent in It
description:
By Shakeel Ahmed — AI Growth Lab | November 10, 2026

Originally published on AI Growth Lab

On November 9, 2026, Meta released Muse Ember, its smallest AI model. It costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, with a 1-million-token context window. Meta built it for the repetitive work AI agents do all day: tool calls, routing, extraction, coding subtasks, and reading long documents.

That price is the whole story. The moment an AI agent costs almost nothing to run, every app starts hiring one. This article explains what Muse Ember is, what 10 cents actually buys, why cheap agents change who can build AI products, and where the small model still falls short.

What Is Muse Ember?

Meta's Muse family is the company's line of AI models for coding and agents, built by Meta Superintelligence Labs. Muse Ember is the smallest and cheapest member of that family. It went live on November 9 as muse-ember-1.0 on the Meta Model API and inside Muse Code, Meta's coding agent. It is also listed on OpenRouter.

Here is the short answer to what it does: Ember is built for the high-volume steps that make up most of an agent's workload. A modern AI agent does not make one big decision. It makes hundreds of small ones — call a tool, read the result, decide the next step, extract a fact from a document, route a request to the right place, repeat. Each of those steps is a separate call to a model, and each call costs money. Ember exists to make those calls cheap.

Meta's launch post describes it plainly: Ember is designed "for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing." It accepts text, images, audio, video, and PDFs as input and returns text. It can take in a million tokens at once — roughly 750,000 words — and write up to 512,000 tokens in reply.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg put it this way in a post on X: Ember is "our smallest model that delivers higher intelligence per dollar than others in its class." That phrase — intelligence per dollar — is the metric that matters here, and it is worth understanding properly.

What Does 10 Cents Actually Buy?

The headline price is $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens. But the real math is more interesting than the headline, because there are three prices, not one.

What you send Price per million tokens
Input, up to 200,000 tokens $0.10
Cached input, up to 200,000 tokens $0.004
Output $0.50
Input, above 200,000 tokens $0.30
Output, above 200,000 tokens $1.50

A request with 100,000 regular input tokens and 10,000 output tokens costs about $0.015 — a cent and a half. If all the input tokens qualify for the cached rate, the same request costs about $0.0054 — about half a cent.

Compare that with the big models. Claude Fable 5.2, launched the same day, costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens — making Ember 80 times cheaper per token on both input and output.

But the fairest comparison is with the model Ember is actually measured against: Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5. Ember's per-token prices are identical to Haiku 5.5's standard rate. The savings come from somewhere else. Independent benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis found that Ember matches Haiku 5.5's best score while using fewer tokens per job — so the same task costs about $0.14 with Ember and $0.41 with Haiku 5.5. Same price per token, one-third the bill. The model is cheaper because it is more efficient, not because the rate card is lower.

There is a catch in the price table worth knowing. Above 200,000 input tokens, Ember's rates triple to $0.30 input and $1.50 output. For the long-document work Meta advertises, that jump matters. A million-token context window is only cheap for the first 200,000 tokens.

Why Does Cheap Change Everything?

AI agents have been expensive to run at scale, and that cost has quietly decided who gets to build them. An agent that makes hundreds of intermediate calls per task, at frontier-model prices, burns money faster than it creates value. That is why most "AI agent" products so far have been demos, or have been limited to a handful of large companies that can afford the bill.

Ember attacks exactly that bottleneck. Meta's launch post positions it as a subagent that can handle hundreds of intermediate steps without sending every request to a larger frontier model. The pattern the industry is settling on is a division of labor: the big model plans, the small model executes. A frontier model decides what to do; a cheap model like Ember does the repetitive work of doing it — calling tools, parsing documents, running coding subtasks — hundreds of times per task, at a fraction of a cent each.

When the cost of the repetitive layer falls this far, three things change at once:

  • Small teams can afford agents. A solo developer or a small business can now run an agent that works all day, because the bill is measured in cents per task rather than dollars.
  • Agents can run continuously. At $0.14 per task, an agent can check, monitor, sort, and route work around the clock. At frontier prices, that same work had to wait for a human to ask for it.
  • Every app gets an agent layer. The same way every app eventually got search, notifications, and a settings page, every app is about to get an agent that handles the repetitive work inside it.

The demand side is already visible. A Chinese AI agent app just hit 1.5 million daily users — and nobody in the West noticed. People want agents that do things for them. Until now, the cost of running them has been the wall. Ember is a serious attempt to take that wall down.

Is It Actually Good, or Just Cheap?

Cheap means nothing if the model cannot do the job. So the benchmark numbers matter, and Meta invited an independent check. Artificial Analysis, an independent evaluation firm, put Ember through its Intelligence Index, version 5, on the day of launch.

At maximum reasoning effort, Ember scored 36 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, effectively tied with Claude Haiku 5.5 at 36.2 (Ember itself measured 35.8) and well ahead of OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna, which scored 28. At a lower reasoning setting, Ember scored 34 at $0.12 per task. Artificial Analysis calls Ember the cheapest model on its leaderboard scoring 36 or higher.

Meta's own claim is stronger: Ember "delivers more intelligence per dollar than Claude Haiku 5.5 or GPT-6 Luna at any reasoning setting," matching Haiku's best score at about a third of the cost and beating every Luna setting.

Three honest caveats. First, these are benchmark estimates — your production bill will vary with workload shape, retry rate, and output length. Second, the Intelligence Index measures general capability; it does not prove Ember handles your specific task as well as Haiku does. Third, the gap to the top is real: Meta's own Muse Spark 1.3 scores 37, one point above Ember, but costs $2.39 per task — about 17 times more. Ember trades a little capability for a lot of savings, and that trade is the entire point.

Ember is also the first model trained using Muse Wonder Full, Meta's newer training approach. Meta has expanded the Muse family fast since Muse Spark launched in April, followed by Muse Spark 1.3 and the Muse Wonder models in October. Ember is the bottom of that family by size — and, deliberately, the top of it by value.

The Catch — What Ember Cannot Do

No model this cheap is a frontier model, and Ember does not pretend to be one. Its limits matter as much as its price.

  • It is built for narrow, repeatable jobs. Tool calls, routing, extraction, coding subtasks, long-document parsing. Ask it to do open-ended research, novel reasoning, or creative work, and the bigger models will beat it.
  • It is a subagent, not the boss. Ember is designed to work under a larger model that plans and checks its work. Running it without that supervision is asking a junior employee to run the company.
  • The price jumps past 200,000 tokens. The $0.10 rate applies only up to 200,000 input tokens. Past that, input costs $0.30 and output $1.50 per million. Long-document work is still cheap, but not as cheap as the headline suggests.
  • It is Meta's first version of this idea. The Muse family is months old, and the tooling around it — evaluations, routing patterns, failure modes — is still being worked out in public.

None of this is a reason to dismiss Ember. It is a reason to use it for what it is: the cheap, tireless worker inside a system where a bigger model still does the thinking.

What This Means for Your Next App

If you build software, the practical question is not whether Ember is the best model. It is whether your product can afford an agent layer now — and the answer changed on November 9.

Start with the routing pattern. Use a frontier model for planning and judgment, and route the repetitive steps — tool calls, extraction, parsing, subtask execution — to Ember. That is the architecture Meta is selling, and it is the architecture that makes the economics work. Claude can now read your bank account — and the agent wave behind it is the same one Ember is built for.

If you are a solo developer, the more important number is $0.14 per task. That is the cost of letting an agent do a complete job — not a single call, a whole job. A hundred agent jobs a day costs $14. A thousand costs $140. Those are numbers a small business can budget for, and that is new.

And if you are watching the job market rather than building products, the same shift cuts both ways. AI layoffs in 2026 are hitting some roles while others are hiring — the map is more complicated than the headlines. Cheap agents do not replace the people who design the work. They replace the repetitive steps inside it — which is exactly the work Ember is built to do.

The agent era has been waiting on one thing: a model cheap enough to run all day without asking permission. Ember is not the smartest model Meta has ever shipped. It is the cheapest one that is good enough. For most apps, that is the one that matters.

Sources: Meta — Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember · VentureBeat — Meta's Muse Ember nearly matches Claude Haiku 5.5 at one-third the estimated per-task cost · AlphaSignal — Meta Releases Muse Ember to Cut AI Agent Costs by 3x

title: Automation bias: when teams trust AI blindly
description:
Automation bias is the reason a pull request full of AI-generated code often slips through review faster than one a colleague wrote by hand. The code looks tidy, the tests are green, and somewhere in the back of your mind sits the thought: the machine probably knows what it's doing. That is exactly where things get dangerous.

I care about this topic because I use AI tools every day and genuinely like them. As a team lead, though, I keep asking what happens to our attention when a tool is almost always right. Research has known the answer since the nineties, only back then the tool was called an autopilot. In this article I apply those findings to everyday development work and show you how to counter the effect in your team without demonizing AI.

In short

Automation bias means people follow automated suggestions more than they should and miss errors the system does not report. Studies on AI-generated code show exactly this pattern, including a false sense of security. The biggest pitfall: a second reviewer alone does not fix it; you need clear accountability, review depth by risk and practice with real mistakes.

What you will learn in this article

  • What automation bias is and which two types of error it causes
  • How to spot automation bias in code review, agent work and incidents
  • What studies found about AI assistants and code security
  • Seven countermeasures for your team and a 45-minute workshop to practice

What is automation bias?

Automation bias describes how people give the advice of an automated system more weight than other signals. Contradicting hints then get brushed aside, even when they are right. The term comes from aviation and medical research. In the nineties, Kathleen Mosier, Linda Skitka and colleagues studied how pilots work with automated cockpit systems. Their finding was uncomfortable: well-trained professionals followed wrong indications even though other instruments showed the opposite.

A closely related idea is automation complacency. It means we monitor a system less carefully because it has run reliably for a long time. In 2010, Raja Parasuraman and Dietrich Manzey showed that both effects share a root: our attention is limited, and we direct it to wherever we suspect the bigger risk. When the automation works well, our attention drifts elsewhere.

Two types of error: accepting and overlooking

Research distinguishes two errors that map directly onto software development. With an error of commission, you follow a suggestion without weighing it against other information. One example is the AI-suggested IAM policy with a wildcard in the actions, which you accept because the deployment finally works afterwards.

With an error of omission, the system fails to report a problem, and you don't notice it either because you relied on the system. For instance, the AI review praises a pull request but does not mention that a new endpoint skips the authorization check. Since there is no comment about it, nobody looks there. This second type is trickier, because there is nothing to trip over.

How automation bias shows up in everyday development

To make this concrete, let's take a fictional team building a ticket shop for concerts. The team uses an AI assistant in the IDE, lets an agent handle smaller tasks as pull requests and has set up an AI review that runs before the human review. All sensible. Still, typical patterns appear in four places.

Code completion

A developer builds the event search. The AI suggests a database query that inserts the search term via string concatenation. She reads the line and, since it looks plausible, hits Tab. Had a colleague shown her this line in a review, she would probably have said “SQL injection” right away. The difference is not knowledge but attitude: you check a colleague, you accept a suggestion.

Agent pull requests

The agent is asked to extend the discount logic with group tickets. It delivers a clean pull request with new tests, all green. However, nobody checks one thing: the agent wrote the tests itself, tailored to its own implementation. A rounding error for groups of ten or more therefore lives in both the code and the test. Green tests feel like independent proof, but in this case they are not.

AI review before the human

The AI review leaves three small style comments and nothing else. Then the human reviewer sees the result, thinks “the AI already checked the big stuff” and only looks at the three comments. Without noticing, the team has turned two reviews into one and a half. I covered the question of who is responsible for what in detail in AI code review: team rules for Copilot approvals.

Incident analysis

At night, checkout goes down. Right away, the on-call engineer pastes logs into an AI chat and gets a convincing explanation: the database is overloaded. As a result, the team scales up the database, but the error stays. In fact, the real cause, an expired certificate at the payment provider, was in the log, but the first plausible answer ended the search. Experts call this the anchoring effect: the first hypothesis colors everything that follows.

What research says about automation bias and AI code

By now there are solid studies on AI assistants in programming. I find two of them particularly revealing, because together they show the whole pattern.

Two studies on AI code and security

In 2021, Hammond Pearce and colleagues tested GitHub Copilot in 89 scenarios with security-critical weaknesses, based on MITRE's “Top 25” list. Of the roughly 1,700 generated programs, about 40 percent were vulnerable. Admittedly, the study is older, and models have improved a lot since. Still, the core point remains: a language model produces likely code, not verified code.

Even more revealing for automation bias is the study by Neil Perry, Megha Srivastava, Deepak Kumar and Dan Boneh from Stanford. Participants with an AI assistant wrote significantly less secure code than the comparison group without one. At the same time, they were more likely to believe their code was secure. In other words, that is the effect in a nutshell: quality drops while the feeling of safety rises. One more detail matters: people who were more skeptical of the AI and worked with it more actively, for example by rephrasing prompts, ended up with fewer vulnerabilities.

What the DORA report says about trust

Google Cloud's 2025 DORA report fits the picture too. According to Google, 90 percent of respondents now use AI at work, but 30 percent trust it only a little or not at all. The report calls AI an amplifier: it makes whatever already works or fails in an organization more pronounced. To me this means: a team with a weak review culture does not automatically get a better one through AI, but a faster weak one.

🎬 The trust spiral behind automation bias – this animated diagram only runs on my site: watch it on sascha-ms.de

Why a second reviewer is not enough

The obvious reflex is: then let two people review. Unfortunately, aviation research offers little hope here. In 1998, Mosier and colleagues also studied two-person crews, and they were no better than individuals at catching errors the automation failed to report. When both assume the system and the other person are paying attention, responsibility spreads out until nobody holds it. A second review only helps if it is clear what it should check in addition.

Why good teams are especially prone

This sounds paradoxical, but it is well documented. Automation bias grows with high workload, with time pressure and with a system that has been reliable for a long time. The literature calls the last effect “learned carelessness”. An AI assistant that is right in 95 out of 100 cases is therefore more dangerous for your attention than one that botches every second suggestion. With the bad tool, you stay alert. With the good tool, however, you train yourself out of checking.

In addition, presentation plays a role. Suggestions that are displayed prominently and in detail seem more trustworthy. AI code arrives neatly formatted, with comments and sometimes even with a rationale. As a result, it looks like the work of an experienced colleague. Our brain gratefully takes that shortcut.

Curbing automation bias in your team: seven countermeasures

You cannot switch the effect off entirely; it is human. However, you can change the conditions under which your team works with AI. The following countermeasures are easy to introduce and build on what research describes as effective.

1. Make accountability explicit

One of the most reliable findings: people who must account for the result rely less blindly on automation. In practice, whoever opens a pull request owns every line in it, no matter who or what wrote it. “The AI did it that way” is not a justification. Say this out loud in your team once and add it to your team agreement.

2. Reasons instead of checkmarks

Add a short question to your pull request template: “Which parts come from an AI, and what did you check or change in them?” For most pull requests, two sentences are enough. It is less about control than about a brief moment of pausing. If you have to write down what you checked, you check something.

3. Scale review depth by risk

Not all code needs the same attention, so divide your repository into zones. For documentation and tests a quick look is enough; for authentication, permissions, payments and data migrations you need a deliberate, independent review. That way you focus scarce attention where an error of omission gets really expensive.

4. Think first, then ask

For incidents and architecture decisions a simple rule helps: before anyone asks the AI, the team writes down its own hypothesis. Afterwards, the AI may add to it or disagree. This weakens the anchoring effect because the first answer no longer comes from the machine by default. Besides, the team keeps learning instead of just collecting answers.

5. Practice with real mistakes

In 2008, Bahner, Hüper and Manzey showed that training with deliberately flawed suggestions works better against automation bias than merely pointing out that errors can happen. Moreover, this translates nicely to teams. I show how in the workshop further down.

6. Take time pressure out of reviews

High workload demonstrably amplifies the effect. If your team is measured by how fast pull requests get merged, you reward exactly the behavior that fuels automation bias. Measure how many defects show up after the merge instead, and schedule fixed review times rather than squeezing reviews between two meetings.

7. Verify independently

Don't let AI code be judged only by the same AI that wrote it, and don't rely solely on tests created in the same step. Independent checks include acceptance criteria written beforehand, static analysis, security scanners or a test written by a human. What matters is that the check does not share the same assumptions as the code.

A 45-minute workshop against automation bias

Countermeasure number five works best when you experience it together. The following agenda fits into an extended retro or a learning slot. You need a facilitator and five short code snippets in the style of your AI suggestions.

Time Step What happens
5 min Intro The facilitator briefly explains automation bias and the two types of error without giving away the exercise.
10 min Review round Everyone reviews five AI suggestions alone and marks each “accept” or “change”. Two snippets contain a deliberately planted error.
10 min Reveal The facilitator shows the errors. The team collects who found what and why the other errors slipped through.
15 min Find patterns Discuss together: when did we read carefully, when did we just skim? What lulled us into a sense of safety?
5 min Agreement Agree on one concrete experiment for the next two weeks, for example the question in the PR template.

The attitude matters: this is not about who finds the most errors. If someone misses an error, that is precisely the effect you are exploring, not a personal failure. Without psychological safety in the team, this exercise quickly turns into a test, and then nobody learns anything.

Good errors for the exercise are ones that look plausible: a missing permission check, a swapped comparison operator at a boundary, a time zone mistake, an overly broad permission or a retry without an upper limit. Either write the snippets yourself or let an AI generate them and plant the errors by hand afterwards.

Questions for your next retro

If you want to raise the topic without a workshop, take one of these questions to your next retrospective. You can find out how to structure a retro in my guide How to run a retrospective.

  • Which AI suggestion in the last sprint should we have looked at more closely?
  • Was there a production bug that a review could have caught? What role did AI play in it?
  • Where do we review AI code more thoroughly than code from colleagues, and where less thoroughly?
  • Which parts of our system should nobody ever accept unchecked, no matter who wrote the code?
  • What would need to change so that nobody feels rushed during review?

Common mistakes in dealing with automation bias

The most common mistake is a blanket ban. After all, banning AI tools pushes their use into private browser tabs and removes any chance of developing good rules together. Blanket distrust is just as unfortunate: if every AI suggestion has to be checked three times, the benefit is gone and the team works around the rule.

Another mistake is the blame question. When a bug from AI code reaches production, asking “Who waved this through?” is understandable but not very helpful. It is more productive to ask which conditions made waving it through likely. Time pressure, unclear responsibility and missing risk levels are almost always involved.

Finally: metrics that reward speed only. Of course, more merged pull requests per week look good on a dashboard. If defects after release rise at the same time, you have built automation bias into your goals.

How to turn this into a fixed guardrail in the review is shown in the pull request template for AI-generated code with an automated check.

My take

I consider automation bias one of the underrated topics in using AI within teams. Most discussions revolve around models, costs and data protection. Those matter. Yet the biggest weak spot sits between screen and chair, and I explicitly don't mean that in a derogatory way. We are simply not built to watch something attentively for long periods when it almost always works.

At the same time, I disagree with the narrative that AI makes developers lazy or dumb. The Stanford study also shows the opposite: people who work with the tool actively and critically benefit from it. For me, this is above all a leadership task. As a team lead, I can create conditions in which looking closely is normal: enough time, clear accountability and a culture in which “I didn't understand this” is a good review comment.

How to measure the impact of AI on your team without anyone feeling watched is the topic of my article Metrics for AI-generated code: measure impact, not people.

FAQ

What is automation bias in simple terms?

Automation bias is the tendency to trust automated suggestions more than other information. As a result, people accept wrong suggestions or miss errors the system does not report.

What is the difference between automation bias and automation complacency?

Automation bias concerns decisions: you follow the suggestion instead of other evidence. Complacency concerns monitoring: you look less closely because the system has been reliable for a long time. Both stem from limited attention and often occur together.

Does AI-generated code make software less secure?

Not automatically. Studies do show, however, that people with an AI assistant can write less secure code and still consider it more secure. What matters is how critically the team handles the suggestions.

Should teams ban AI tools?

A ban usually just pushes usage out of sight. Clear accountability, review depth by risk and regular practice with flawed suggestions are more effective.

Your next step

This week, add a question to your pull request template asking which parts come from an AI and what was checked. It takes five minutes and changes how your team looks at AI code. Now I'm curious about your view: when did you last catch yourself simply waving an AI suggestion through? Feel free to tell me in the comments.

Sources

  • Wikipedia: Automation bias (overview with references to Mosier et al. 1997/1998, Parasuraman & Manzey 2010, Bahner et al. 2008)
  • Parasuraman, R. & Manzey, D. H. (2010): Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation: An Attentional Integration. Human Factors 52(3)
  • Bahner, J. E., Hüper, A.-D. & Manzey, D. (2008): Misuse of automated decision aids. International Journal of Human-Computer Studies 66(9)
  • Perry, N., Srivastava, M., Kumar, D. & Boneh, D.: Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants? (arXiv 2211.03622)
  • Pearce, H. et al.: Asleep at the Keyboard? Assessing the Security of GitHub Copilot’s Code Contributions (IEEE S&P 2022)
  • Google: 2025 DORA report (State of AI-assisted Software Development)
  • DORA: 2025 State of AI-assisted Software Development
