title: Once Upon Agentic AI (Part 1): Create your own agent and forge its tools with Strands Agents
description:
On Day1, three heroes that nothing destined to cross went on a journey to write the same legend. TheWitcherish from the Order of Developers, Amagash from the Order of Agents, and Tagazok from the Order of Builders.
And high above it all, an Orchestrator agent watched over this world.

The series follows the adventure in three parts:

  • This article: Create your first agent, equip it with a Vended tool, then write a tool of your own.
  • Part 2: MCP (Model Context Protocol) explored via the Strands Agents Harness SDK.
  • Part 3: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation, where an agent answers from documents it looks up) and A2A (Agent2Agent, a protocol that lets agents talk to other agents), with an orchestrator agent leading specialized agents.

By the end of Part 1, your agent tells a story, looks up a spell in a real rules API, and rolls real dice with a power you wrote. You'll also be able to prove each of those from the log.

Get started

To complete our heroes quest, you need Python, uv, a terminal, and AWS credentials with access to Amazon Bedrock.
As our three heroes share one adventure, you write the code behind each step of their quest with Strands Agents, an open source SDK for AI agents in Python and TypeScript.

The code lives in aws-samples/sample-once-upon-agentic-ai. The main branch contains skeletons with # TODO markers.

git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-once-upon-agentic-ai.git ~/sample-once-upon-agentic-ai
cd ~/sample-once-upon-agentic-ai
uv sync
export AWS_PROFILE=YOUR_AWS_PROFILE AWS_REGION=YOUR_AWS_REGION

No AWS profile yet? The Strands Agents Amazon Bedrock model provider guide shows how to set up AWS credentials (with aws configure, environment variables, a boto3 session, or aws login) and lists the IAM permissions your agent needs to invoke a model. Strands picks those credentials up on its own.

Why do we call AI Agents... agents?

Well, agents do have agency, that is why we call them agents. Both words come from the Latin agere, "to act". A model on its own only answers. An agent decides what to do next and acts on it, using the tools you give it.

An agent has three parts: a model, a system prompt with its instructions, and tools it may use. When you send a message, the model decides whether to call a tool. It reads the result, then answers or calls another tool. That cycle is the agent loop. Strands runs it for you, handling model calls, tool runs, and conversation history while you write the instructions and tools.

Here is what each part gives our heroes:

Our heroes need to... Which means... Strands gives us...
Think and decide A brain that reads and chooses what to do A model on Amazon Bedrock (default model provider)
Know who they are A standing instruction A system prompt
Act beyond words Reaching outside the model Tools: ready-made ones from strands.vended_tools, or your own with @tool

Step 1 gives the model its system prompt. Steps 2 and 3 give it tools.

Step 1: Does an agent need more than one line?

"Our heroes had just arrived in the realm. No map, no weapons, not a single spell." Your first agent arrives the same way: a voice, and nothing in its hands.

Summons it with debug logs, a system prompt, and one call:

from strands import Agent
import logging

logging.getLogger("strands").setLevel(logging.DEBUG)
logging.basicConfig(
    format="%(levelname)s | %(name)s | %(message)s",
    handlers=[logging.StreamHandler()]
)

agent = Agent(
    system_prompt="You are a game master for a fantasy role-playing game"
)

response = agent("Hi, I am an adventurer ready for adventure!")

Agent(system_prompt=...) gives the model an instruction for every turn. Here it makes the agent the storyteller of a fantasy role-playing game. Without a model argument, Strands uses Amazon Bedrock with Claude Sonnet 4.6 by default. Bedrock is a serverless AWS service that runs models from several providers for you behind its APIs, so trying another model means changing a model ID, not rewriting your agent.

cd ~/sample-once-upon-agentic-ai/1_strands_basics
uv run python simple_agent.py

The debug logs show what the SDK does:

DEBUG | strands.models.bedrock | config=<{'model_id': 'global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6', ...}> | initializing
DEBUG | strands.tools.registry | tool_count=<0> | tools configured
DEBUG | strands.models.bedrock | request=<{'modelId': 'global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6', 'messages': [...], 'system': [...]}>
DEBUG | strands.event_loop._retry | stop_reason=<end_turn> | model call succeeded, ...

One request, no tools, and stop_reason=<end_turn>: the model finished in one turn. The agent opened a scene:

The torchlight flickers as you step into the worn wooden tavern. The smell of ale and woodsmoke fills the air. A grizzled barkeep eyes you from across the room.

Then the barkeep added: "We don't get many fresh faces in Thornhaven these days." One sentence summoned a tavern and named a town. No map, no weapons: tool_count=<0>. Keep DEBUG on. The agent sounds like it knows the rules, but it has no book to check them in.

Step 2: Does the agent already know Fireball?

"Before conquering anything, they first had to equip themselves."
Our heroes enter a shop that promises everything they need. One of them is hungry. "No, we don't do burgers here," the shopkeeper answers, "but there's plenty of other stuff that should interest you."
Our heroes expected a few trinkets; they found a treasure.

A tool is a function described to the model, which decides whether to call it. A vended tool comes ready-made in strands.vended_tools. Here, http_request calls web APIs:

from strands.vended_tools import http_request

agent = Agent(tools=[http_request], system_prompt=...)

The system prompt points to Open5e, an open fantasy-RPG rules API, then asks: "What does the Fireball spell do, and how much damage does it deal?" Copy step 1's logging block, then run:

cd ~/sample-once-upon-agentic-ai/2_vended_tools
uv run python agent_with_vended_tools.py

Here is the trace of what the SDK does:

DEBUG | strands.tools.registry | tool_count=<1> | tools configured
DEBUG | strands.event_loop._retry | stop_reason=<tool_use> | model call succeeded, ...
DEBUG | strands.tools.executors._executor | tool_use=<{..., 'name': 'http_request', 'input': {'method': 'GET', 'url': 'https://api.open5e.com/v2/spells/srd_fireball/'}}> | streaming
Tool #1: http_request

The first turn ends with stop_reason=<tool_use>. The model built the URL, Strands ran it, and the result began {"status": 200, "status_text": "OK", ...}. Only then did the agent answer:

Casting Time: Action
Range: 150 feet
...
Failed save: The target takes 8d6 fire damage.

The API's JSON says "range": 150 and "casting_time": "action"; the reply repeats both. You wrote no code to choose the tool: the model chose it, and the log proves it. But a shop only sells tools someone else made.

Step 3: Is a function already a tool?

"Saddlebags full and hearts light, our heroes continued on their way."
Two of them stride ahead. Behind them, TheWitcherish leafs through the grimoire he has just acquired.

Suddenly, he shouts "WAIT!" and announces an extraordinary power. The power: "It's 13h37." The party is not impressed. Then comes a better idea: "you can write your own powers!" How? "All we have to do is create a function, then declare it as a tool."

You turn a function into a tool with a decorator, a line beginning with @ above the function. In Strands, it is @tool. The custom tools docs explain how Strands reads the function's docstring and type hints to build the tool specification shown to the model.

Our custom tool is a dice roller, trimmed here:

from strands import Agent, tool

@tool
def roll_dice(faces: int = 6) -> int:
    """Roll one die with a given number of faces and return the result.
    ...
    """
    import random
    return random.randint(1, faces)

dice_master = Agent(tools=[roll_dice], system_prompt=...)

The system prompt makes the agent "Lady Luck", who rolls four dice for each ability score and drops the lowest. When the agent is built, the log shows the new tool being registered:

DEBUG | strands.tools.registry | tool_name=<roll_dice>, tool_type=<function>, is_dynamic=<False> | registering tool
DEBUG | strands.tools.registry | tool_count=<1> | tools configured
agent built, tools: ['roll_dice']

The solution prints roll_dice.tool_spec, the specification sent to the model:

{'name': 'roll_dice', 'description': 'Roll one die with a given number of faces and return the result.\n\n...', 'inputSchema': {'json': {'properties': {'faces': {'default': 6, ..., 'type': 'integer'}}, 'type': 'object'}}}

The docstring became the description, the type hint became 'type': 'integer', and the default became 'default': 6. The model reads this specification, not your code, so a clear docstring helps it choose the tool.

Time to roll the dice!

Run the chapter:

cd ~/sample-once-upon-agentic-ai/3_custom_tools
uv run python agent_with_dice_roll_tool.py

The trace shows each step the SDK takes:

DEBUG | strands.event_loop._retry | stop_reason=<tool_use> | model call succeeded, ...
DEBUG | strands.tools.executors._executor | tool_use=<{..., 'name': 'roll_dice', 'input': {'faces': 6}}> | streaming
...
Tool #1: roll_dice
...
Tool #16: roll_dice
DEBUG | strands.event_loop._retry | stop_reason=<end_turn> | model call succeeded, ...

Lady Luck requested all 16 dice in one turn. Strands ran the tool 16 times, returned the results, and the second model call answered:

STRENGTH
Rolls: 3, 1, 1, 3 -> Drop the 1 (one of them) -> 3 + 1 + 3 = 7
...
CHARISMA
Rolls: 2, 6, 5, 3 -> Drop the 2 -> 6 + 5 + 3 = 14

The 16 tool results in the full log carry every one of those numbers, in the same groups Lady Luck used: 3, 1, 1, 3; 1, 2, 4, 3; 3, 2, 1, 2; and 2, 6, 5, 3.

The log is the record. When I asked step 1's tool-free agent the Fireball question, it also said 8d6, so the reply alone can't tell you whether a tool ran. tool_count, stop_reason and each Tool # line can.

Tagazok decided to write his own custom tool decorated with @tool: def fire_sword():
That is AWSome!

Follow the adventurers

In Part 2, our heroes seek help beyond their own strength. We equip them with an MCP server as another monster, greater and mightier, awaits them!

Until then, three habits for your own agent:

  • Start with the system prompt. Settle the agent's role and rules before you add tools.
  • Write the docstring for the model. Read the tool_spec before the model does.
  • Let the model choose. If you catch yourself writing if statements to pick a tool, that rule belongs in the system prompt.

P.S.: Their adventure is also a comic book. If you would like your own copy, the Once Upon Agentic AI with Strands Agents page lists where to buy it in North America, Europe and Asia Pacific.

title: Stop invoking the whole graph to test one node: unit tests and checkpoints for my LangGraph agent
description:
After part 3, my LangGraph graph worked. It also had exactly one test: run it, look at the verdict, shrug. Every edit to judge_node meant rerunning the whole graph and hoping the retries would still stop after three calls, and hope is a lousy CI stage. The spend policy of my agent, the code that decides when the copilot is allowed to pay for LLM calls, got audited the way I check soup: with a fork and a squint.

A comment on part 3 named the two missing pieces: stop testing through the framework, because the nodes are pure functions and deserve unit tests, and add checkpoints between runs. This part is both. What I have now: thirteen tests that run in 0.26 seconds without a single LLM call, and a checkpoint that parks the graph right before the model starts costing money.

The JobCopilot mirror is unreachable from this machine, so the code below is a checked template rebuilt from the published contracts of parts 1-3 (AgentState, route_after_parse, judge_node(state, chat), build_graph(chat)). Before publishing, align node names, prompt wording, and the THRESHOLD = 60 / MAX_CALLS = 3 constants with your repo. The numbers below come from a real run in my sandbox (langgraph 1.2.20, pydantic 2.14.3, Python 3.14).*

The router is twelve lines, so it gets a truth table

The router from part 3, route_after_parse, decides between ok, retry, and give_up. It is the entire economy of my agent in one pure function: no LLM, no framework, no network. A truth-table test costs nothing to write:

# test_copilot.py
import pytest

from nodes import route_after_parse
from state import MAX_CALLS, AgentState


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "error, attempt, expected",
    [
        (None, 0, "ok"),
        ("schema: 1 validation error", 1, "retry"),
        ("schema: 1 validation error", 2, "retry"),
        ("schema: 1 validation error", MAX_CALLS, "give_up"),
    ],
)
def test_router_branches(error, attempt, expected):
    state = AgentState(error=error, attempt=attempt)
    assert route_after_parse(state) == expected


def test_router_budget_boundary():
    """The retry budget runs out exactly at attempt == MAX_CALLS, not one past it."""
    assert route_after_parse(AgentState(error="x", attempt=MAX_CALLS - 1)) == "retry"
    assert route_after_parse(AgentState(error="x", attempt=MAX_CALLS)) == "give_up"

That boundary test is the whole point of having MAX_CALLS as a constant instead of a magic number inside the loop. Off-by-one errors in retry budgets are invisible in a happy-path demo: the model cooperates, the router never reaches the edge. This test visits the edge on purpose, so the day I change 3 to 4, it fails loudly instead of quietly burning one extra paid call per job description.

Coming from React, this was my first genuinely comfortable pytest moment. I test pure functions the same way I test reducers.

Node tests: the fake chat, and what the prompts actually say

judge_node(state, chat) takes its LLM callable as an argument, a design decision from part 3 that pays off here. Unit testing it is just handing it a fake, and my fake records the prompt it was sent:

def recording_chat(raw: str):
    sent = {}

    def chat(prompt: str) -> str:
        sent["prompt"] = prompt
        return raw

    return chat, sent

The LLM call becomes free, deterministic, and inspectable. A test can ask what the node actually asked the model, not only what it did with the answer:

def test_first_pass_asks_about_the_jd():
    chat, sent = recording_chat('{"match_score": 72, "missing_skills": ["Terraform"]}')
    state = AgentState(jd_text="Senior Frontend (React, TS)", context="<chunks>")

    patch = judge_node(state, chat)

    assert "Senior Frontend (React, TS)" in sent["prompt"]
    assert "RESUME EXCERPT" in sent["prompt"]
    assert "PREVIOUS" not in sent["prompt"]  # no repair talk on a fresh judge


def test_retry_prompt_quotes_the_model_back():
    chat, sent = recording_chat('{"match_score": 70, "missing_skills": []}')
    state = AgentState(
        error="Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)",
        last_raw="Sure! The match is quite good, I'd say around 70 out of 100.",
    )

    judge_node(state, chat)

    assert "PARSER ERROR" in sent["prompt"]
    assert "around 70 out of 100" in sent["prompt"]  # its prose, quoted back

The second test is the repair trick from part 1 turned into a regression check. If a future refactor "simplifies" the repair prompt and stops quoting the model's own prose back at it, nothing will crash: the graph reruns, the verdict looks plausible, and repair quality rots in silence. The test can't grade repair quality, but it can check the mechanism survived.

The test that actually caught a design mistake of mine is about patch shape:

def test_judge_returns_a_state_patch_nothing_else():
    chat, _ = recording_chat('{"match_score": 72, "missing_skills": ["Terraform"]}')
    patch = judge_node(AgentState(jd_text="x", context="y"), chat)

    assert patch["attempt"] == 1
    assert patch["match_score"] == 72
    assert patch["verdict"] == "match"
    assert patch["error"] is None
    assert set(patch) == {"last_raw", "attempt", "match_score", "missing_skills", "verdict", "error"}

My first draft of that last line asserted that the error case writes verdict: None into the patch. It failed, because the error patch carries no verdict key at all. Writing the assertion forced me to confront something the design already knew: an undecided verdict should be absent, not None. The router reads state.error, so a verdict: None in the patch is a lie the next reader has to interpret. The test made the "no decision, no key" rule explicit, which is the one thing a comment cannot do.

Match this anecdote to how judge_node actually evolved in your repo; the assertion above ("verdict" not in patch on a failed parse) follows the part 3 code published earlier. Also recheck the ParseOk field name: part 1 used ParseOk(match=JobMatch(...)), the part 3 draft read result.data.*

Testing the loop through the graph, still no LLM

Node tests check the parts. One test per promise that belongs to the graph itself: the repair loop recovers, and the retry budget stops.

import json

from graph import build_graph
from state import AgentState, MAX_CALLS


def test_budget_loop_ends_cleanly():
    calls = {"n": 0}

    def chat(prompt: str) -> str:
        calls["n"] += 1
        return "I'd say around 70 out of 100."  # prose, never JSON

    final = build_graph(chat).invoke(AgentState(jd_text="Junior Python Backend"))

    assert final["verdict"] == "error"  # invoke returns state as a dict
    assert final["attempt"] == MAX_CALLS
    assert calls["n"] == MAX_CALLS  # the loop stopped itself


def test_repair_loop_recovers():
    calls = {"n": 0}

    def chat(prompt: str) -> str:
        calls["n"] += 1
        if calls["n"] == 1:
            return "Sure! The match is quite good, I'd say around 70 out of 100."
        return json.dumps({"match_score": 70, "missing_skills": ["Terraform"]})

    final = build_graph(chat).invoke(AgentState(jd_text="Senior Frontend Engineer (React, TS)"))

    assert final["verdict"] == "match"  # invoke returns state as a dict
    assert final["match_score"] == 70
    assert final["attempt"] == 2

Both are end-to-end runs and both are free: a fake chat goes in, assertions come out. The division of labor I settled on: node tests own the details (which prompt fired, the exact shape of the patch), graph tests own the promises between nodes (the budget exhausts, the loop recovers, fail exits without raising).

The whole suite: thirteen tests, 0.26 seconds. One real LLM round trip takes longer, so the suite can run before every commit, which a suite with an LLM inside never could.

Two honest notes from the way there. First, final.verdict raises AttributeError: app.invoke() returns the merged state values as a plain dict, not my pydantic AgentState. The framework hands you channel values; the attribute access I reached for was my model, not the graph's interface. Second, invoke(AgentState(...)) is input, not a stored run: every invoke is a fresh run unless a thread_id says otherwise. Which leads straight into checkpointing.

The dict-return behavior is checked against langgraph 1.2.20; reconfirm on your pinned version.*

Checkpointing: state leaves the stack

With a checkpointer, LangGraph saves state after every node. A run stops being a black box that either finishes or throws. You can stand between nodes and look around:

import json

from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver

from graph import build_graph
from state import AgentState


def compliant_chat(score: int = 70):
    def chat(prompt: str) -> str:
        return json.dumps({"match_score": score, "missing_skills": ["Terraform"]})

    return chat


JD = "Senior Frontend Engineer (React, TypeScript, 5+ years)"

app = build_graph(compliant_chat(), checkpointer=MemorySaver(), interrupt_before=["judge"])
config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "jd-42"}}

Two settings changed from part 3's build_graph: checkpointer=MemorySaver() turns on state snapshots (in-memory is fine for a batch run inside one process), and interrupt_before=["judge"] tells the graph to stop right at the LLM node's door. Run it, inspect, resume:

1. run stops before the LLM call
2. next: ('judge',) | values: {'jd_text': 'Senior Frontend Engineer (React, TypeScript, 5+ years)',
   'context': '<top-8 resume chunks>', 'attempt': 0, 'missing_skills': []}
3. resume finished: next: () | values: {..., 'attempt': 1,
   'match_score': 70, 'missing_skills': ['Terraform'], 'verdict': 'match'}

Step 2 is the part I did not expect to enjoy this much. next: ('judge',) is the graph parked, and it tells me where it is:

stopped = app.invoke(AgentState(jd_text=JD), config)
snap = app.get_state(config)
print(snap.next)    # ('judge',) parked at the LLM door
print(snap.values)  # jd + resume chunks, attempt: 0, no score yet

The snapshot holds the job description and the extracted resume chunks with zero LLM calls spent. In copilot terms: I can check exactly what the judge will see before the judge sees it. That is a human-in-the-loop door I never planned to build; it fell out of the checkpoint for free.

Then app.invoke(None, config), where None means "continue, no new input", and step 3 confirms the resume worked: attempt: 1, not 2. The retrieve node did not run again. The run picked up exactly where it parked, including the LLM call it owed. And the part that makes this actual infrastructure: threads are isolated.

fresh = app.invoke(AgentState(jd_text=JD), {"configurable": {"thread_id": "jd-43"}})
snap = app.get_state(config)
print(fresh)        # jd-43's own run, fresh attempt
print(snap.values)  # jd-42's checkpoint, exactly where we left it

thread_id is the boundary between "this job description's run" and "every other run". When JobCopilot chews through a night batch of job descriptions, each gets its own thread_id, and every run stays inspectable after the fact, including the ones that errored. It also opens the door to durable storage later: swap MemorySaver for a persistent checkpointer and a crashed batch run resumes instead of restarting from zero. That one is on my todo list, not in my code, and this post only claims runs I actually executed.

One more honest surprise: on step 2, snap.values["match_score"] raised KeyError. Not every state field lands in the snapshot. With my pydantic state the checkpoint carries only fields written at least once, and untouched None fields are simply not there.

The outputs above are verbatim from my test run (MemorySaver + interrupt_before + pydantic state, langgraph 1.2.20). Worth repeating on your pinned langgraph.*

What changed this week

My agent's spend policy went from "run it and look" to a test suite I trust. The one-line version: test the router as a truth table, test the nodes with a fake chat, test the budget through the graph, and let checkpoints turn runs into resumable threads.

Three things this React dev learning Python took from it:

  • The patch-shape assertion turned out to be the best test in the file. It pins a contract: an undecided verdict is absent, not None. Comments describe intent; assertions enforce it.
  • The fake chat makes the LLM deterministic. Prompt content, the repair mechanism, the retry budget: all of it tested in a quarter of a second.
  • interrupt_before plus thread_id turned the graph into something more than a function call: a stored, inspectable process. next: ('judge',) might be my favorite bit of Python output so far.

Next up: the parts of the copilot that talk to the real world, or swapping the in-memory checkpointer for persistent storage if something breaks first. In case you missed it, part 3: Stop calling functions: my first LangGraph graph, where state does the calling.

Follow along if you want to watch the rest of the copilot get built, including the parts that break. Build log plus daily code at t.me/novamind_hub.

How do you test nodes that wrap an LLM call: fakes, or recorded real responses? And has checkpointing paid off in your graph?

title: El secreto para no saturar el contexto de tu IA: El patrón de agentes en capas
description:
La imagen de portada pertenece a jonakoh_

Si como yo, has utilizado la suscripción de Opencode OpencodeGo quizás te cueste llegar a fin de mes con los tokens que se ofrecen.

Tras un año usando Opencode te puedo decir que la solución no está en los prompts, sino en la forma en que implementamos distintos patrones arquitecturales para hacer el trabajo. Podemos expresar estos patrones haciendo uso de las capacidades de definir agentes dentro de un espacio de trabajo con OpenCode. Este feature desata el verdadero potencial de la herramienta. 

Hoy te enseñare el primer patrón que he descubierto haciendo utilización de los agentes mediante la creación de un tablero Kanban para demostrar su implementación.

Tipos de agentes en Opencode

En Opencode tenemos dos tipos de agentes:

  • Primarios: Son los agentes a los que se puede acceder desde la caja de interacción de la ventana principal de Opencode (shift+tab).build y plan son agentes primarios.

  • Sub-agentes: Son agentes que pueden ser invocados por los agentes primarios. El agente general y explore subagentes.

Si en nuestro proyecto creamos una carpeta llamada .opencode con una sub-carpeta llamada agents podemos definir tanto agentes primarios como secundarios en nuestro proyecto.

Layered Agent Pattern

Primero visualicemos su forma mas general antes de ir a la implementación:

En este caso vamos a hacer tenemos un esquema lineal para abrir la mente sobre la utilización de estos agentes, de a poco iremos añadiendo mas complejidad en futuras entregas.

El agente primario es el orquestador, que funciona como un bus principal donde está todo el historial de cambios del proyecto. Como es un bus principal, el objetivo es mantenerlo limpio con un contexto sumamente acotado y que pueda tener todos los mensajes de principio a fin sin necesidad de compactar ni de crear nuevas conversaciones, como se ve en la imágen:

Los subagentes tienen contextos vacíos al comienzo de cada petición, esto permite que la atención del modelo no se diluya. 

Otra cosa fundamental es acotar bien las restricciones de los agentes, esto permitirá utilizar menos tokens y reducir la incertidumbre de los agentes, permitiendo que tengan menos libertad y opciones para realizar, esto permitirá que el modelo divage menos se centre en acabar la taréa

FastKanban

El proyecto a desarrollar es un proyecto de juguete diseñado para este blog, que es un Kanban que permite crear proyectos y cada proyecto tiene su propia pizarra Kanban. Puedes definir distintas columnas y también arrastrar notas de una columna a otra, es bastante simple para no saturar el blog y poder completarlo en pocos prompts.

La definición de los agentes depende del proyecto a desarrollar, no existe una formula, es parte de la ingeniería del proyecto. Para este proyecto decidí usar el siguiente Stack Tecnologico:

  • Next.JS: Framework web fullstack.
  • Sqlite: Base de datos en un archivo. 

Estas decisiones fueron tomadas para facilitar el proceso de creación. 

La carpeta de mi proyecto tiene los siguiente contenidos:

.
└── .opencode
    └── agents
        ├── auditor.md
        ├── backend.md
        ├── database.md
        ├── frontend.md
        ├── integrador.md
        ├── orchestrator.md
        └── qa.md

Los contenidos de cada archivo son:

auditor.md

---
description: "Audita el código buscando antipatrones y fallos de arquitectura. Solo lectura."
mode: subagent
steps: 8
permissions:
  - action: "*"
    resource: "*"
    effect: deny
  - action: read
    resource: "*"
    effect: allow
  - action: shell
    resource: "git diff*"
    effect: allow
---

Eres el auditor de calidad.

OBJETIVO
Detectar código duplicado, funciones huérfanas o antipatrones mediante `git diff`.

FORMATO DE SALIDA (máximo 12 líneas)
`ruta:línea severidad hallazgo` (ordenado por alta, media, baja). Si no hay fallos: `OK`.

Como podemos observar los permisos son limitados, primero se deniegan todas las acciones, para luego definir las acciones permitidas. En este caso el auditor puede leer archivos pero no ejecutar comandos de shell libremente.

backend.md

---
description: Implementa rutas de API y lógica de servidor en Next.js.
mode: subagent
steps: 8
permissions:
  - action: "*"
    resource: "*"
    effect: deny
  - action: read
    resource: "*"
    effect: allow
  - action: edit
    resource: "*"
    effect: allow
  - action: glob
    resource: "*"
    effect: allow
---

Eres el desarrollador backend de Next.js.

OBJETIVO
Implementar los endpoints (API Routes del App Router) requeridos por el orquestador.

REGLAS
- Cambios mínimos. Limítate a la carpeta `src/app/api/`.
- Conéctate limpiamente con Prisma. No edites componentes gráficos (frontend).

FORMATO DE SALIDA (máximo 20 líneas)
- Archivos tocados (rutas).
- Endpoints implementados.
- Bloqueos o decisiones pendientes.

Aquí debemos ser mas permisivos para que el agente pueda trabajar

database.md

---
description: Crea esquemas de base de datos y migraciones con Prisma y SQLite.
mode: subagent
steps: 8
permissions:
  - action: "*"
    resource: "*"
    effect: deny
  - action: read
    resource: "*"
    effect: allow
  - action: edit
    resource: "*"
    effect: allow
  - action: glob
    resource: "*"
    effect: allow
  - action: shell
    resource: "*"
    effect: allow
---

Eres el especialista en base de datos.

OBJETIVO
Implementar esquemas en `prisma/schema.prisma` y funciones con SQLite mediante Prisma.

REGLAS
- Cambios mínimos. No toques archivos de UI ni rutas de API.
- Motor: SQLite. ORM: Prisma.

FORMATO DE SALIDA (máximo 20 líneas)
- Archivos tocados (rutas).
- Comandos ejecutados y resultado (OK/FALLO).
- Decisiones o bloqueos.
No vuelques código completo en la respuesta.

frontend.md

---
description: Implementa componentes y páginas de la interfaz en Next.js y Tailwind CSS.
mode: subagent
steps: 8
permissions:
  - action: "*"
    resource: "*"
    effect: deny
  - action: read
    resource: "*"
    effect: allow
  - action: edit
    resource: "*"
    effect: allow
  - action: glob
    resource: "*"
    effect: allow
---

Eres el desarrollador frontend.

OBJETIVO
Implementar vistas y componentes en Next.js utilizando Tailwind CSS.

REGLAS
- Cambios mínimos. Limítate a `src/app/` (vistas y componentes visuales).
- No modifiques esquemas de base de datos ni lógica de servidor interna.

FORMATO DE SALIDA (máximo 20 líneas)
- Archivos tocados (rutas).
- Componentes creados o modificados.
- Bloqueos o decisiones pendientes.

---
description: Ejecuta pruebas, typecheck y compilación del proyecto Next.js. Solo lectura.
mode: subagent
steps: 10
permissions:
  - action: "*"
    resource: "*"
    effect: deny
  - action: read
    resource: "*"
    effect: allow
  - action: glob
    resource: "*"
    effect: allow
  - action: shell
    resource: "npm run *"
    effect: allow
  - action: shell
    resource: "npx tsc *"
    effect: allow
  - action: shell
    resource: "npx vitest *"
    effect: allow
---

Eres QA del proyecto.

OBJETIVO
Verificar la compilación, tipos y pruebas del código sin alterarlo (solo lectura).

FORMATO DE SALIDA (máximo 15 líneas)
- Comando ejecutado y resultado (OK/FALLO).
- Error exacto con `archivo:línea` si aplica.
- Siguiente acción recomendada.

Y por ultimo el orquestador, como veremos el orquestador esta bastante limitado y tiene todos los subagentes como recursos a su disposicion. Se enfoca en la comunicación y acotar la petición con preguntas:

---
description: Pregunta al usuario, define el alcance mínimo y delega en el equipo de Next.js y base de datos. No lee ni edita código.
mode: primary
steps: 12
permissions:
  - action: "*"
    resource: "*"
    effect: deny
  - action: question
    resource: "*"
    effect: allow
  - action: subagent
    resource: "backend"
    effect: allow
  - action: subagent
    resource: "frontend"
    effect: allow
  - action: subagent
    resource: "database"
    effect: allow
  - action: subagent
    resource: "qa"
    effect: allow
  - action: subagent
    resource: "auditor"
    effect: allow
---

Eres el orquestador de un equipo que construye una aplicación Next.js con Prisma y SQLite.

TU ROL
- Hablas con el usuario y delegas. No lees archivos, no escribes código y no ejecutas comandos.
- Usa la herramienta `question` para decisiones de alcance. Si la petición es clara, delega directo.

DESCOMPOSICIÓN Y FLUJO
- Si una tarea mezcla áreas distintas (DB, API, UI, tests), divídela antes de delegar.
- Cada llamada a un subagente pide un cambio mínimo y verificable en una sola área.
- Orden recomendado: Esquema DB → API/Backend → Componentes Frontend → Tests → Auditoría e Integración.

AHORRO DE TOKENS (OBLIGATORIO)
- No repitas contexto; envía a cada trabajador solo lo que necesita.
- Limita los informes de los subagentes a un máximo de 20 líneas.
- Responde en español, breve y directo.

Habiendo mostrado las instrucciones de cada agente vamos con los prompts que se hicieron para el desarrollo del proyecto.

Desarrollo 

Para desarrollar yo opto por usar un archivo llamado prompts.md que es mi fuente de verdad por si algún día necesito recrear el proyecto. también de esta manera puedo trabajar mejor el formato de cada petición.

Prompt 1: Vista de proyectos


Crea la vista inicial (#1: Dashboard de Proyectos) para la aplicación FastKanban usando Next.js (App Router, TypeScript y Tailwind CSS).

Requerimientos de la vista:
1. Estado Vacío (sin proyectos):
   - Mostrar un botón principal cuadrado con bordes punteados (border-dashed) que diga "Agregar proyecto".
2. Lista de Proyectos (con datos presentes):
   - Renderizar una cuadrícula (grid) de tarjetas de proyectos.
   - Cada tarjeta debe mostrar el nombre del proyecto y un preview temporal que diga "Proyecto 1" (placeholder mientras se implementa la vista detallada del Kanban).
   - Incluir el botón "Agregar proyecto" al final de la lista.
3. Funcionalidad mínima:
   - Manejar un estado local/simulado para alternar entre el estado vacío y la lista de proyectos al hacer clic en "Agregar proyecto".

Instrucciones para los agentes:
- Limitarse estrictamente a la Vista #1.
- No implementar el tablero Kanban detallado aún.

Prompt 2: DB Proyectos

Implementa la base de datos para la vista de proyectos:
- Los proyectos tienen un nombre.
- Una fecha de creación.
- Una fecha de actualización.
- Un Blob para el preview (Por ahora un placeholder).

Prompt 3: Tablero Kanban


Crea un tablero de Kanban para los proyectos:

1. Sidebar:
    - Un botón para crear colas.
        - Cuando se presione el botón debe aparecer un dialog para escoger el color de la cola y el nombre.
            - Para el color un color picker. 
            - Para el nombre un input estilizado. 

2. El tablero de kanban con las colas:
    - Cada cola tiene que tener el nombre y su color en la parte superior.
    - Un espacio mas oscuro para delimitar la colulmna.
    - Cada cola ocupa una columna con un overflow.

3. Cuando se haga click en la cola:
    - Aparece un dialog para agregar la nota con soporte para markdown.
    - El dialog tiene un look como de postit con el color correspondiente a la cola.
    - El texto debe ser blanco o negro dependiendo del color de cada cola.
    - No debe tener un campo para el titulo de la nota explicito.
    - El titulo de la nota es el primer header de la nota y si no tiene se pone como (sin titulo).
    - Hay un hint al principio que indica que el titulo es el primer header. 

4. La nota en la cola:
    - Se representa como un titulo con su contenido parcial oculto con ...

5. Cuando arrastro una nota:
    - La puedo cambiar de cola lo que hara mutar so color.
    - Hay una animación drag and drop con framer-motion.

6. Esquema de datos:
    - La nota tiene que tener los campos:
        - Titulo.
        - Fecha de cracion.
        - Fecha de actualización.
        - Cola a la que pertenece.
        - Proyecto al cual pertenece (FK)
    - La cola debe tener los campos:
        - Titulo
        - Fecha de creación
        - Color
        - Proyecto al cual pertenece (FK)
Cualquier detalle omitido debera ser tomado en cuenta para la creación la compatibulidad


 

Prompt 4: Limpieza y detalles

1. La nota al arrastrarla debe quedar por encima de todos los elementos de la pagina.
2. Añadir soporte para quitar colas (un botón X arriba a la derecha de cada cola).
3. Añadir soporte para quitar notas (Un botón X arriba a la derecha de cada nota).
4. En la pantalla principal al crear un proyecto debe existir un dialogo que te permita definir el titulo del proyecto. 
5. Soporte de edición de los titulos de proyecto y las notas: Si clickeo cualquier de una cola o un proyecto debo poder editarlo. Se indica con un lapiz y un background gris al hacer hover en el elemento. 
6. Verificar que todos los elementos tengan un CRUD completo en el frontend.
7. Agregar un botón de navegación para volver a la ventana de proyectos.

Prompt 5: Ultimos detalles

Corrige los puntos.

1. Integra los snapshots y mejora los cards de proyectos.
    - Un header gris con el nombre 
    - En el cuerpo un snapshot del kanban creado
    - Si no hay un kanban reemplazar por una tarjeta en blanco 
2. Modo oscuro:
    - Para la vista de proyectos y vista del kanban.

Y estos son los prompts que utilice en este proyecto. Por la misma naturaleza del proyecto no se necesitaron mas recursos.

Adjunto algunas imágenes del resultado

Conclusión

En lo personal este patrón me ha ayudado a ahorrar tokens al momento de crear una gran variedad de proyecto, si bien este no es el único patrón de mi caja de herramientas es una base solida para ir mejorando. Es adaptable a cada necesidad y se pueden encadenar distintas rutinas de utilizacion de herramientas de auditoria como SonarQube, ReactDoctor, entre otras. Cada agente puede tener un stack de herramientas a las que puede recurrir y eso hace que esta forma de plantear la utilización de la herramienta sea bastante flexible. 

Si bien este es el inicio de una serie de artículos sobre ingeniería de agentes aplicada a Opencode creo que es una base solida para ir construyendo intuición sobre una utilización mas avanzada de la herramienta

¿Que opinas de este patron de diseño?. Dímelo en la caja de comentarios.

title: 0/55 three nights in a row: product bug or test bug?
description:
Our nightly evaluation gate went 0/55 three nights in a row. The third time, the product was completely fine and the harness was the one lying. Telling those apart is the hardest testing problem we have hit this year, and the discipline that solved it is simple to state: no fix gets pushed until the red run has a named cause with evidence.

The setup. We sell conversational AI employees, so the thing that must work is a conversation. The nightly harness provisions a real employee through MCP for each of 55 cases across 6 suites (booking, student FAQs, email orders, ERP lookups, log review, YouTube backoffice), replays the conversation against production, and asserts two things per case: the right tools ran, and a judge model scores the reply against a rubric. The gate fails below 80% on product-backed cases. This is evaluation-driven development: the cases are written from the use case's intent, and the nightly is the reference curve, not the target.

Night one: 0/55, cause named. Every conversation died with a 401 on turn one. The client sent the standard X-Api-Key header; the auth code only matched a converted-underscores variant (x_api_key) because of how the framework lowercases parameter names. One customer-facing symptom, one line of auth code, every external client broken. Fixed, and a regression test now covers all three accepted spellings.

Night two: 0/55, a different cause. The policy engine's gate hook read arguments from a function signature that had been refactored away. Every reply became "name 'kwargs' is not defined". Two things made this one instructive. First, the error was invisible in the product: users just saw the fallback reply. Second, we had a day earlier merged a fix whose tests were green, because no test imported the module that broke. The suite now has a static check that fails when a handler references variables its own signature does not define.

Night three: 0/55, and the product was fine. Probing by hand, a booking conversation worked end to end: the agent checked the calendar, offered slots, booked, confirmed. But the gate still said 0.304. Reading the transcripts line by line found three harness defects stacked on top of each other. The fixtures (calendar events, client catalogs) were injected into the system prompt, so the agent never needed to call a tool, and tool-expecting cases failed with zero calls. A skill assignment wrote one table while activation read another, so assigned skills were silently inert. And the response contract changed shape, so the gate was reading evidence from an empty field. None of these were product bugs. All of them made the product look dead.

The discipline that paid. Each red run got a named cause with evidence before any fix was pushed: an API probe that reproduces the failure in isolation, or a transcript line that proves the claim. The alternative is what we did the first day: two theories, two pushed fixes, both wrong, four CI cycles wasted. Reading the actual log before theorizing sounds obvious. Under a red nightly at midnight it is not obvious at all; it is the only thing that works.

What the gate measures now. With the harness fixed, the number finally means what it says: the 0.304 pass rate measured a real gap, the gap between what the product serves today (booking, email handoff, lead capture) and what the case suites contract (ERP flows, invoicing, scheduled reports). That is not overfitting, that is a roadmap with a number on it. The gate only blocks on the product-backed suites, and the full 55 keep running as the curve.

If you are building anything conversational, the takeaway is one sentence: separate the judge from the judged, and never let either of them skip a named cause. The product behind this one is Optimly, and the nightly curve is how it earns the right to ship on a Tuesday afternoon.

title: How Often Do AI Labs Ship New Models? Release Cadence of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek and Mistral (2024-2026)
description:
Research scope: This study counts releases listed in the official API changelogs of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek and Mistral, read on November 10, 2026. Each date is the first day a new text model name appeared in the API (experimental, preview or generally available), January 2024 to October 2026. It measures how often models ship, not their quality or price, and counts depend on how each developer names and bundles models.

Short answer: Across 11 full quarters from January 2024 to September 2026, five developers released 135 new text models in their public APIs. Counting January to September only, releases rose from 23 models in 2024 to 44 in 2025, then held at 40 in 2026. We call the main pattern the Decimal Clock: the median gap between new version numbers fell from 112 to 63 days, while whole-number generations still arrived 308 to 496 days apart.

What did we count?

We audited text model releases across five provider changelogs on November 10, 2026. The primary sources include the OpenAI API changelog, the Anthropic Claude Platform release notes, the Google Gemini API release notes, the DeepSeek API news page, and the Mistral changelog. For the Claude 3 family, we included Anthropic's launch announcements from March 4 and March 13, 2024, which predate its formal platform release notes. Each row in our dataset represents a distinct text model name, defined as a new family, a new version number, or a new tier, on the exact date it first surfaced in the public API.

We excluded several categories to keep the count focused strictly on distinct text model releases. Our count omits dated snapshots of an existing name, such as gpt-4o-2024-08-06 or DeepSeek-V3-0324, along with generic latest aliases. It leaves out models restricted to approved organizations, tool-specific releases for computer use, deep research, or search, and third-party models hosted by a provider. We also excluded audio, image, video, embedding, moderation, and OCR models.

Across the 11 quarters from Q1 2024 to Q3 2026, the five developers released 135 text models across 101 combined launch days. Mistral released 42 models across 28 launch days, while OpenAI published 40 models across 26 launch days. Anthropic introduced 22 models across 20 launch days, Google added 19 models across 17 launch days, and DeepSeek delivered 12 models across 10 launch days.

Developers differ in how many model sizes they drop at a single time. OpenAI averaged 1.54 models per launch day, closely matched by Mistral at 1.50 models per launch day. DeepSeek averaged 1.20 models per launch event, Google posted 1.12, and Anthropic averaged 1.10.

Finding 1: Releases doubled in 2025 and moved to the US big three in 2026

Total model releases across the five developers rose through 2024 and 2025 and stayed high in 2026. The count ran at 5 models in Q1 2024, 7 in Q2 2024, 11 in Q3 2024, and 9 in Q4 2024. Volume accelerated to 12 models in Q1 2025, 16 in Q2 2025, and 16 in Q3 2025, reaching a peak of 19 models in Q4 2025, the busiest quarter in the dataset. Activity settled into 2026 with 12 models in Q1, 11 in Q2, and 17 in Q3.

Comparing the identical nine-month stretch from January to September across calendar years shows this expansion clearly. The five providers published 23 models during the first nine months of 2024, 44 models in the same period of 2025, and 40 models in the first nine months of 2026. While the overall volume in 2026 matched the pace set in 2025, the source of those releases shifted heavily toward OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.

OpenAI, Anthropic and Google increased their output in each of these nine-month periods. Together, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google shipped 11 models between January and September 2024, 24 models in that span in 2025, and 32 models in 2026. OpenAI went from 4 models to 14 and then 15; Anthropic scaled from 4 to 5 and then 10; Google increased from 3 to 5 and then 7.

DeepSeek and Mistral moved the other way or stayed low. Mistral went from 10 models in the first nine months of 2024 to 17 in 2025, but dropped to 4 in 2026. DeepSeek held steady at lower volumes, moving from 2 models in 2024 to 3 in 2025 and 4 in 2026. The shift was clearest in Q3 2026, when OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google accounted for 15 of the 17 total releases, compared to just 6 of 16 models in Q3 2025. Mistral listed zero new text models in Q3 2026 before introducing Mistral Large 4 in preview on October 6, 2026.


New text model names by the quarter they first appeared in each developer's official API changelog. Snapshots, aliases, restricted-access and non-text models are not counted.

Finding 2: The Decimal Clock

Our primary finding is the Decimal Clock: on the main model line of each developer, the median time between new version numbers (for example GPT-5.4 to GPT-5.5) fell from 112 days for the 19 gaps that ended in 2024 to 2025 to 63 days for the 21 gaps that ended from January to October 2026, while whole-number generations (for example GPT-5 to GPT-6) still arrived 308 to 496 days apart. We track this metric along each lab's primary text sequence: OpenAI GPT, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, DeepSeek V, and Mistral Large. Shorter gaps mean more point releases between whole-number generations.

From January to October 2026, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google each shipped six new version numbers along their primary lines. OpenAI shipped GPT-5.3, 5.4, 5.5, 5.6, 6, and 6.1. Anthropic published Claude 4.6, 4.7, 4.8, 5, 5.1, and 5.5. Google deployed Gemini 3.1, 3.5, 3.6, 3.7, 3.8, and 4.

This tempo represents a sharp break from 2025. Across all twelve months of 2025, OpenAI shipped five main-line versions, Anthropic shipped four, and Google released two. Those 2025 releases included OpenAI GPT-4.5, 4.1, 5, 5.1, and 5.2, Anthropic Claude 3.7, 4, 4.1, and 4.5, and Google Gemini 2.5 and 3.

Comparing gaps that closed in 2024 to 2025 against those closing between January and October 2026 shows how the cadence contracted. OpenAI saw its median interval between version updates fall from 98 days to 53 days. Anthropic shortened its median gap from 87 days to 56 days. Google registered the most dramatic acceleration, dropping its median gap from 238 days to 52 days. Across all five providers, the median time separating version numbers dropped from 112 days to 63 days.

The fastest updates in 2026 arrived in a matter of days. OpenAI moved from GPT-5.3 on February 24 to GPT-5.4 on March 5, a gap of just 9 days. Anthropic moved from Claude Opus 4.8 on May 28 to Claude Fable 5 on June 9, an interval of 12 days. Google advanced from Gemini 3.7 Flash on August 13 to Gemini 3.8 Flash on September 2, taking 20 days.

DeepSeek and Mistral operated on a more extended schedule. DeepSeek recorded a median gap of 112 days across 3 version intervals in 2024 to 2025, followed by 173 days across 2 intervals in 2026. Mistral Large posted a median gap of 149 days across 3 intervals in 2024 to 2025, followed by 308 days for its single gap in 2026. These samples are small.


Main lines only: OpenAI GPT, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, DeepSeek V and Mistral Large. Each dot is the first API date of a new version number.


Median days between consecutive new version numbers on each main line, grouped by the year the gap ended. DeepSeek and Mistral rest on 1 to 3 gaps.

Finding 3: Whole-number generations still take about a year

While point releases sped up in 2026, whole-number generations stayed far apart. The median interval across all eight whole-number model transitions in the dataset was 387.5 days. Developers iterated on decimal increments at high frequency, but whole-number versions still arrived roughly ten to sixteen months apart.

The three longest transitions took well over a year. Mistral Large 2 to Mistral Large 3 took 496 days, running from July 24, 2024 to December 2, 2025. DeepSeek V3 to DeepSeek V4 took 484 days, spanning December 26, 2024 to April 24, 2026. Claude 3 to Claude 4 required 444 days, stretching from March 4, 2024 to May 22, 2025.

Generational transitions inside OpenAI and Anthropic clustered close to the one-year mark. GPT-5 to GPT-6 took 392 days, running from August 7, 2025 to September 3, 2026. Claude 4 to Claude 5 arrived after 383 days, dating from May 22, 2025 to June 9, 2026.

The three shortest transitions belong to Google and Mistral. Gemini 2.0 to Gemini 3 took 342 days between December 11, 2024 and November 18, 2025, while Gemini 3 to Gemini 4 arrived 329 days later on October 13, 2026. Mistral Large 3 to Mistral Large 4 recorded 308 days between December 2, 2025 and October 6, 2026. In 2026, the decimals sped up while the whole numbers stayed near one year apart.


Days between the first API release of consecutive whole-number versions on each main line.

Finding 4: Google moved to generally available Flash releases

Google changed how new models first appear in its API. All 12 Google models first listed in 2024 and 2025 appeared as experimental or preview releases. In 2026, 6 of Google's 8 new models launched with general availability on the day they first appeared, starting with Gemini 3.5 Flash on May 19, 2026.

Most of Google's 2026 releases were Flash models: 6 of its 8 new models were Flash or Flash-Lite. The company released Gemini 3.5 Flash on May 19, Gemini 3.6 Flash on July 21, Gemini 3.7 Flash on August 13, and Gemini 3.8 Flash on September 2. That cadence delivered four successive Flash versions within 106 days.

After Google listed Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview on February 19, 2026, it did not introduce another non-Flash Gemini model until Gemini 4 Argon arrived on October 13, 2026.

Across all five developers, the proportion of models launching without general availability held relatively stable. Non-GA models represented 21.9% of total releases in 2024, 19.0% in 2025, and 18.2% in 2026. These figures include Mistral Labs models and DeepSeek's temporary V3.2-Speciale, which both counted as not generally available at launch.

Finding 5: New tier names replace size words

In 2026, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and DeepSeek each introduced tier names that were not in their 2024 and 2025 lineups. OpenAI released its final mini and nano models within our observation window on March 17, 2026, with GPT-5.4 mini and GPT-5.4 nano. When OpenAI launched GPT-5.6 on July 9, 2026, it introduced Sol, Terra, and Luna, and followed with Astra alongside GPT-6 on September 3, 2026. Exactly 8 of the 16 models OpenAI published between January and October 2026 used these new naming conventions.

Anthropic also broadened its tiered naming structure beyond its established sizes. On June 9, 2026, the developer introduced Claude Fable 5, creating a fourth tier alongside Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku. It expanded that tier on September 1, 2026, with the introduction of Claude Fable 5.1.

Other providers also drifted away from conventional naming schemes. Google dropped the Pro and Flash designations for its primary generation launch, introducing Gemini 4 as Gemini 4 Argon on October 13, 2026. DeepSeek V4, launched on April 24, 2026, came as two models: V4 Pro and V4 Flash.

Mistral preserved its established tier naming of Large, Medium, Small, and Ministral while releasing specialized models across specific disciplines. Across Mistral's 43 total rows, 9 models targeted software development under the Codestral and Devstral lines. Another 6 rows represented reasoning models under the Magistral label, and 3 rows covered mathematics through the Mathstral and Leanstral series.

What this means for teams that build on these APIs

With version gaps at the big three sitting at a median of 53 to 56 days, an engineering team pinned to specific model identifiers encounters a new version roughly every two months from each provider. Managing updates can no longer be handled as an annual project. Engineering groups must treat prompt evaluation and model migration as continuous routines rather than rare maintenance events.

Teams should keep model identifiers stored strictly in configuration files and environment variables rather than hardcoded inside application logic. Decoupling the codebase from explicit model tags reduces migration friction when newer decimals land. A gateway such as Tokely lets you switch the model name without changing the integration.

New tier names like Sol, Terra, Luna, Fable, Argon, and Flash require independent testing against existing production workloads. Teams cannot rely on legacy size words or familiar brand tiers to deduce performance characteristics, latency profiles, or pricing structures. Direct evaluation against your own task distributions is necessary before routing production traffic to newly released model tiers.

Methodology and limitations

We compiled this dataset by reviewing official changelogs on November 10, 2026, verifying each entry against its public source URL on that date. Each release date reflects the timestamp assigned by the provider in its official changelog. These entry dates can differ by a day or so from blog announcements.

Release counts depend heavily on how individual developers package, brand, and bundle their models. A lab that introduces multiple sizes on a single day logs multiple models in this dataset, which is why launch days should be considered alongside raw model counts. In addition, the cadence medians calculated for DeepSeek and Mistral rest on small samples of 1 to 3 gaps, meaning individual release decisions sway their metrics significantly.

Our analysis deliberately omits providers and models that do not meet strict documentation criteria. We excluded xAI because its release notes list updates by month rather than specific calendar days and do not list all earlier Grok models. OpenAI's gpt-oss open-weight models do not appear in the OpenAI API changelog and are not tracked here.

Our version gap calculations track main lines only, covering GPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek V, and Mistral Large. While OpenAI's o-series and Mistral's specialized coding, math, and reasoning lines appear in the raw dataset, we excluded them from the median gap figures. This study measures API release velocity over time and does not measure output quality, inference latency, or pricing changes.

Download the data

One CSV with 139 rows contains the raw data across the observation window, covering developer, date, quarter, model ID, line, version, tier, stage, source URL, and verification date. Cite as: Tokely, "How Often Do AI Labs Ship New Models? Release Cadence of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek and Mistral (2024-2026)", November 2026, https://tokely.me/blog/ai-model-release-cadence-2026.

Originally published at tokely.me.

title: How we did entity resolution with a vector DB and Argon
description:
This article was originally published on the Actian blog.

In this tutorial, you'll build an entity resolution pipeline in Python that finds the same product listed twice across two catalogs. Actian VectorAI DB blocks each record to its 10 nearest neighbors, a similarity threshold settles the clear-cut pairs, and Gemini 4 Argon decides only the uncertain band, returning a match decision with a one-sentence reason. Everything except the Argon calls runs on your own machine.

On the Abt-Buy benchmark, the threshold alone reached an F1 of 0.813. With Argon on the uncertain pairs, F1 rose to 0.915 and precision to 0.998, for $0.76 per 1,000 records. All code is in the companion repo. If you're in a hurry, follow steps 1 to 3 and skip to step 8.

Results at a glance

Stage Abt-Buy result
Blocking Kept 10,810 of 1,180,452 possible pairs (99.08% removed) and 99.0% of true matches
Threshold only F1 0.813
With Argon on the uncertain band F1 0.915, precision 0.998
Sent to Argon 13.2% of candidate pairs, 1,001 of 7,570 on the test split
Cost $1.41 at OpenRouter's charges, or $0.76 per 1,000 records in the test split

Prerequisites

  • You need Docker with the Compose plugin.
  • You need uv, the Python package manager, which installs a compatible Python for you.
  • You need Ollama to run the embedding model locally.
  • You need a Gemini 4 Argon key, either an OpenRouter key with a few dollars of credit or a Google AI Studio or Google Cloud key with billing turned on. Argon has no free tier, and the Abt-Buy run cost $1.41.
  • You need about 3 GB of free disk for the database image and the embedding model. Everything runs on a CPU.

VectorAI DB needs no separate install, because step 1 runs Community Edition in Docker. Each benchmark fits under its 5,000-vector cap, one at a time. Install uv if you don't have it.

# macOS or Linux
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

# Windows (PowerShell)
irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex

How the pipeline works

Entity resolution, also called record linkage or entity matching, runs in three steps. Blocking cuts the pairs down to candidates, comparison scores each candidate, and matching makes the final call. This build gives each step its own tool.

  • VectorAI DB does the blocking, returning each record's nearest neighbors from the other table so the pipeline scores 10 candidates per record.
  • EmbeddingGemma, run locally through Ollama, turns each record into a 768-dimensional vector.
  • A similarity threshold auto-matches confident pairs and rejects clear non-matches.
  • Gemini 4 Argon decides the uncertain band in between and gives a one-sentence reason.
  • resolve.py connects them and scores the results against the benchmark's known matches.

Records are embedded and blocked in VectorAI DB, and the similarity score routes each candidate pair to an auto-match, a rejection, or Argon

The examples use Abt-Buy from the Leipzig benchmark collection, with 1,081 Abt products, 1,092 Buy products, and a gold file of 1,097 true matches. Comparing every Abt record with every Buy record would mean 1,180,452 pairs.

1. Start VectorAI DB

Clone the companion repo and move into the project folder. Every command from here on runs in this folder.

git clone https://github.com/actian-devs/developer-content.git
cd developer-content/blog/entity-resolution-vectorai

The repo's docker-compose.yml starts VectorAI DB. The ACTIAN_VECTORAI_ACCEPT_EULA=YES line accepts Actian's license for you, so read it before you start the container.

services:
  vectorai:
    image: actian/vectorai:1.0.2
    container_name: vectorai
    ports:
      - "6573:6573" # REST
      - "6574:6574" # gRPC (Python SDK)
      - "6575:6575" # Local UI
    volumes:
      - ./vectorai_data:/var/lib/actian-vectorai
    environment:
      - ACTIAN_VECTORAI_ACCEPT_EULA=YES
    restart: unless-stopped

docker compose up -d
docker ps

The container should show Up. The Python SDK talks to it over gRPC on port 6574.

The Community Edition's 5,000-vector cap covers the whole server, and deleted vectors kept counting against it until the container restarted. The harness drops its own old collections. If it still reports the cap, run docker compose restart vectorai.

2. Pull the embedding model

EmbeddingGemma is about 620 MB.

ollama pull embeddinggemma

Ollama serves it on localhost:11434, and the harness calls it there. Nothing leaves your machine at this stage.

3. Install Python dependencies

The repo already includes pyproject.toml, and its uv.lock pins the exact versions used, such as actian-vectorai-client 1.0.3 and google-genai 2.31.0.

[project]
name = "entity-resolution-vectorai"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Entity resolution with VectorAI DB blocking and Gemini 4 Argon on the ambiguous band"
requires-python = ">=3.11,<3.14"
# `uv run resolve.py` reads this, creates .venv and installs these on first run
dependencies = [
    "actian-vectorai-client",  # VectorAI DB client (gRPC)
    "google-genai",            # Gemini API, for the Argon pass
    "pandas",
    "numpy",
    "pydantic",                # Argon's structured-output schema
    "requests",                # benchmark download
    "matplotlib",              # score-distribution chart
]

[project.optional-dependencies]
st = ["sentence-transformers"]   # in-process embedding models: uv sync --extra st, then --embed-backend sentence-transformers

uv sync

From here on, start each command with uv run. You don't need to activate an environment.

4. Load and embed the records

The source table goes into each point's payload, because step 5 filters on it, so an Abt record is only ever compared with Buy records. Embedding is the slowest step on a CPU, so the harness caches the vectors, and reruns skip it. The code below is the core of load() in er/data.py, embed()in er/embed.py, and load_records() in er/block.py.

import numpy as np
import requests
from actian_vectorai import Distance, PointStruct, VectorAIClient, VectorParams

def to_text(row, fields):
    # "name: Sony Bravia 40in LCD TV | price: $899.99" (empty fields are skipped)
    return " | ".join(f"{f}: {row[f].strip()}" for f in fields if row[f].strip())

def embed(texts, model="embeddinggemma", url="http://localhost:11434", batch=64):
    out = []
    for i in range(0, len(texts), batch):
        r = requests.post(f"{url}/api/embed", json={"model": model, "input": texts[i:i + batch]}, timeout=600)
        r.raise_for_status()
        out.extend(r.json()["embeddings"])
    v = np.asarray(out, dtype=np.float32)
    return v / np.linalg.norm(v, axis=1, keepdims=True)   # unit length, so cosine score = dot product

vectors = embed([text for _, _, text in records])          # records: (source, record_id, text)

with VectorAIClient("localhost:6574") as db:
    if db.collections.exists("er_abt_buy"):   # start clean, so the step can be rerun
        db.collections.delete("er_abt_buy")
    db.collections.create("er_abt_buy", vectors_config=VectorParams(
        size=vectors.shape[1], distance=Distance.Cosine))
    points = [PointStruct(id=i, vector=v.tolist(), payload={"source": src, "record_id": rid, "text": t})
              for i, ((src, rid, t), v) in enumerate(zip(records, vectors))]
    for start in range(0, len(points), 500):   # upsert in batches
        db.points.upsert("er_abt_buy", points[start:start + 500])

5. Block with VectorAI DB

The blocking query runs once per Abt record and asks for its K nearest Buy records, with a must filter on the source field so the search only returns records from the other table. Zeakis et al. evaluated 12 language models on 17 entity resolution benchmarks, including how well their embeddings block. This is the core of neighbors () in er/block.py.

from actian_vectorai import Field, FilterBuilder, VectorAIClient

K = 10
TOTAL_RECORDS = len(records)   # Abt + Buy: a limit this high returns every Buy record
abt_ids = [rid for src, rid, _ in records if src == "abt"]
abt_vectors = vectors[:len(abt_ids)]   # records lists every Abt record first
other_source = FilterBuilder().must(Field("source").eq("buy")).build()

def search(db, vectors, limit):
    out = []
    for i in range(0, len(vectors), 100):   # search_batch takes up to 100 queries per call
        out += db.points.search_batch("er_abt_buy", [
            {"vector": v.tolist(), "limit": limit, "filter": other_source, "with_payload": True}
            for v in vectors[i:i + 100]])
    return out

ranked, todo, limit = {}, list(range(len(abt_ids))), K * 10   # over-fetch, then keep the top K
with VectorAIClient("localhost:6574") as db:
    while todo:
        short = []
        for i, hits in zip(todo, search(db, abt_vectors[todo], limit)):
            ranked[abt_ids[i]] = sorted(((h.payload["record_id"], h.score) for h in hits),
                                        key=lambda x: -x[1])[:K]
            if len(hits) < K and limit < TOTAL_RECORDS:   # stop once the limit covers the table
                short.append(i)
        todo, limit = short, min(limit * 4, TOTAL_RECORDS)   # retry any record still short

Over-fetch when you filter

On VectorAI DB 1.0.2 with the 1.0.3 Python client, a search_batch call with limit=10 and the source = buy filter came back short for 1,075 of the 1,081 Abt records, with 3.9 results on average. The filtered results looked like the Buy records among roughly the limit nearest records overall. The predicate filters guide says filters apply during the search, so treat this as what 1.0.2 did on this collection.

Raising hnsw_ef to 256 changed nothing, and 1.0.2 rejects adding a payload index to an existing collection. Asking for 10 × K and keeping the top K fixed it. Every record got its 10 candidates, and 99.95% of them matched an exact brute-force search. On customer or supplier data, the samemust clause can rule out a pair completely, such as a different country. Raise the limit until every record gets its K, because the more records a filter excludes, the fewer of the nearest records pass it.

Read the reduction ratio and pair completeness together

The reduction ratio is the share of all pairs that blocking removed. Pair completeness is the share of true matches that survived blocking, and it caps recall for the whole pipeline.

import pandas as pd

candidates = {(abt_id, buy_id): score for abt_id, hits in ranked.items() for buy_id, score in hits}
n_buy = len(records) - len(abt_ids)
gold = set(map(tuple, pd.read_csv("data/abt-buy/abt_buy_perfectMapping.csv").astype(str).values))
rr = 1 - len(candidates) / (len(abt_ids) * n_buy)
pc = len(gold & candidates.keys()) / len(gold)
K Candidate pairs Reduction ratio Pair completeness
1 1,081 99.91% 81.9%
3 3,243 99.73% 94.5%
5 5,405 99.54% 97.0%
10 10,810 99.08% 99.0%
20 21,620 98.17% 99.7%

K = 10 removed 99.08% of the comparison space and kept 99.0% of the true matches. K = 20 adds 0.7 points of pair completeness for twice the candidates. Pick the smallest K whose pair completeness you can live with.

One square per 1,000 pairs on Abt-Buy. VectorAI DB kept 10,810 of the 1,180,452 possible pairs, and Argon read 1,001 of them

6. Score the candidates and set the band

The baseline is a best-match threshold, where each Abt record's nearest candidate is a match if its similarity clears one cutoff. On the test split, the best cutoff was 0.562, with precision 0.820, recall 0.806, and F1 0.813. One global cutoff over all 10 candidates per record scored only 0.522.

All 136 false matches sit inside the band, between 0.56 and 0.84, mixed in with true matches

The harness holds out 30% of the Abt records as a development split to set the cutoff and both band edges, and every result is reported on the remaining 70%.

  • The upper edge is the lowest score above which best matches reach 95% precision on the development split. Best matches above it are auto-matched.
  • The lower edge is the highest score below which at most 5% of true matches fall, capped at the baseline's cutoff. Pairs below it are rejected.
  • Near-ties are second- or third-ranked candidates within 0.03 of their record's best, and they also enter the band. 18% of true matches aren't their record's top candidate.

This code comes from er/bands.py, which also holds the helpers rank_and_gap(), best_match(), and best_threshold().

import numpy as np

def band_edges(cand, gold, target_precision, max_miss):
    pairs = sorted(cand.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1], reverse=True)
    s = np.array([score for _, score in pairs])
    y = np.array([p in gold for p, _ in pairs], dtype=float)
    precision_above = np.cumsum(y) / np.arange(1, len(y) + 1)
    ok = np.where(precision_above >= target_precision)[0]
    upper = s[ok.max()] if len(ok) else s[0] + 1e-9   # nothing reaches the target: auto-match nothing
    missed_below = (y.sum() - np.cumsum(y)) / y.sum()   # share of matches scoring below each position
    lower = s[np.where(missed_below <= max_miss)[0].min()]
    return float(min(lower, upper)), float(upper)

def near_tie_band(cand, info, lower, upper, max_rank=3, max_gap=0.03):
    band = []
    for pair, score in cand.items():
        rank, gap = info[pair]   # rank among the record's candidates, distance below its best
        if score < lower:
            continue
        if (rank == 1 and score < upper) or (2 <= rank <= max_rank and gap <= max_gap):
            band.append(pair)
    return band

lower, upper = band_edges(dev_best, dev_gold, target_precision=0.95, max_miss=0.05)
lower = min(lower, best_cutoff)   # never reject a pair the baseline accepts
band = near_tie_band(test_candidates, info, lower, upper)

The edges landed at 0.562 and 0.841. The band held 1,001 of the 7,570 test candidates, and 206 of the baseline's 279 errors sat inside it. If Argon decided every band pair correctly, recall could rise from 0.806 to 0.897. Measure that share on your own data first, because errors outside the band can't be fixed by a second pass.

The hard pairs differ by a detail an embedding blurs. The Sharp LC37D44U scored 0.832 against an Abt listing for the LC37D64U, while the correct LC-37D64U scored 0.814 as the second candidate. Here's the first pair as the embedding model and Argon see it.

Record A (Abt): name: Sharp AQUOS 37' Black LCD HDTV - LC37D64U | description: Sharp AQUOS 37' Black LCD HDTV - LC37D64U/ 1920 x 1080p Pixel Resolution/ Up To 60,000 Hours Lamp Life/ Built-In ATSC/QAM/NTSC Tuner/ 10,000:1 Dynamic Contrast Ratio/ 4ms Response Time/ 4-Wavelength Backlight System/ Black Finish

Record B (Buy): name: Sharp AQUOS LC37D44U 37' LCD TV - LC37D44U | description: Sharp AQUOS LC-37D44U - 37' Widescreen LCD HDTV - 7500:1 Dynamic Contrast Ratio - 6ms Response Time | manufacturer: Sharp

7. Send the band to Argon

Each band pair goes to Argon and comes back as structured output, a match or no-match with a one-sentence reason. Peeters, Steiner and Bizer found that the best LLMs, given no or few examples, match pre-trained language models fine-tuned on thousands of labeled pairs. This snippet is the core of the Adjudicator class in er/adjudicate.py, calling the Gemini API directly with GEMINI_API_KEY.

import json
from google import genai
from google.genai import types
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Verdict(BaseModel):
    match: bool
    reason: str   # one sentence, logged for audit

PROMPT = """You are resolving product records from two catalogues.
Decide whether Record A and Record B describe the same product: same model, size, and variant.
Answer from the records only. Give a one-sentence reason.

Record A: {a}
Record B: {b}"""

client = genai.Client()   # reads GEMINI_API_KEY from the environment

def adjudicate(a_text: str, b_text: str) -> tuple[Verdict, int, int]:
    resp = client.models.generate_content(
        model="gemini-4-argon",
        contents=PROMPT.format(a=a_text, b=b_text),
        config=types.GenerateContentConfig(
            response_mime_type="application/json",
            response_schema=Verdict,
            temperature=0,
            thinking_config=types.ThinkingConfig(thinking_level="LOW"),
        ),
    )
    usage = resp.usage_metadata
    # thinking tokens are billed at the output rate, so count them with the visible answer
    out_tokens = (usage.candidates_token_count or 0) + (usage.thoughts_token_count or 0)
    return Verdict.model_validate_json(resp.text), usage.prompt_token_count or 0, out_tokens

Every verdict goes to a log with its reason, and the loop skips pairs already in the log, so a rerun never pays twice.

import os

text_of = {(src, rid): text for src, rid, text in records}

os.makedirs("results", exist_ok=True)
log_path = "results/argon_verdicts.jsonl"
done = set()
if os.path.exists(log_path):   # pairs already paid for on an earlier run
    with open(log_path) as f:
        done = {(r["abt"], r["buy"]) for r in map(json.loads, f)}

tokens_in = tokens_out = 0
with open(log_path, "a") as log:
    for abt_id, buy_id in band:
        if (abt_id, buy_id) in done:
            continue
        verdict, t_in, t_out = adjudicate(text_of["abt", abt_id], text_of["buy", buy_id])
        tokens_in += t_in
        tokens_out += t_out
        log.write(json.dumps({"abt": abt_id, "buy": buy_id, **verdict.model_dump()}) + "\n")
        log.flush()   # a crash mid-run keeps every verdict written so far

The runs in the article reached Argon through OpenRouter, which reports the exact charge per call. Thinking was set to LOW, because thinking tokens are billed and a match decision doesn't need deep reasoning. Set your key in the environment before you run the harness.

# macOS or Linux
export OPENROUTER_API_KEY="<YOUR_OPENROUTER_API_KEY>"

# Windows (PowerShell)
$env:OPENROUTER_API_KEY="<YOUR_OPENROUTER_API_KEY>"

The --budget-usdflag adds up the exact cost of every call across all runs and stops before the cap.

Argon got 960 of the 1,001 band pairs right, or 95.9%, including every hard pair the threshold had wrong. Forty of its 41 mistakes were true matches it declined.

  • In 19 cases, one record was too vague to confirm, such as a microwave listed with no model number or color.
  • In 7 cases, a variant, color, or bundle differed, such as a black camera against the silver one.
  • In 14 cases, the model numbers differed, and several look like labeling errors in the benchmark itself.

8. Run the full pipeline

Component Version
VectorAI DB actian/vectorai:1.0.2
Embedding model EmbeddingGemma (embeddinggemma) through Ollama
Adjudicator gemini-4-argon, run on 23 October 2026 through OpenRouter, thinking level LOW
Datasets Abt-Buy and Amazon-Google, downloaded 19 October 2026 
uv run resolve.py --dataset abt-buy --argon-backend openrouter --workers 2 --budget-usd 10

Swap in --dataset amazon-google for the second benchmark, or add --no-argon to run blocking and the threshold without any API calls. Here's the trimmed output from the Abt-Buy run.


abt-buy: 1081 abt + 1092 buy records, 1097 true matches

Blocking (all records, hnsw_ef=256):
  K=1   candidates=  1,081  reduction ratio=0.9991  pair completeness=0.8186  returned/record: mean 1.0, min 1, short 0
  K=3   candidates=  3,243  reduction ratio=0.9973  pair completeness=0.9453  returned/record: mean 3.0, min 3, short 0
  K=5   candidates=  5,405  reduction ratio=0.9954  pair completeness=0.9699  returned/record: mean 5.0, min 5, short 0
  K=10  candidates= 10,810  reduction ratio=0.9908  pair completeness=0.9900  returned/record: mean 10.0, min 10, short 0
  K=20  candidates= 21,620  reduction ratio=0.9817  pair completeness=0.9973  returned/record: mean 20.0, min 20, short 0

Test split: 7,570 candidates, 767 true matches
  Global cutoff, all candidates (reference, 0.7672): P=0.5734 R=0.4785 F1=0.5217
  Best-match threshold (baseline, 0.5618): P=0.8196 R=0.8057 F1=0.8126
  Band [0.5618, 0.8405) + near-ties (rank <= 3, gap <= 0.03): 1,001 pairs (13.2% of candidates), holding 206/279 of the baseline's errors; recall ceiling 0.8970
  With Argon: P=0.9985 R=0.8449 F1=0.9153  (960/1001 band verdicts correct, $1.4081)

The results, measured

Dataset Reduction ratio Pair completeness F1, threshold F1, with Argon Share sent to Argon Cost per 1,000 records
Abt-Buy 99.08% 99.0% 0.813 0.915 13.2% $0.76
Amazon-Google 99.69% 94.1% 0.597 0.691 14.0% $0.58

On Abt-Buy, Argon rejected 135 of the 136 false matches the threshold had accepted and picked up 59 true matches that were a record's second- or third-best candidate. Amazon-Google is harder, because its software titles vary in edition, version, and packaging. Argon was right on 76.4% of that band.

The 1,001 Abt-Buy calls cost $1.41, and the 1,338 Amazon-Google calls cost $2.42. Argon's list price doubles on 1 December 2026, according to Google's Gemini API pricing page. On a CPU-only laptop with 8 GB of RAM, embedding the Abt-Buy records took 771 seconds, blocking took 35 seconds, and the Argon calls took 54 minutes with 2 requests in parallel.

Why it runs on your own infrastructure

VectorAI DB and the embedding model run on your machines, so the embeddings, the blocking, and the resolved entities stay inside your network. Only the band leaves, two records at a time. For regulated data, you have two options.

  • De-identify the band by masking names, emails, and account numbers, and send only the fields that decide the match.
  • Keep the second pass local by swapping adjudicate() for a call to a model you host. A local model wasn't measured, so expect different numbers.

When the Argon pass is worth it

Run it when the band holds most of the threshold's errors and Argon decides band pairs at least 10 points more accurately than the threshold.

Dataset Threshold's errors in the band Threshold right on band pairs Argon right on band pairs F1 gain
Abt-Buy 206 of 279 (74%) 79.4% 95.9% +10.3
Amazon-Google 500 of 697 (72%) 62.6% 76.4% +9.4

Doubling the band's width on Abt-Buy sent 78 more pairs to Argon for $0.12 more, and F1 moved from 0.9153 to 0.9160. To check your own data, label about 200 band pairs by hand and compare how often the threshold and Argon get them right. That sample costs about 30 cents in Argon calls.

Wrapping up

The second pass got the Sharp TVs right. The threshold picked the LC37D44U because its vector scored higher, while Argon matched the LC37D64U by its model number and logged why. Blocking removed 99% of the comparison space, data-driven band edges kept the paid work to 13.2% of candidates, and Argon read the part numbers the embedding blurred.

What's next

  • Point the loader at your own customer, supplier, or product records and put your exclusion rules in the blocking filter's must clause.
