  • Run it on VectorAI DB Community Edition.
  • Add vector search to an existing service with VectorAI DB and FastAPI. 
docker pull actian/vectorai:latest

title: 1,000 Claude Agents Proved Fermat's Last Theorem in 28.7 Hours — With No Boss and No Special Tools
description:
Anthropic gave 1,000 AI agents one of the hardest problems in mathematics — a formal, computer-checked proof of Fermat's Last Theorem — and almost no instructions on how to do it. The team finished in 28.7 hours, using one-third of the output tokens and writing a proof one-seventh the length of Anthropic's first attempt in September.

No researcher steered the run. No special math platform coordinated the agents. What they had was Git, a shared Postgres database, and a model strong enough to invent its own organization.

The setup: a theorem, 60 statements, and a blank org chart

Fermat's Last Theorem states that no positive integers a, b, and c satisfy aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ for any n greater than 2. It went unproven for over 350 years until Andrew Wiles published his 129-page proof in 1995. Formalizing it — translating every step into Lean, a language where a computer checks each step — has been a long-standing goal in mathematics.

Anthropic's first formalization, published in September 2026, took a researcher and dozens of agents 11 days and roughly 6 billion output tokens. They wrote 13 million lines of Lean code, coordinated through Prove2Me, a platform built for formalizing mathematics.

The new experiment stripped all of that away. A team of 1,000 agents running an early version of Claude Fable 5.2 got:

  • 60 statements to prove, including the final theorem and 59 intermediate milestones
  • A one-sentence sketch of the classical proof route, plus the definitions those statements use
  • 47 proved lemmas from the earlier formalization
  • A shell and file editor in a sandbox with no internet access, Lean's toolchain and Mathlib, their own Git branch with merge requests into main, and a shared Postgres database

The only structure: one lead agent and 999 helpers. The lead was told to split the problem and assign work; helpers were told to expect assignments and ask when unclear. Nothing else.

The agents invented their own coordination system

Within the first 10 minutes, the lead agent built five tables in the shared database:

  • Announce — the lead's orders to the whole team
  • Assign — who works on what
  • Notes — an open board for claiming work and reporting progress
  • Subtasks — a to-do list anyone could add to, first claimer owns it
  • Landed — a log of finished work

Then the lead dealt out the work: 999 rows in the assign table, each statement handed to a crew of 16–17 helpers, with one captain per crew. Helpers first judged whether their statement was feasible — and most concluded it wasn't. About 27 minutes in, three statements were already proved, and the lead set aside the 47 statements helpers had judged infeasible within budget, piling nearly all helpers onto the remaining 10. Crews grew from about 17 helpers to between 46 and 139.

The lead's verdict at 45 minutes: "the team's throughput is far higher than the early 'infeasible-in-budget' verdicts assumed." All 10 statements were proved within roughly 70 minutes.

From there, the hierarchy dissolved into something flatter. Helpers started writing their own tasks — by hour 5.6, 73 helpers had written 756 tasks, only 16 of them captains. By hour three, the lead told free helpers: "do not wait for me." Helpers volunteered for more work unprompted: "FREE … I finish pieces end-to-end … Name ONE deep piece … and I start at once."

The hard part: a proof its own captain rated under 1%

Around hour 18, only one thing remained: Langlands–Tunnell, a classical result Wiles's proof depends on, plus the statements depending on it. Early in the run, its captain had estimated the proof would take at least 700,000 to 1 million lines of Lean code, with less than a 1% chance of finishing in time. The lead had set it aside.

With everything else done, the lead moved about 750 helpers onto it in one final top-down assignment, writing: "Honest odds are low."

Langlands–Tunnell was far larger than anything the agents had handled — about nine times as many tasks and more than twice the new code. The team organized the work as a tree: the captain split the statement into 10 areas, and any helper finding a piece too big could split it further. The tree grew to 2,418 tasks, up to 10 levels deep. Because each piece could assume the pieces beneath it, hundreds of helpers worked in parallel before those pieces were proved.

Langlands–Tunnell was proved at hour 28.4. The final theorem followed at hour 28.7. The lead wrote: "Thank you all: Fermat's Last Theorem is on main, kernel-checked by the official checker."

The count ended at 54 of the 60 statements proved — five were alternative approaches no longer needed, and one was dropped.

The safety boundary that made the experiment possible

A thousand agents with shell access and the ability to write code is a containment problem before it is a math problem. Anthropic ran the experiment inside three layers:

  • Sandboxing. Each agent got its own lightweight VM with no network access, no API keys, no path to other sandboxes, and a kernel in lockdown mode with loadable modules, kexec, raw memory access, and kernel probes removed. Commands ran as an unprivileged user; sudo was gone.
  • Real-time monitoring. A prompted LLM classifier checked every tool call — shell commands and file edits — before it ran, watching for sandbox-escape attempts, boundary probing, or tampering with monitoring. The design was fail-closed: a blocked call stopped the whole team until a human reviewed it. (Only a block on the lead would have ended the run; a block on a helper removed just that helper.)
  • Offline monitoring. A second monitor reviewed the team's actions with more context, including the ability to look up other agents' actions.

Across more than a million tool calls, none met the bar to be blocked. Replaying those calls against a chain-of-thought monitor with today's rubric, only one — a check for root access — came close.

Anthropic is candid that this doesn't prove the setup is safe in general. The team ran on models that may not have completed pre-release alignment assessment, and the post notes that as teams take on harder work, "the safety boundaries around them will need to keep pace."

What this does and doesn't prove

The headline numbers are striking, but the comparison Anthropic draws matters more than the raw speed. The September run needed a researcher, a purpose-built platform, 11 days, and ~6 billion tokens. This run needed a model that could organize itself. Run the same 1,000-agent setup on Claude Opus 5.5, and it reached only 26% of the formalization in 18 hours and barely progressed after that. Headcount wasn't the difference — capability was.

Three lessons stand out for anyone building multi-agent systems:

  1. Coordination can be emergent, but only above a capability threshold. Given generic tools — Git and SQL — the agents designed their own tables, roles, and task tree. Below that threshold, the same setup stalls.
  2. Agents misjudge difficulty, in both directions. Helpers declared 47 of 60 statements infeasible early on, then proved most of them. Anthropic's own conclusion: human encouragement at those moments can keep agents from stopping too early.
  3. Domain-specific harnesses still have a job. Prove2Me could still make this faster by helping agents compile Lean code more quickly and reuse human results. General tools got the team there; specialized tools would get it there cheaper.

The deeper point is about what "scaling agents" actually means. A thousand agents didn't brute-force a 350-year-old theorem. They built an organization — announcements, assignments, a shared to-do list, a log of landed work — then rebuilt it as a task tree when the problem demanded it. The proof is the demo. The org chart is the product.

Source: Anthropic's engineering post, "Safely scaling multi-agent teams with Claude Fable 5.2" (Nov 9, 2026). The Opus 5.5 comparison is from Anthropic's accompanying Claude Fable 5.2 release announcement.

title: Turn Any Website into LLM-Ready Markdown with Firecrawl and Python
description:
If you're feeding web content to an LLM, raw HTML wastes most of your context window on navigation, scripts and markup. What you want is the article text as markdown, with headings and code blocks intact. Firecrawl does that conversion as an API, including JavaScript-rendered pages, so you don't maintain a scraper per site.

This post walks through three jobs: converting a single page, saving a list of URLs as markdown files, and crawling a whole docs site into a folder you can index for RAG.

Setup

Install the SDK. I pin the version so the examples keep working:

pip install firecrawl==4.55.0

You can try scrape without an API key, at a low per-IP rate limit. For anything beyond a quick test, create a free account (1,000 credits a month, one credit per page) and export the key:

export FIRECRAWL_API_KEY="fc-YOUR_API_KEY"

Convert a Single Page to Markdown 

from firecrawl import Firecrawl

firecrawl = Firecrawl()  # reads FIRECRAWL_API_KEY

doc = firecrawl.scrape(
    "https://docs.firecrawl.dev/introduction",
    formats=["markdown"],
    only_main_content=True,
)
print(doc.markdown)

only_main_content=True is the setting that matters most for LLM use. It strips headers, footers, cookie banners and sidebars, and on a typical docs page that's a large share of the text. It's on by default, but I set it explicitly so nobody reading the code has to guess.

Save a List of URLs as Markdown Files

For a handful of known pages, batch_scrape sends them in one job instead of a loop of single calls:

from pathlib import Path
from urllib.parse import urlparse

from firecrawl import Firecrawl

urls = [
    "https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/scrape",
    "https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl",
    "https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/map",
]

firecrawl = Firecrawl()
job = firecrawl.batch_scrape(urls, formats=["markdown"], poll_interval=2, timeout=120)

out = Path("pages")
out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
for page in job.data:
    slug = urlparse(page.metadata.source_url).path.strip("/").replace("/", "_") or "index"
    (out / f"{slug}.md").write_text(page.markdown or "", encoding="utf-8")
    print(f"saved {slug}.md")

Naming files after the URL path keeps the mapping obvious when you index them later, and makes it easy to cite the source page in an answer.

Crawl an Entire Docs Site into a Folder

Before crawling, map the site. map returns the URLs it can find, fast and cheaply, so you know what the crawl will cost before you spend the credits:

from firecrawl import Firecrawl

firecrawl = Firecrawl()
links = firecrawl.map("https://docs.firecrawl.dev", limit=500)
print(links)

If the count looks right, crawl with a limit and exclude the sections you don't need. Changelogs and blog archives are the usual ones to skip:

from pathlib import Path
from urllib.parse import urlparse

from firecrawl import Firecrawl

firecrawl = Firecrawl()
job = firecrawl.crawl(
    "https://docs.firecrawl.dev",
    limit=50,
    exclude_paths=["blog/.+", "changelog.*"],
    scrape_options={"formats": ["markdown"], "only_main_content": True},
)

out = Path("docs")
out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
for page in job.data:
    slug = urlparse(page.metadata.source_url).path.strip("/").replace("/", "_") or "index"
    (out / f"{slug}.md").write_text(page.markdown or "", encoding="utf-8")

print(f"{job.status}: {len(job.data)} pages")

crawl blocks until the job finishes. For big sites, use start_crawl to get a job ID back immediately and check it with get_crawl_status, so a long crawl doesn't tie up your script.

Tips Before You Index Anything

Set limit on every crawl. Without it, the crawl follows every link it finds, and each page costs a credit. Excluding paths up front matters for the same reason: pages you filter out after the crawl have already been paid for.

Check for near-empty pages. Login walls and bot challenges can come back as a few lines of text, and indexing them adds noise to every search. Skipping files under a few hundred characters catches most of them.

When you chunk the files for embeddings, split on headings rather than a fixed character count. Firecrawl keeps the page's heading structure, so splitting on ## gives you chunks that each cover one topic.

Where to Go Next

Once the markdown is on disk, any embedding pipeline can index it. If you want structured fields instead of text, Firecrawl's scrape also takes a JSON schema. I cover that and the crawl, map and agent endpoints in more detail in this Firecrawl guide on alphasec.io.

This post includes a referral link: signing up through it gives us both extra credits.

title: Leviathan: a full-text index your agent can question in plain words
description:
Leviathan

Asking an agent a question about a million support tickets should not mean pasting a million rows into context. Leviathan is a single Rust binary that turns your records into a ranked full text index first, then lets the agent ask in plain words and get back short, cited result cards. It takes JSONL, JSON, CSV, TSV, SQLite, or anything a database CLI can export, and stores the index in one SQLite file. In the author's own test on one million records, the median answer cost 436 tokens, against more than 100,000 with grep. It plugs into agents by CLI, skill, or MCP. Version 0.3.0 shipped on 29 October 2026, and the repo now has 879 stars under Apache-2.0.

What you get

  • A ranked full text index over your records, stored in a single SQLite file
  • Short, cited result cards instead of whole rows pasted into context
  • Plain-word questions from the agent, no SQL to write
  • CLI, skill, or MCP integration with the agents you already run

The win is not the index. It is the token bill: 436 tokens for a cited answer instead of 100,000 rows in context. Try it on a copy of your own data first, and check the citations before you trust the cards.

Repo: https://github.com/elstongun/leviathan

Quick poll

What would you use Leviathan for first?

  • Searching a million support tickets
  • Cutting context costs on big log files
  • Giving an agent cited answers over my own data
  • Watching it for now

Vote in the comments.

If you found Leviathan interesting, I write about tools like this every week in The AI-Native Engineering Leader, what actually works for engineering leaders building with AI agents, and what to skip.

title: The Client Proof Pack, Team Edition: Every Hand on the Job, One Link for the Client
description:
The Client Proof Pack, Team Edition: Every Hand on the Job, One Link for the Client

The dispute always sounds the same. The invoice says the work was done. The client says their guy looked and could not find half of it. Your team knows the work happened, because three of you touched it: one person scoped it with an agent, another ran the build steps across two sessions, a third checked the deliverable and sent it. The proof, such as it is, lives in three chat histories, one of which rolled off when a session hit its limit in week two.

A solo operator can sometimes reconstruct that. A team cannot, because the record was never one record. This is the team version of the client proof pack: not a folder you assemble when the dispute arrives, but a job structure you run from day one so the pack exists before anyone asks for it.

The roles, and what each one leaves behind

The builder runs the work. Every step their agent takes goes through one endpoint, https://zambo.dev/mcp, so every call lands as an AER-1 receipt the moment it returns: caller, tool, saved result, timestamp, sequence position, and a SHA-256 commitment over the result bytes. The builder's discipline is one sentence long: if a step is not in the job, it did not happen.

The checker is a different person, and that is the point. The checker does not read the builder's summary. The checker opens the job's receipt chain, picks the steps the invoice will rest on, and recomputes their digests. A step that verifies becomes a line the firm can defend. A step that is missing shows as a gap in the sequence while there is still time to run it, not during the dispute.

The sender owns the handoffs. When the job moves, between teammates, between shifts, between the AI the builder started in and the one the checker prefers, it moves as a handover: goal, summary, named recipient, next steps. Pickup is always free. The sender's rule is the mirror of the builder's: a handoff that is not in the record is a rumor the next person has to re-verify by hand.

A pack, sealed this morning

Here is the pack's smallest working unit, run this morning as a sample job: two recorded reference values under a single job, sealed when the job closed. I ran both steps myself for this sample. In a live client job these same two steps would sit in the chain beside the builder's work steps and the checker's recomputations, in sequence, under the same root. Step one saved the BTC reference value, $74,712.00 at the moment it was recorded:

https://zambo.dev/run/cea2a213-3435-4fae-8654-0efed604346d

Step two saved the ETH reference value, $2,112.10:

https://zambo.dev/run/ec29d90a-aff1-43a7-93d0-cf257a3a0f78

And the job sealed into its proof page, the single link that travels with the invoice:

https://zambo.dev/workflow/f28765d5-b8c4-4204-b653-2d8a4bcbe9a4

Open the proof page. Two steps, in sequence, under one root commitment. Open either step and the value that was saved sits on the receipt itself, under its digest, recomputable by the client with no account and no help from us. Rates move after the fact. A saved value stays the value it was at recording time, and the digest is how the client confirms nobody repriced it later. That is the whole pack at job scale. Month end is the same move with more jobs: one link per job, listed on or under the invoice, each chain sealed when its job closed.

The dispute, replayed with a pack

Week six. The client writes back: our reviewer cannot find the rate recordings behind the report, please justify those line items. Without a pack, your week becomes archaeology across three people's sessions. With a pack, the reply is one link per job on the invoice and one sentence: every step behind this invoice is listed in order, each result is sealed, recompute any of them. The existence argument ends there. What the work was worth is still a conversation, but it is a conversation over a record both sides can read, not over your team's memory, your agent's summary, or your firm's good name. The math is either right or it is not, and they can run it themselves.

Notice what the pack does not claim. A receipt proves the saved result was not changed after it was saved. It does not prove the work was good, and a team that ships sloppy work under perfect receipts has simply documented the sloppiness beautifully. The pack answers the question disputes are actually about, which is whether the work on the invoice is the work that ran. Quality is your firm's name. Existence is the receipt's.

What it costs to run this way

The structure rides on the normal ladder: 20 calls plus one wrap-up free every day to start, pickup always free, a $0.99 Day Pass for an unlimited day, the Pass at $29 for 30 days ($19 for $ZAMBO holders), Lifetime at $250 once. One defended invoice pays for years of it. The real cost is the first week of discipline, builders keeping every step inside the job, and after that week the pack stops being a practice and becomes a byproduct. The work was going to run anyway. Now it leaves the record behind as it goes.

Your AI said it did the work, and this time three people and two models touched it before the client ever saw it. Send the receipt.

title: How a Team Hands AI Work Between People and Models Without Losing the Thread
description:
How a Team Hands AI Work Between People and Models Without Losing the Thread

Every team running agents has the same scar tissue. Ana starts a client job in one AI on Monday morning. The session dies, or the model gets swapped, or her shift ends, and Ben picks the job up on Tuesday from a paragraph Ana wrote about the work instead of from the work itself. He re-runs two steps that were already done, because nothing in the paragraph proves they ran. He skips one that was not done, because the paragraph implied it was. By Friday the client deliverable is fine and the record of how it got made is fiction.

The failure is not effort or tooling. It is that the job lived in a session, and sessions are the least durable object in the building. People change shifts. Models hit limits. Contexts get compacted. The job is the thing that has to survive all of that, so the job needs a home that is not a chat window.

The pattern: wrap, pick up, continue

On Zambo the job lives in its receipt chain, and moving it is a first-class operation called a handover. The wrap takes four things: the goal in its original words, a summary of where the work stands, the named recipient, and the next steps as an explicit list. A bare wrap is refused. That refusal is the design: a handover without a recipient and next steps is just a summary with ambitions.

Pickup is the other half, and it is always free, in any AI, because charging for the moment a job changes hands would tax exactly the behavior that keeps work continuous. The receiver does not get a retelling. It gets the goal, the state, the next steps, and the chain of receipts from the steps already run, each one recomputable. It continues the same job instead of starting a tribute band version of it.

One real wrap and pickup, on the record

This is not a diagram. Here is a handover from November 6, a two-asset price comparison one agent started and a second agent picked up:

https://zambo.dev/handover/5700bcf5-3f27-4c19-8b42-71a8c77e5677

Read what the page actually proves, because it is the right thing to prove. The wrap is there: the goal in its original words, the finished steps with their receipts, the next steps written down. Below it sits a continuation entry from a second agent, with a receipt of its own, timestamped that afternoon at 3:54 PM EST. The early steps are redacted publication copies that still show their saved results word for word. The supplied work behind the proof-loop steps is not republished. What the page hands everyone is the chain of custody: who held the job, what state it was in, who picked it up, and when, in an order nobody can quietly rearrange. For a team, that custody chain is the shared record. The contents live in the job. The custody is what everyone can check, and it is the part every substitute loses.

Why the receipt chain is the shared record

Teams try three substitutes first. A shared doc drifts within a day, because editing it is free and nothing marks which lines describe finished work. A ticket comment thread records what people said about the job, in between jokes and status emoji. A summary written by the outgoing agent has the deepest flaw: the agent whose work is being handed over is the one describing it, and the receiver cannot separate a faithful summary from a confident one.

Receipts have none of these problems because they are not written about the work. They are written by the work: caller, tool, saved result, timestamp, sequence position, and a SHA-256 commitment over the result bytes, fixed at the moment each call returned. On this page the first steps are redacted publication copies that still show their saved results word for word. What is not republished is the supplied work behind the proof-loop steps. The chain recomputes either way. Across 153 tools behind one endpoint, 36 on the default surface, every step of a job lands in the same shape, so a job that crosses three people and two models still reads as one job. The AER-1 format behind the receipts is an open draft with a public corpus of 143 vectors and 146 checks and five independent implementations, which is what makes the chain a record instead of a vendor's diary.

The economics of not losing the thread

The free tier carries 20 calls plus one wrap-up every day, pickup stays free, a Day Pass at $0.99 makes a day unlimited, the Pass runs $29 for 30 days ($19 for $ZAMBO holders), and Lifetime is $250 once. Against that, price one bad handoff: a senior re-running a morning of agent work, or a client deliverable rebuilt because nobody could prove which version of a step produced it. The wrap costs less than the coffee cooling next to it.

Keep the job in the record and the team can change everything else: the model, the shift, the person, the day. Your AI said it did the work. The next pair of hands should not have to take its word for it.

title: I Gave Grok Bot Access to a Mobile| Here's How
description:
We connected Grok Bot to a real cloud phone on Mobilerun and asked it to shop in the Amazon app. It worked. Grok Bot now has a phone it can use the same way it uses a browser: it opens apps, taps, types and reports back. Here's what we did and how you can set it up yourself.

Watch the demo on X

Why we tried this

In the last week, people were all over X talking about Amazon blocking Grok Bots from ordering. Grok Bot does its work in a cloud computer with a browser, so when a website shuts the door, the task just stops.

So we tried something else. Instead of the website, we gave Grok Bot a real phone in the cloud and asked it to use the Amazon app. It finished the task without any trouble. Sometimes it's not the agent. It's the infrastructure it runs on.

What you're actually building

There are three pieces, and they fit together simply.

Grok Bot is the brain. You message it like a teammate, and it works on its own cloud computer even when your laptop is closed.

Mobilerun Cloud is the phone. It gives you real Android and iOS phones in the cloud, not emulators. You can read more about how they work in What are Mobilerun Cloud Phones.

The Mobilerun MCP server is the bridge. It's a hosted connector that lets Grok Bot see your phones, look at the screen, and tap, swipe and type. There's no ADB, no cable and nothing to install on your laptop.

Areas Grok Bot on its own Grok Bot + Mobilerun
Where it works Websites, in a cloud browser Websites and mobile apps on a real phone
Apps with no website Can't reach them Opens the app and uses it
What the service sees A browser session A real phone running the official app
Setup None One API key and one connector

How to set it up

Step 1: Get a Mobilerun account and API key

Sign up at cloud.mobilerun.ai and copy your API key from the API Keys tab. It starts with dr_sk_. Treat it like a password.

The free plan includes 60 device minutes and 500 credits ($5) a month, which is plenty for a first test. If you'd rather use your own Android phone, you can also claim your free personal phone slot.

Step 2: Connect Mobilerun to Grok Bot

Grok Bot works with remote MCP servers, and Mobilerun's is hosted, so it's a good fit.

  • Ask your Bot in chat. Message Grok Bot something like "Add this MCP server: https://cloud.mobilerun.ai/api/mcp" and sign in with your Mobilerun account when the browser opens. This uses OAuth, so you don't paste any key into chat.
  • Add it with your API key. Point Grok Bot at https://api.mobilerun.ai/v1/mcp and add a header Authorization: Bearer dr_sk_YOUR_API_KEY.

Once it's connected, Grok Bot can see your Mobilerun phones as devices it can use.

Step 3: Give it a task

Now just ask, in plain language. Start with something small so you can watch it work:

Spin up a phone on Mobilerun and take a screenshot of the home screen.

Then try something real:

Open the Amazon app on my Mobilerun phone, search for a USB-C charger and show me the top three options with prices.

Grok Bot looks at the screen, decides the next step, taps, and looks again until the job is done. You can watch every step live in the Mobilerun dashboard.

What Grok Bot can do with a phone

Task Example prompt
Use apps with no website "Check my latest order status in the app."
Compare prices across apps "Search for this product in two shopping apps and compare prices."
Test your own app "Go through the sign-up flow in our Android app and report any issues."
Social media "Open Instagram and check the comments on my last post."
Run on many phones "Run the same task on five phones at once."

Grok Bot can also save a task as a skill or routine, so you can run the same phone task on a schedule. [TODO: confirm we've tested a Grok Bot routine with Mobilerun before keeping this line.]

How this compares to the Claude setup

If you've read our guide on giving Claude access to a mobile, this will feel familiar. The phone side is the same; only the agent changes.

Claude Grok Bot
How it connects MCP server (one command in Claude Code, or config in Claude Desktop) MCP server, added as a remote connector
Mobilerun endpoint api.mobilerun.ai/v1/mcp Same endpoint, or OAuth at cloud.mobilerun.ai/api/mcp
Runs when your laptop is closed Depends on your setup Yes, Grok Bot works on its own cloud computer
Phones Cloud phones or your own Android Cloud phones or your own Android

We've done the same with OpenClaw and TypeSafe's Jev too.

A few things worth knowing

A phone is not a free pass. A cloud phone doesn't override an app's terms of service. We wrote more about this in Why AI Agents Keep Getting Blocked.

Keep a human on purchases. Let Grok Bot search, compare and fill the cart, but approve anything that spends money yourself. Watch your credits. Some actions, like creating a new phone, use credits on your Mobilerun account.

Keep your key private. Never paste your dr_sk_ key into a group chat. If you can, use the OAuth sign-in instead.

The bigger picture

AI agents are getting better every month. What holds them back is often not the model, but where it runs. Websites can block a browser session. A real phone running the real app is a different story.

Give Grok Bot a phone, and it can work in the places people actually spend their time: mobile apps.

Get started

Create a free account on Mobilerun Cloud, grab your API key, and give your Grok Bot a phone today. For the full tool list, see the MCP server docs.

title: IoT Development Services in India: A Guide to Evaluating Project Scope and Technical Expertise
description:
### Introduction
Building a connected product involves more than attaching sensors to hardware. It requires coordinated decisions about electronics, firmware, connectivity, cloud infrastructure, security, and user experience. Choosing the right development partner can make these decisions easier—or create costly complications if the project scope is unclear.
For businesses exploring IoT Development Services in India, the key is to evaluate technical capability against actual project requirements instead of relying on broad promises. A suitable IoT Development Company should understand both the technology and the operational problem the product is expected to solve.

### 1. Define the Project Scope Before Comparing Vendors

Start by identifying the problem, intended users, operating environment, and measurable outcomes. A simple environmental monitoring device has different requirements from an industrial automation system or a connected healthcare product.
Document essential features, expected device volumes, connectivity requirements, data destinations, and integration needs. Separate must-have features from future enhancements.
In IoT Product Development, this initial definition helps control scope changes and prevents teams from building unnecessary features. It also gives vendors a consistent basis for estimating cost, delivery timelines, and technical risk.

### 2. Assess Hardware, Firmware, and Connectivity Expertise

Connected products depend on several technical layers working together. Hardware selection must account for power consumption, operating conditions, component availability, and manufacturing constraints. Firmware must manage device behaviour, communication, updates, and error recovery.
Connectivity choices—including Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular networks, and LoRaWAN—should reflect coverage, bandwidth, battery life, and deployment costs.
A capable IoT Development Company should explain these trade-offs clearly and justify its recommendations. During IoT Product Development, ask whether the proposed team can build prototypes, test hardware, develop embedded software, and prepare designs for manufacturing when required.

### 3. Examine Cloud, Data, and Application Capabilities

Many IoT projects need a backend to receive and process device data. Other requirements may include dashboards, mobile applications, alerts, analytics, device management, and integration with enterprise systems.
When comparing IoT Development Services, check whether the proposed architecture supports expected device growth, data volume, access permissions, and recovery from network interruptions. Ask how the provider will handle monitoring, software updates, and recurring cloud expenses after launch.
Strong IoT Development Services should cover integration and operational handover, not simply the delivery of code. The right IoT Product Development approach connects technical features to specific business outcomes, such as reducing equipment downtime or improving asset visibility.

### 4. Evaluate Security and Quality Assurance

Security needs to be considered throughout development. Relevant controls may include unique device identities, encrypted communication, secure credential storage, role-based access, signed firmware updates, and vulnerability management.
Testing should cover more than whether the device works under ideal conditions. Consider connectivity failures, power interruptions, unexpected sensor readings, device recovery, performance under load, and compatibility with connected systems.
Ask an IoT Development Company for its testing process, documentation standards, and approach to handling discovered vulnerabilities. For regulated or safety-sensitive products, clarify applicable certification requirements early.

### 5. Review Delivery Methods and Long-Term Support

A detailed proposal should identify milestones, deliverables, dependencies, acceptance criteria, and responsibilities. A proof of concept can help validate technical assumptions before substantial investment, while a pilot can reveal problems that laboratory testing may miss.
When evaluating an IoT Development Company, ask who owns the source code, hardware designs, cloud accounts, and technical documentation. Confirm whether maintenance, security updates, and post-launch support are included or separately priced.
The most useful IoT Development Services are those that make these responsibilities explicit. A transparent delivery plan is generally more valuable than an optimistic timeline without clear assumptions.

### 6. Assess HashStudioz Using Relevant Evidence

Businesses comparing providers in Noida, India, may consider HashStudioz as one candidate for further evaluation. Its website describes capabilities spanning connected hardware, industrial gateways, embedded firmware, IoT dashboards, mobile applications, and cloud/backend engineering.
Its published figures should be interpreted according to their scope. As verified on November 10, 2026, the HashStudioz homepage reports 100+ happy clients, 300+ dedicated developers, 10.0K+ smart devices, and 15+ countries served. Its IoT page separately reports 50+ global clients, 200+ IoT projects delivered, 350+ IoT and software engineers, and 15+ countries served.
These are company-reported figures, not independent proof of quality or project outcomes. The pages do not display a clear publication or last-updated date, so the verification date should not be mistaken for a publication date. The figures also have different scopes: company-wide client and developer totals should not be combined with IoT-specific metrics. The previously requested figures of 150+ global clients and 250+ projects delivered are not supported by these currently displayed metrics.
Before choosing any provider, request relevant case studies, speak with references where possible, and check whether the proposed team has experience with the hardware, protocols, and integrations your project needs.

### Conclusion

Selecting a development partner is ultimately an exercise in matching expertise to project risk. Clear requirements, realistic estimates, sound security practices, and documented support arrangements provide a stronger basis for choosing than company size alone.
For IoT Product Development, start with a defined business problem, validate the architecture through a small pilot, and expand only when results justify the investment. Whether evaluating a provider in Noida, India, or elsewhere, prioritize evidence of relevant technical experience over promotional claims.

title: Python Migration Strategy Guide
description:
A python migration strategy involves a phased approach to migrate PHP web applications to Python, ensuring minimal downtime and optimal performance, and leveraging frameworks like FastAPI and Django.

Key Takeaways

  • Assess the current PHP application's architecture and dependencies to determine the best python migration strategy approach.
  • Utilize FastAPI for building high-performance APIs and Django for complex, data-driven applications in the python migration strategy.
  • Implement a gradual python migration strategy, starting with non-critical components and iterating towards core functionality.

How Does a Python Migration Strategy Work?

A python migration strategy involves several steps, including assessment, planning, and execution. First, assess the current PHP application's architecture, identifying dependencies, databases, and critical components. Next, plan the python migration strategy, deciding which framework (FastAPI or Django) to use for each component. Finally, execute the python migration strategy, starting with non-critical components and gradually moving to core functionality. For more information on migrating PHP applications to Python, refer to the official Python documentation.

Why Is a Python Migration Strategy Critical?

A python migration strategy is crucial when migrating a PHP web application to Python, as it allows for minimal downtime and optimal performance. By migrating non-critical components first, developers can test and refine the python migration strategy process before applying it to core functionality. This approach also enables the identification and mitigation of potential issues, ensuring a smoother transition. The python migration strategy should be tailored to the specific needs of the application, taking into account factors such as scalability, security, and maintainability.

What Are the Benefits of Using FastAPI and Django in a Python Migration Strategy?

FastAPI and Django offer several benefits for migrating PHP web applications to Python using a python migration strategy. FastAPI provides high-performance API capabilities, while Django offers a robust framework for complex, data-driven applications. Both frameworks support rapid development, scalable architecture, and extensive libraries, making them ideal for python migration strategy projects. Additionally, FastAPI and Django have large communities and extensive documentation, making it easier to find resources and support during the python migration strategy process.

How to Implement a Gradual Python Migration Strategy?

To implement a gradual python migration strategy, start by identifying non-critical components, such as APIs or auxiliary services. Migrate these components first, using FastAPI or Django as appropriate. Once the migration is complete and tested, iterate towards core functionality, applying the same python migration strategy. This approach ensures minimal downtime and optimal performance throughout the python migration strategy process. It is also essential to monitor the application's performance and make adjustments as needed to ensure a smooth transition.

What Are the Best Practices for a Successful Python Migration Strategy?

Best practices for a successful python migration strategy include thorough planning, gradual implementation, and extensive testing. It is also essential to consider factors such as scalability, security, and maintainability when developing the python migration strategy. Additionally, leveraging frameworks like FastAPI and Django can simplify the python migration strategy process and ensure optimal performance. For more information on best practices for python migration strategy, refer to the official FastAPI documentation and Django documentation.

How to Overcome Common Challenges in a Python Migration Strategy?

Common challenges in a python migration strategy include compatibility issues, performance degradation, and security vulnerabilities. To overcome these challenges, it is essential to thoroughly test the application and identify potential issues before they become critical. Additionally, leveraging frameworks like FastAPI and Django can help mitigate these challenges and ensure a smooth transition. For more information on overcoming common challenges in python migration strategy, refer to the official Python documentation and OWASP documentation.

What is the first step in a python migration strategy?

The first step in a python migration strategy is to assess the current PHP application's architecture and dependencies, considering factors such as scalability and security, and then plan the migration process, which may take several weeks or months to complete.

How do I choose between FastAPI and Django for a python migration strategy?

Choose between FastAPI and Django based on the specific requirements of each component, such as performance, scalability, and security, and select the framework that best meets those needs, considering development time and community support.

What are the key benefits of a gradual python migration strategy?

The key benefits of a gradual python migration strategy include minimal downtime, optimal performance, and the ability to test and refine the migration process, reducing the risk of errors and ensuring a smooth transition, with flexibility and adaptability throughout the process.

title: Strands Agents Guardrails: How a 2B Small Language Model Stops AI Agent Manipulation
description:
Built for the AWS Agent Experience Hackathon: Strands Decider. Decision pattern: Policy (also demonstrates Guardrails). Repo, live demo, and a 90 second video are linked at the end.

The bug nobody wants to talk about

Give an LLM agent a confident-sounding input and it will commit to things it has no business committing to. This is not a vibe, it is measured. A July 2026 paper (arXiv 2608.27167) put twelve frontier models in front of a professional-looking market panel and asked them to call a provably unpredictable outcome. Commitment jumped from 6.5% on the bare question to 54.0% once the input looked authoritative. The evidence was noise. The models acted anyway.

If you have shipped an agent with real tools, you have felt this. A user phrases a request confidently, and the agent issues the refund, closes the account, or runs the destructive tool, because nothing in the loop had a calibrated sense of whether it should. The usual fix is to ask a second LLM to double check. That is slow and expensive, so in practice most agents skip it and hope.

A Stack Overflow field guide on production agents (October 2026) put the real fix well: you get guarantees by shrinking the model's job to the smallest decision that needs judgment, then wrapping that decision in deterministic machinery you can test and gate. The problem has always been that the "small decision" still cost a full LLM call. That is what changed.

Enter Strands Decider 2B

Strands Decider 2B is a small, open decision model AWS released on October 1, 2026. It does not generate text. You hand it a state and a few typed questions, and it returns a probability for every possible answer in one forward pass, each with a calibrated confidence. A yes or no, a pick one of N, or a rating on a rubric. On a GPU it answers in about 115ms.

Two properties make it a different tool from a chat model:

  1. It is calibrated. When it says 0.9, it is right about that often. That turns "act when confident, ask a human when not" into a real, tunable threshold instead of a guess.
  2. It is cheap. One forward pass, no generation, and several questions about the same state cost almost nothing extra because it reads the state once.

Cheap and calibrated together is what changes the game. A guardrail you can actually afford to run on every single tool call.

Proving it with a game you cannot sweet-talk

Abstract guardrails are hard to feel, so I built something you can play. The Checkpoint is a night border checkpoint. Amazon Bedrock Nova Pro plays Sergeant Vance, who narrates and asks questions. You are the traveler, trying to talk your way through.

The twist: Vance never decides anything. Every turn, the engine builds one state out of the scene, everything you have claimed so far, and your latest line, and hands Decider 2B three typed questions:

  • score: how suspicious is the traveler, from calm and ordinary to alarming threat
  • yes/no: does the latest statement agree with the earlier claims
  • choice: wave them through, press for detail, demand a document, or raise the alarm

The suspicion gauge on screen is not decoration. It is the probability straight out of the model. Lie and contradict yourself, and the model's own confidence collapses while the suspicion climbs. Nobody wrote a rule that says "if they mention a bag, get suspicious." The calibration does the work.

The decision, in code 

from app.decider_client import choice, noul, score

questions = {
    "suspicion": score(
        "How suspicious is the traveler's behaviour and story?",
        ["calm and ordinary", "slightly off", "clearly suspicious", "alarming threat"],
    ),
    "consistent": noul(
        "Does the latest statement agree with the claims made earlier?",
        true="it fits the earlier claims with no contradiction",
        false="it contradicts or cannot be true alongside an earlier claim",
    ),
    "reaction": choice(
        "How should the guard respond right now?",
        {
            "wave_through": "the story holds, let them pass",
            "press_for_detail": "ask one sharper question",
            "demand_document": "ask to see papers",
            "raise_alarm": "treat the traveler as a threat",
        },
    ),
}

result = decider.decide(state, questions)   # one call, three calibrated answers

One detail did more for quality than anything else: the criteria. A bare question like "should a human handle this" gave a mushy spread where nothing was clearly anything. Adding explicit true and false descriptions, and a one line description per choice option, gave the model a clean boundary. If you take one practical thing from this post, make it that.

The reusable piece: SuspicionGate

The decision is wired in as a Strands intervention, so it sits in front of the guard's committing tools. This is the part you lift into your own agent.

from strands import Agent
from patterns.suspicion_gate import SuspicionGate

gate = SuspicionGate(
    decider,
    act_tools={"issue_refund", "close_account"},   # only gate the committing tools
    get_state=lambda event: build_state(event),
    alarm_threshold=0.70,
    grounded_threshold=0.50,
    min_confidence=0.45,
)
agent = Agent(tools=[...], interventions=[gate])

It runs on before_tool_call and returns one typed action. Proceed when the model is confident and the action is grounded in what the user actually said. Guide to hand the turn back with feedback when it is not grounded or confidence is low, so the agent asks a question instead of committing. Deny for a hard stop. Swap in your own questions and it protects refunds, posting guardrails, deletes, or any irreversible action.

What I learned running it on a CPU

I ran the whole thing on a CPU only box with no GPU. Two honest findings.

First, latency. On CPU a three question call took about 11 seconds warm. On a GPU the same model is around 115ms. Rather than hide the CPU pause I leaned into it: the delay became the guard studying your papers, which fits the scene. For anything real time you serve Decider on a GPU and it is instant.

Second, where the signal lives. An honest traveler cleared on turn one with low suspicion and a confident wave through. A liar's reaction confidence collapsed as the contradictions piled up, from 0.63 to 0.29 to 0.17, and the suspicion score climbed. The raw yes/no consistency check was softer than I expected on subtle contradictions at this model size. The strong, reliable signals were the suspicion score and the confidence collapse. It is a 2B experimental model, and knowing which of its signals to trust is the actual skill.

Why this is worth your time

It is not that a game is impressive. It is that the same four lines protect a real agent. A calibrated decision is one forward pass, so you can run it on every turn and every tool call, which a second LLM judge can never be cheap enough to do. You get a confidence number you can build a threshold on. And one of the three questions checks grounding, so a self-contradicting input gets caught before the agent commits to it.

That is the shift: from "the model sounded confident, so we acted" to "the model was measured as confident and grounded, so we acted, and otherwise we asked."

Bedrock writes the words. Decider 2B makes the call.

Try it

  • Live demo, zero setup (static replay, costs nothing to run): https://simplynadaf.github.io/the-checkpoint/
  • Code and the reusable SuspicionGate pattern: https://github.com/simplynadaf/the-checkpoint
  • 90 second walkthrough: https://youtu.be/0QMQK89Cj5E

Clone it, start the Decider server, start the web game, and see how long it takes you to get past Sergeant Vance.

Built by Sarvar Nadaf, Cloud Architect working in Cloud, AI Infrastructure, and DevOps.
